summary: Combined findings of 17 scanners (architecture-scan, cicd-scan, configuration-scan, domain-language-scan, evolution-scan, functionality-scan, iac-scan, maintainability-scan, network-scan, observability-scan, performance-scan, reliability-scan, risk-synthesis-scan, security-scan, storage-scan, tech-stack-scan, testing-scan): 369 findings — 2 high, 23 medium, 65 low, 279 info. Generated by merge_findings.py; see each scanner's own file for its narrative summary.

findings.title: Layered crate hub around a session-loop engine, with execution pushed across a process boundary
findings.description: The `codex-rs` Cargo workspace declares 133 member crates and the manifest graph reads as **four layers**. At the bottom sits `codex-protocol` (68 in-workspace dependents) plus small `utils/*` crates. Above it are service crates: `config`, `sandboxing`, `network-proxy`, `execpolicy`, `exec-server`, `rollout`/`state`, model clients. `codex-core` is the engine hub: it depends on 61 workspace crates and is depended on by 23, and it runs every conversation as an **async actor**: a bounded submission channel in, an unbounded event channel out. The top layer is frontends and API: `app-server` exposes the engine over JSON-RPC on stdio, Unix socket or WebSocket, and `tui` consumes it through `app-server-client` rather than linking `core`. Anything the model executes is transformed by `codex-sandboxing` into an OS-sandboxed child process, or shipped to a remote `exec-server`, so the **execution boundary is a process boundary** by construction. The structure optimises for many entry points sharing one engine and for moving execution off the host, at the price of a very large `core`.

findings.title: codex-core: the conversation engine that owns sessions, turns, tool dispatch and policy decisions
findings.description: `codex-core` is responsible for running a thread: it holds the `Session` and `CodexThread` types, the `submission_loop` that consumes user submissions, the tool-call pipeline including `exec` and `apply_patch`, and the in-engine glue for config, exec policy, hooks, MCP and guardian review. It re-exports network-policy types from `codex-network-proxy` and turn-input types from `codex-protocol`, which is why frontends rarely need the lower crates. It depends on **61 workspace crates** and 23 depend on it, including `app-server`, `exec`, `cli`, `mcp-server` and every `ext/*` extension except `ext/skills` and `ext/extension-api`. Replacing it means replacing the product; it is the one component with no substitute.

findings.title: Execution cluster: sandboxing, platform sandboxes, exec-server, arg0 dispatch and process hardening
findings.description: Nine crates together own **how a model-requested command becomes a confined child process**. `codex-sandboxing` is the platform-neutral manager: it picks a `SandboxType` and rewrites an argv into a Seatbelt, Linux or Windows wrapper invocation. `linux-sandbox` (bubblewrap launcher, seccomp, Landlock), `windows-sandbox-rs` (restricted token) and `bwrap` (a bundled bubblewrap build) are the platform backends. `execpolicy` is a rule engine deciding allow/prompt/forbid per command prefix, used by `core` and `config`. `exec-server` plus `exec-server-protocol` turn process spawning into a JSON-RPC service that can run locally or on a remote environment. `arg0` multiplexes the single `codex` binary into these helpers by executable name or first argument, and `process-hardening` runs pre-main to disable core dumps and ptrace. `network-proxy` belongs here functionally but sits below `protocol` in the graph (see the violations group).

findings.title: Frontends and the app-server API layer
findings.description: `app-server` is the **product API**: it hosts `codex-core`, wires in every `ext/*` extension, and speaks `app-server-protocol` JSON-RPC over the transports in `app-server-transport` (stdio, Unix socket, WebSocket, and a remote-control mode with its own kill switch). `app-server-client` is the in-tree consumer library. `tui` is a client of that API and does not link `core`; `exec` (headless) links both the client and `core`; `cli` is the binary shell that mounts every subcommand, including `mcp-server`, `exec-server`, `responses-api-proxy` and `cloud-tasks`. The 54-dependency `app-server` and 44-dependency `cli` are hubs by role, not by accident: they are the composition roots.

findings.title: Two extension clusters: in-tree ext/* contributors and external MCP, plugin, skill and hook surfaces
findings.description: Two different things are called extensions. The **in-tree** `ext/*` crates (agent, goal, guardian-v2, image-generation, mcp, memories, queue, skills, web-search, git-attribution, connectors) implement contributor traits from `ext/extension-api` and are registered by `app-server`; ten of them still depend on `core` directly, so they are engine plugins compiled into the binary, not a stable public extension point. The **external** surfaces are the crates for third-party code: `rmcp-client` launches MCP servers as stdio child processes or connects over HTTP, `mcp-server` exposes Codex itself as an MCP server (its own header still calls it a prototype), `codex-mcp` holds the MCP bindings and capability negotiation, `plugin` and `utils/plugins` model marketplace plugin packages, `skills` loads skill folders, and `hooks` runs user-configured hook commands with a trust gate.

findings.title: Sokrates primary decomposition: right at the top, misleading at two seams
findings.description: The 17-component `primary` decomposition matches the crate layering well for `core engine`, `app-server API`, `TUI frontend`, `persistence` and `configuration`. Three placements mislead. **`network-proxy` is filed under `sandboxing & policy`** but in the manifest graph it is a dependency of `protocol`, i.e. it sits in the bottom layer under everything; the component view therefore shows the vocabulary layer depending on the sandbox layer. **`apply-patch` is filed under `core engine`** while it depends on `exec-server`, making the engine component appear to depend on the executor at a point where the real edge is a helper-dispatch one. **`shared infrastructure` is a remainder bucket** defined as `.*/codex-rs/.*` minus every other component, so it collects `otel`, `git-utils`, `utils/*` and unassigned crates without a shared responsibility. The `by-layer` decomposition is closer to the truth for direction questions.

evidence.note: network-proxy is below protocol, not beside the sandbox

findings.recommendation: Move `network-proxy` (and `execpolicy`) into a `policy vocabulary` component next to `protocol`, move `apply-patch` into the exec-server component, and split `shared infrastructure` into `observability (otel)` and `utils`. Then the component dependency view will show the same direction as the manifests.

findings.title: codex-protocol is the shared vocabulary that 68 crates agree on
findings.description: `codex-protocol` defines the **serde-typed contract** for everything that crosses a seam inside Codex: `SandboxPolicy`, `AskForApproval`, `PermissionProfile`, thread and turn items, MCP policy, the `Event`/`Submission` pair. 68 of 133 crates depend on it and it has no dependency on `core`, so it holds as the one-directional floor of the workspace. Its versioning is by serde attributes rather than by version numbers: renames and aliases such as `on-failure` for `OnRequest` are the compatibility mechanism, and a `legacy_events` module keeps older wire shapes decodable. That makes the contract wide but shallow: any field added here reaches every layer at once.

findings.title: app-server-protocol: the versioned JSON-RPC contract between engine and clients
findings.description: `app-server-protocol` is the **external API contract**: request, response and notification types with schema export for TypeScript and other SDKs, organised into `v1` and `v2` modules that are both exported. Thirteen crates depend on it, on both sides of the process boundary (`app-server`, `app-server-client`, `tui`, `exec`, `cli`, `core`). The contract is what lets `tui` be a pure client. It is also the reason `core` depends on `app-server-protocol` rather than the reverse: the engine produces API-shaped items directly, which couples the engine to the API version.

findings.title: exec-server-protocol: the engine-to-executor contract that makes execution location-independent
findings.description: `exec-server-protocol` defines the JSON-RPC envelope the engine uses to spawn and control processes through `exec-server`: `InitializeParams`, `ExecParams`, environment capabilities, and a **network-policy round trip** in which the executor asks the engine whether a connection should be allowed and receives an `ExecServerNetworkPolicyDecision`. Because the same contract runs over a local WebSocket or a Noise-encrypted relay to a remote environment, the sandbox can be on another machine without the engine changing. 17 crates depend on `exec-server`, including `apply-patch`, `arg0` and the `ext/*` crates that need to run commands, which makes the executor the second hub after `core`.

findings.title: ext/extension-api: trait-based contributor seam for in-tree extensions
findings.description: `ext/extension-api` defines a family of **contributor traits** (`ToolContributor`, `McpServerContributor`, `ContextContributor`, `TurnLifecycleContributor`, `ApprovalReviewContributor` and others) plus an `ExtensionRegistryBuilder` that `app-server` fills. The seam is intended to let features be added without touching `core`. It is only half enforced: `extension-api` itself does not depend on `core`, but ten of the twelve `ext/*` implementations do, so the traits bound what an extension *provides* to the engine while the extension still reaches freely into engine internals. findings.title: The TUI does not link the engine: it is a client of the app-server API
findings.description: `tui` has no dependency on `codex-core`; it drives conversations through `app-server-client` and types from `app-server-protocol`. This is the strongest layering rule the workspace enforces and it has held: the interactive frontend cannot bypass the API and must work with what a remote or embedded client would see. The one leak (direct `exec-server` and `sandboxing` imports for local helpers) is recorded under violations.

findings.title: codex-core is the god crate the repo's own guidance says not to grow
findings.description: AGENTS.md states the rule: `codex-core` has become bloated and contributors should **resist adding code to codex-core**. The manifests show the rule losing: `core` depends on 61 of 133 workspace crates, the largest fan-out in the tree, and 23 crates depend on it, so it is both the widest consumer and the second-widest provider. Extension crates that were split out (`ext/*`) mostly still link `core`, the `codex_thread`/`session` modules carry config, exec, MCP, hooks, guardian and compaction concerns, and `core` re-exports lower-layer types as its own API. The cost is that most changes rebuild and re-test the whole engine and that the compile-time seam around the engine constrains almost nothing.

evidence.snippet: Over time, the `codex-core` crate (defined in `codex-rs/core/`) has become bloated because it is the largest crate, so it is often easier to add something new to `codex-core` rather than refactor out the library code you need so your new code neither takes a dependency on, nor contributes to the size of, `codex-core`.
To that end: **resist adding code to codex-core**!

findings.recommendation: Pick the next two extractions by dependency count: hook and MCP execution (`hook_runtime`, `hook_mcp_executor`, `mcp_*`) into the existing `hooks`/`rmcp-client` crates, and the `sandboxing`/`exec` modules into the execution cluster. Make `ext/*` crates depend on `extension-api` only, so the extension seam constrains both directions.

findings.title: The vocabulary crate depends on the policy engine, the network proxy and the HTTP client
findings.description: `codex-protocol` is named and used as the shared vocabulary, and Sokrates' decomposition files it that way. Its manifest, however, pulls in `codex-execpolicy` (the rule engine), `codex-network-proxy` (the egress proxy implementation with its TLS stack) and `codex-http-client`. The uses are real: `environment.rs` embeds `RequirementsExecPolicy` and `EnvironmentNetworkPolicy`, `error.rs` wraps `HttpError`. The effect is that every one of the 68 dependents of `protocol` transitively compiles the proxy and the policy engine, and that those two crates can never depend on `protocol` types themselves, which is why `network-proxy` defines its own policy vocabulary that `core` then re-exports. The evident intent (a leaf types crate) is inverted at this seam.

findings.title: TUI skips the API layer for exec-server and sandboxing

These support local concerns (sandbox warnings at startup, Windows sandbox setup prompts, plugin browsing) but they mean the TUI has knowledge of the executor that a remote client cannot have, and they are the reason the exec-server has 17 dependents. findings.title: No production cycles; one 21-crate cycle exists through dev-dependencies
findings.description: A manifest pass over all 133 crates finds **zero production dependency cycles**: the workspace is a DAG at build time. findings.title: Engine runtime: one actor per thread, bounded submissions in, unbounded events out
findings.description: Each conversation runs as a Tokio task: `submission_loop` reads `Submission`s from a **bounded** `async_channel` and everything the session emits goes out on an **unbounded** event channel that the API layer drains. Backpressure therefore exists on the input side only; an idle or slow consumer of events lets them accumulate. Tool calls, MCP calls and sub-agents are spawned as further tasks and report back through the same event sender, which is the ordering assumption every frontend relies on.

findings.title: Three process-crossing RPC seams: app-server JSON-RPC, exec-server JSON-RPC, MCP stdio and HTTP
findings.description: Codex crosses process boundaries in three places, all JSON-RPC. **Client to engine**: `app-server` over stdio, a Unix socket, a WebSocket, or the remote-control channel. **Engine to executor**: `exec-server` over a local WebSocket or a Noise-encrypted relay, with a forwarding mode that relays frames without parsing them. **Engine to tools**: `rmcp-client` spawns MCP servers as stdio children through the executor's `ExecBackend` or talks streamable HTTP. The exec-server seam crosses the trust boundary described under security-boundaries; MCP servers cross it in the other direction (they are untrusted third-party code but run outside the command sandbox).

findings.title: Trust map: five entry points for untrusted input, one structurally enforced boundary
findings.description: Untrusted data enters Codex through five doors. **Model output** (tool calls, commands, patches) arrives in `core` from the model clients. **User project files** and `AGENTS.md` are read into context by the engine. **Third-party code** enters as MCP servers, plugins, skills and hooks through the extensibility crates. **API clients** connect to `app-server` over stdio, Unix socket, WebSocket or remote control. **Remote executors** connect to `exec-server` over a relay. Of these, only model-requested commands cross a boundary that is **enforced by structure**: they are rewritten by `codex-sandboxing` into an OS-sandboxed child process, with an `execpolicy` and `AskForApproval` gate in front. Project trust (`trust_level` per project directory) selects which approval and sandbox profile applies. MCP servers, hooks and extensions run in the engine's own trust domain as ordinary child processes or in-process code: the boundary there is policy (approval, hook trust) rather than structure. `security-scan` judges what crosses each door; this finding records where the doors are.

findings.title: Command sandbox: Seatbelt on macOS, seccomp plus Landlock or bubblewrap on Linux, restricted token on Windows, via arg0 re-exec
findings.description: `SandboxManager` picks one backend per host and rewrites the argv. On **macOS** the command is wrapped in `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -p <profile>` with a generated Seatbelt policy (the path is pinned to defeat PATH tampering). On **Linux** the binary re-executes itself as `codex-linux-sandbox`, which launches bubblewrap with `--unshare-user --unshare-net` and read-only binds, or falls back to in-process `no_new_privs`, a seccomp network filter and Landlock filesystem rules, which the code now labels legacy. On **Windows** a restricted-token or elevated backend from `windows-sandbox-rs` is used when enabled. The single `codex` binary provides all helpers through `arg0` dispatch, and `process-hardening` disables ptrace and core dumps and strips `LD_PRELOAD`-style variables before `main`. The **executor path** (`exec-server`) refuses a request it cannot confine rather than running it open, which is the fail-closed half of the design.

findings.title: Network confinement: OS-level cut-off by default, opt-in managed egress proxy with domain policy
findings.description: Network confinement has two structural layers. The **base layer** is part of the sandbox: `network_access` is `false` by default in both `ReadOnly` and `WorkspaceWrite` policies, Linux installs a seccomp network filter or unshares the network namespace, and the child is told through `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1`. The **managed layer** is `network-proxy`: an HTTP and SOCKS5 proxy with allowed and denied domain lists, `Limited` (GET/HEAD only) versus `Full` modes, optional MITM hooks, a credential broker, and a policy decider that can route decisions back to the engine (and, via `exec-server-protocol`, to a remote engine). The proxy is `enabled: false` by default and its default mode is `Full`, so it only narrows traffic when a deployment turns it on and configures domains. Sandboxed commands reach the proxy through loopback, which the Seatbelt and bwrap profiles leave open for that purpose.

evidence.note: child is told the network is off

findings.title: Escape hatches: one flag disables both gates, plus policy variants and proxy switches that widen the boundary
findings.description: Seven distinct switches relax the boundaries, all explicit. `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` sets approval to `Never` and sandbox to `DangerFullAccess` in one move (`cli` and `exec`). `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` disables the hook trust gate. `SandboxPolicy::DangerFullAccess` and `SandboxPolicy::ExternalSandbox` are protocol-level ways to run open (the latter trusts a container to confine). `network_access: true` on a policy re-enables outbound traffic. `AskForApproval::Never` removes the human from the loop. In the proxy, `dangerously_allow_non_loopback_proxy` and `dangerously_allow_all_unix_sockets` widen the managed layer. Config-requirements (`config_requirements.rs`) can pin approval policies in managed deployments, which is the gating mechanism above these flags. The naming convention (`dangerously_*`) makes the hatches greppable, which is the design's main control.

findings.title: Open defaults: Windows sandbox is disabled by default and the in-process path degrades to no sandbox
findings.description: `WindowsSandboxLevel` defaults to `Disabled`, and `get_platform_sandbox` then returns `None` on Windows. `SandboxManager::select_initial` maps that to `SandboxType::None` with `unwrap_or`, so on a default Windows install a command whose policy says `WorkspaceWrite` runs **without any OS confinement**, with only the approval gate in front. The degradation is silent at the manager level; the compensating control lives one layer up in `core::safety`, where `assess_patch_safety` only auto-approves when `get_platform_sandbox` returns a backend and otherwise asks the user or rejects, and the TUI adds a startup prompt to enable the Windows sandbox. The `exec-server` path refuses instead of degrading. So the open default is deliberate, the confined mode exists (restricted-token and elevated backends), and the single wall on a default Windows install is the approval prompt. The trade-off is documented in the enum rather than in the docs folder, whose `sandbox.md` is a link to an external page. Two smaller open defaults sit beside it: MCP servers are launched with `sandbox: None`, and the managed network proxy is off by default, so a plain configuration relies on the OS cut-off alone.

evidence.note: the compensating control: auto-approval requires a platform sandbox

findings.recommendation: Make the in-process path match the executor: when the policy requires confinement and the host cannot provide it, have `select_initial` return an error or force the `UnlessTrusted` approval policy instead of `SandboxType::None`, so the guarantee is in the sandbox layer rather than in a caller-side safety check. Headless `exec` and app-server clients get no startup prompt today. Consider a manifest-level default of `RestrictedToken` once the Windows backend is considered stable.

findings.title: Two aggregate CI entry points, four release tag families, two schedules
findings.description: The trigger surface is deliberately narrow: blocking-ci runs on every pull request and on pushes to main and is the single merge-blocking entry point; postmerge-ci runs only on pushes to main for the heavier suites. Releases are driven by four tag families - rust-v*.*.* (main CLI release), codex-zsh-v*.*.* (patched zsh helper), python-v* (Python SDK to PyPI), rusty-v8-v*.*.* (V8 builds). Two scheduled workflows exist (rust-release-prepare every 4 hours, close-stale-contributor-prs daily), three issue-triage workflows react to issue events, and cla.yml uses pull_request_target. Roughly half of the 27 workflow files are workflow_call reusables invoked by the two entry points, which keeps the required-check list in one version-controlled place.

findings.title: Workspace version is 0.0.0 on main; release commits must stamp the real version
findings.description: codex-rs/Cargo.toml carries workspace version 0.0.0 in regular history, yet the release workflow's tag-check job fails unless the pushed rust-v tag exactly matches the version in Cargo.toml. Together these imply that release tags are not cut on ordinary main commits: some step outside the repo's visible automation (a release branch, manual commit, or external tooling) writes the real version into Cargo.toml and tags that commit. No workflow or script in the repo performs this version bump, so the version-stamping half of the release process lives outside what is checked in here.

findings.title: PRs get Bazel tests + fast checks; the full cargo-nextest 5-platform matrix runs post-merge
findings.description: The merge-blocking suite runs `bazel test //...` on a 4-target matrix (macOS arm64/x64, Linux gnu/musl; arm Linux disabled as flaky) plus fast cargo-native checks (fmt, clippy, cargo-shear, benchmark smoke test). The full cargo-nextest test suite - macOS aarch64, Linux x64 (remote-env) and arm64, Windows x64 and arm64, largely on self-hosted runners with sccache - runs only after merge via postmerge-ci calling rust-ci-full, with an opt-in '**full-ci**' branch-name trigger for developers who want the full suite pre-merge. This trades PR latency for a window where platform-specific cargo test regressions are only caught post-merge; the Bazel PR matrix and the opt-in escape hatch are the compensating controls.

findings.title: Hand-rolled path-based change detection scopes the fast PR jobs
findings.description: rust-ci's first job diffs the PR against its base with plain git (explicitly avoiding an external action) and emits booleans (codex, argument_comment_lint, workflows) that gate the downstream jobs, so a docs-only PR skips Rust jobs. Any change under .github/ flips the 'workflows' flag and forces the full fast bundle - a safe default that prevents CI edits from skipping their own validation. Manual dispatches force everything on.

evidence.snippet: - name: Detect changed paths (no external action)
evidence.note: deliberate avoidance of third-party path-filter actions
CI changes force the full run

findings.title: Single always()-guarded required job closes the skipped-check loophole
findings.description: Instead of listing many required checks in branch protection, blocking-ci funnels all seven gate workflows into one 'CI required' job that runs with always() and executes check_ci_results.py, which fails unless every dependency reports an explicit 'success' - skipped and cancelled count as failures. This closes the classic GitHub Actions hole where a skipped required check appears green, and keeps the required-check list version-controlled in one file. postmerge-ci reuses the same script so the two entry points cannot drift in result interpretation.

evidence.note: fan-in job runs even when dependencies fail

findings.title: Merge gates beyond tests: cargo-deny, codespell, blob-size, unused-deps, clean-worktree checks
findings.description: The PR gate includes cargo-deny (license/advisory/ban checking over the Rust workspace), codespell, a blob-size policy check, repo-checks, cargo-shear with --deny-warnings (unused dependency detection), a custom argument-comment dylint lint, and a CLA gate. Distinctively, nearly every job ends with a 'Check for a clean worktree' step, which fails if any build or codegen step modified tracked files - a repo-wide codegen-freshness gate that keeps generated artifacts (lockfiles, protobuf output, etc.) in sync with their sources.

evidence.snippet: - name: Check for a clean worktree

findings.title: CLA gate uses pull_request_target with write permissions - but never checks out PR code
findings.description: cla.yml runs contributor-assistant on pull_request_target and issue_comment events with contents/pull-requests/statuses write permissions, storing signatures on a cla-signatures branch. pull_request_target with write tokens is the classic CI privilege-escalation trigger, but this workflow never checks out or executes PR code - it only runs the pinned contributor-assistant action - so the risky trigger is used correctly. Worth preserving: any future edit that adds a checkout of the PR head to this workflow would create a serious vulnerability.

only step; no PR code checkout

findings.title: rust-v tag: validate, build, sign, GitHub Release, then fan out to npm/R2/DotSlash/WinGet
findings.description: Pushing an annotated rust-v*.*.* tag runs the whole release: tag-check enforces the tag format (x.y.z with optional -alpha/-beta suffixes) and that it equals the Cargo.toml version; after building and signing, the release job assembles all artifacts plus SHA256SUMS manifests and installer scripts, generates release notes from the tagged commit's message, and creates the GitHub Release (prerelease/latest flags derived from the version suffix). Downstream jobs then publish DotSlash manifests, mirror everything to Cloudflare R2 in two stages (assets, then channel finalize), publish six platform npm packages plus the @openai/codex wrapper and SDK to npm via OIDC trusted publishing (stable and numbered-alpha versions only), open a WinGet PR for stable versions, trigger a Vercel deploy of developers.openai.com, and force-update the latest-alpha-cli branch pointer once R2 and npm have succeeded.

evidence.snippet: # Publish to npm using OIDC authentication.

findings.title: Every platform's binaries are signed: AKV-notarized macOS, cosign Linux, Azure-signed Windows
findings.description: The release pipeline signs artifacts on all three platforms: macOS binaries and DMGs are signed with rcodesign against Azure Key Vault via PKCS11 and notarized with Apple, inside a protected 'codesigning' GitHub environment, with signature-info reports archived for verification; bundled helper binaries (rg, patched zsh) are fetched, signed, and notarized too. Linux artifacts are signed with sigstore cosign via a local composite action; Windows binaries go through an 'azure-artifact-signing' environment. Checksum manifests (codex-package_SHA256SUMS) accompany the release, and the R2 mirror re-verifies digests before advancing channel aliases. This is a notably complete signing story for a CLI distributed through curl-installers and package managers.

evidence.note: macOS signing gated by a protected environment

findings.title: The release path runs no tests - a tag on any commit builds, signs, and publishes
findings.description: rust-release's publish job depends only on tag-check, the build jobs, macOS finalization, and lint asset packaging - no test suite executes anywhere in the release workflow. The integrity model relies on tags being cut from CI-validated main history, but nothing in the pipeline enforces that: anyone with permission to push a rust-v tag on an arbitrary commit (including one never reviewed or tested) triggers a fully signed release to GitHub, npm, R2, and WinGet. Protected environments (codesigning, codex-r2-publisher) can add reviewer gates for signing and mirroring, but the GitHub Release and npm publish steps are not visibly environment-gated in the workflow. A tag-provenance check (verifying the tagged commit is contained in main) or a smoke-test job before publish would close the gap.

evidence.note: release job dependencies contain no test job
any matching tag push starts the release

findings.recommendation: Add a job to rust-release that verifies the tagged commit is an ancestor of main (git merge-base --is-ancestor) and/or run a smoke-test suite on the built artifacts before the publish jobs; alternatively gate the GitHub Release/npm jobs behind a protected environment with required reviewers, and restrict rust-v* tag creation via a tag ruleset.

findings.title: Users receive Codex via npm, curl-installers backed by R2, GitHub Releases, WinGet, PyPI, DotSlash
findings.description: Distribution is artifact-based with many channels: @openai/codex and platform packages on npm; install.sh/install.ps1 bootstrap scripts served from Cloudflare R2 (publish_r2_release.py uploads every release under a versioned prefix with digest verification, then advances mutable codex/channels/latest and codex/install.sh aliases for stable releases); GitHub Releases with SHA256SUMS; WinGet (OpenAI.Codex) via an automated winget-pkgs PR; the Python SDK on PyPI pinning an openai-codex-cli-bin runtime wheel; and DotSlash manifests. The install.sh script verifies the sha256 digest of every downloaded archive against release metadata and falls back from R2 to GitHub Releases on failure, so the payload (though not the bootstrap itself) is integrity-checked end to end.

evidence.note: mutable install channel aliases on R2

findings.title: No workflow deploys a running service - backend deployment lives elsewhere
findings.description: Every pipeline in the repo ends at artifact publication; nothing deploys or promotes a server environment. The only deployment-shaped step is a best-effort curl to a Vercel deploy hook that refreshes developers.openai.com's config schema after stable releases, marked continue-on-error at both job and step level so it can never fail a release. The Codex cloud backend the CLI talks to (chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex, referenced by the models-refresh job) is evidently deployed from a separate private codebase.

evidence.note: deploy hook is best-effort, cannot fail the release

findings.title: All ~195 external action references are SHA-pinned; checkouts drop credentials
findings.description: Every third-party action reference across all 27 workflows (195 of 195 external `uses:` lines) is pinned to a full 40-character commit SHA with a human-readable version comment, and composite actions under .github/actions follow the same rule. Checkout steps consistently set persist-credentials: false so later steps cannot reuse the git token. Combined with mostly-explicit least-privilege permissions blocks and repository guards on scheduled/issue jobs, this is top-tier GitHub Actions supply-chain hygiene; the criticism findings elsewhere in this report should be read against that baseline.

evidence.note: representative SHA-pinned action with version comment

findings.title: The curl-able install bootstrap is a mutable, unsigned R2 object
findings.description: publish_r2_release.py deliberately maintains mutable aliases - codex/install.sh, codex/install.ps1, and codex/channels/latest - that stable releases overwrite in place. Users who bootstrap via the R2-hosted installer execute whatever shell script currently sits behind that alias; unlike the release archives (which the script verifies by sha256 against release metadata), the bootstrap itself has no signature or pinned digest, so R2 write credentials (the codex-r2-publisher environment secrets) are sufficient to silently change what new installs run. This is inherent to every curl-pipe-sh channel and the blast radius is limited to the installer, but it makes the R2 credentials and their environment protection the single most security-sensitive secret in the pipeline.

evidence.snippet: ``codex/install.ps1`` bootstrap aliases from their verified versioned assets.
evidence.note: mutable bootstrap aliases documented in the publisher
R2 credentials scoped to a dedicated environment

findings.recommendation: Require reviewers on the codex-r2-publisher environment if not already enforced, and consider publishing a detached signature or checksum for install.sh at a well-known URL (or serving the installer from GitHub Releases only) so security-conscious users can verify the bootstrap before piping it to a shell.

findings.title: Nine configuration layers, from packaged defaults to MDM
findings.description: Codex composes configuration from **nine ordered layers**, each with an explicit numeric precedence in `ConfigLayerSource::precedence()`. From lowest to highest: packaged defaults (`-10`, the `defaults.toml` compiled into the binary), MDM managed preferences (`0`, macOS only), system config `/etc/codex/config.toml` (`10`), enterprise cloud-managed bundle (`15`), user `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` (`20`), a selected user profile `$CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml` (`21`), project `.codex/config.toml` (`25`), session flags from `-c key=value` (`30`), and two legacy managed-config layers (`40` and `50`). The format is **TOML throughout**; there is no JSON, YAML or dotenv config source, and no `.env` file anywhere in the tree. Environment variables are a **parallel** channel rather than a layer: they are read directly at their point of use (`CODEX_HOME`, `CODEX_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_BASE_URL`) and never merged into the TOML stack. A separate `requirements.toml` stack carries **36 admin constraint keys** that clamp what the config layers may express.

evidence.note: the loader's own documented layer list

evidence.snippet: /// - runtime   e.g., --config flags, model selector in UI

findings.title: Precedence is a numeric total order with per-key deep merge
findings.description: Precedence is **not implicit**: every layer carries an integer rank and `PartialOrd` is derived from it, so 'which source wins' is a single comparison rather than an argument order. Layers are folded lowest-to-highest by `merge_toml_values`, a **recursive per-key merge**: a scalar in a higher layer replaces the lower value, but a table is merged key by key, so setting `[tui] theme = "dark"` in a project config does not erase `[tui]` keys set in the user config. The stack also records **per-key origins**, so the effective value of any key can be attributed to the layer that set it. Two surprises are worth knowing. First, the **legacy managed-config layers outrank session flags** (`40`/`50` vs `30`), so a `-c` override on the command line cannot beat `managed_config.toml` — deliberate, but the opposite of the usual 'CLI wins' intuition. Second, a **selected profile sits at `21`, just above the base user config at `20`**, and therefore *below* project config at `25`: a project can override a setting the operator deliberately selected with `--profile`.

evidence.note: project ranks below session flags, both below legacy managed
the recursive per-key merge used to fold every layer

findings.title: CODEX_HOME anchors user config; project config is found by walking up
findings.description: The user layer lives under `$CODEX_HOME`, which defaults to `~/.codex` and is overridable by the `CODEX_HOME` environment variable — and that override is **strictly validated**: a path that does not exist, or exists but is not a directory, is a **fatal startup error** rather than a silent fall back to the default. That is the right choice, and it is one of the few configuration inputs in the system that fails fast. Project configuration is discovered by **walking up from the working directory** looking for `.codex/config.toml`, plus the repository root found via git, plus `$PWD/config.toml`. Which directories count as roots is itself configurable through `project_root_markers`, defaulting to `[".git"]`; setting it to an empty array disables root detection entirely. Discovered project layers are loaded but **disabled when the directory is untrusted**, so the file is visible in the layer listing for the UI while contributing nothing to the effective config.

evidence.note: the CODEX_HOME override, validated to exist and be a directory

evidence.snippet: /// - cwd       `${PWD}/config.toml` (loaded but disabled when the directory is untrusted)

findings.title: Project config may not set twelve credential- and execution-sensitive keys
findings.description: Project-local `.codex/config.toml` comes from repository contents, so it is treated as a **lower-trust source** and is denied twelve keys outright plus one nested key. The denylist covers exactly the settings that would let a checked-in file redirect where credentials go or what runs locally: `openai_base_url`, `chatgpt_base_url`, `model_provider`, `model_providers`, `notify` (which executes a command), `profile`, `profiles`, `otel`, `responses_api_metadata`, `apps_mcp_product_sku`, the two experimental realtime base URLs, and `features.respect_system_proxy`. The keys are **stripped before the layer is merged**, and the operator gets a startup warning naming each ignored key and telling them to set it in their user config instead. This is a well-designed control and one of the strongest parts of the configuration system: the same keys remain settable from user, system, managed and runtime layers, so the restriction is about *provenance*, not capability. Note the restriction is a **strip, not a rejection** — a project config full of denied keys still loads, it just loses them.

evidence.note: keys removed from the project layer before merge

findings.title: Environment variables are a side channel, not a config layer
findings.description: Codex reads **110 distinct environment variable names**, but they never enter the TOML layer stack — each is read at its point of use with `std::env::var`. Of those 110, roughly **35 are actual configuration** under the `CODEX_*` prefix (`CODEX_HOME`, `CODEX_API_KEY`, `CODEX_SANDBOX`, `CODEX_EXEC_SERVER_URL`, the `CODEX_APP_SERVER_*` overrides); the rest are **environment queries rather than settings** — `HOME`, `PATH`, `TMPDIR`, `USERPROFILE`, terminal-detection probes (`TERM`, `TMUX`, `ZELLIJ`, `WEZTERM_*`, `WT_SESSION`), Cargo and Bazel build variables, and proxy conventions (`HTTP_PROXY`, `NO_COLOR`). A further **eleven names are test-only hooks** (`CODEX_TEST_*`, `CODEX_APP_SERVER_TEST_USER_CONFIG_FILE`) that nonetheless ship in the release binary. The counting script resolves names held in `const` string constants, which is what makes this list usable: 67 of the names are reached only through a constant such as `CODEX_SANDBOX_ENV_VAR`, and a plain grep for string literals would have missed them.

evidence.note: a direct env read, outside the layer stack
config that names an env var to read

findings.title: 491 CLI options, but only about eleven set configuration
findings.description: The workspace declares **491 distinct CLI options** across all binaries and subcommands, and almost all of them select an action or supply an argument rather than set a configuration value. The **configuration-setting subset is about eleven**: the generic `-c/--config key=value`, plus `--model/-m`, `--profile/-p`, `--sandbox/-s`, `--oss`, `--local-provider`, `--cd/-C`, `--add-dir`, `--approve-for-me`, `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, and `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`. The generic `-c` is the interesting one: it takes a **dotted path** (`-c shell_environment_policy.inherit=all`), parses the right-hand side as TOML, and lands as the `SessionFlags` layer. Two named flags are **sugar that expands into config overrides** rather than separate settings — `--approve-for-me` pushes three `-c`-equivalent overrides (`approvals_reviewer`, `approval_policy`, `sandbox_mode`) into the same layer, which keeps the surface honest: there is one place a value can come from, not two.

evidence.note: a named flag that sets a config value

findings.title: Two generations of profiles coexist, and selecting the new one rejects the old
findings.description: Codex has **two profile mechanisms at once**. The legacy form is a `[profiles.<name>]` table inside `config.toml` selected by a `profile = "..."` key or `--profile`; the v2 form is a **separate file** `$CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml` layered on top of the base user config at precedence `21`. The v2 profile is a **restricted subset** — `ConfigProfile` carries about 20 fields (model, provider, approval policy, sandbox mode, reasoning effort, base URL) rather than the full 93-key surface, so a profile cannot express everything a config file can. The migration is handled by **refusing to guess**: if `--profile foo` is passed while the user config still contains a legacy `profile = "foo"` or a `[profiles.foo]` table, the load fails with a message telling the operator to move the settings and delete the legacy selector. Failing loudly on an ambiguous profile is the right call, though it means a user carrying an old config cannot adopt the new flag without editing first.

evidence.note: the v2 profile as its own layer

findings.title: Enterprise cloud config is fetched at startup, cached, and refreshed every 15 minutes
findings.description: A genuine **remote configuration source** exists for enterprise deployments: `codex-cloud-config` fetches a bundle from the backend at startup, caches it on disk, and then **refreshes in the background every 15 minutes**, with a 15-second timeout per attempt and retries. The bundle carries two payloads — cloud `config.toml` fragments that become the `EnterpriseManaged` layer at precedence `15`, and cloud `requirements.toml` fragments that become admin constraints. Failure is **fail-soft**: a timeout or a fetch error logs and keeps the existing cache, so a network outage does not stop the tool from running but does mean an operator can be running against **up to 15 minutes of stale policy** with only a log line saying so. Because the refresh applies to the cache rather than the live session, a policy change made centrally does not take effect in an already-running session — this is the one place in the product where configuration is genuinely dynamic, and its effect is deferred to the next load.

evidence.snippet: "Timed out refreshing cloud config bundle cache from remote; keeping existing cache"

findings.title: Traced: cli_auth_credentials_store, from four sources to a silent plaintext fallback
findings.description: This setting decides **where the operator's API credentials are written**, and tracing it end to end shows every mechanism in the system at once. **Sources**, lowest to highest: the packaged `defaults.toml` sets `"file"`; system, cloud and user `config.toml` may set it; `-c cli_auth_credentials_store=keyring` sets it as a session flag; and an admin `requirements.toml` can **force** it via `apply_exact!`, which overrides the user's choice outright rather than merging with it. Project config **cannot** set it (it is not in the denylist, but it is also not a provenance-sensitive key — it is reachable from a project file). **Default**: `"file"`, meaning credentials go to `$CODEX_HOME/auth.json` written with mode `0600`. **Type coercion**: a closed four-variant enum (`file`, `keyring`, `auto`, `ephemeral`), so a typo like `"kyring"` is a **deserialization error with a caret diagnostic**, not a silent default. **Validation**: none beyond the enum. **The interesting part is what happens after resolution.** On a local dev build the resolver silently rewrites `keyring` and `auto` to `file`, so a developer testing keyring configuration is not exercising keyring at all. And under `auto`, a keyring failure falls back to writing the credential to a plaintext file at `warn!` level — see `secrets-management/plaintext-fallback`.

evidence.note: an admin requirement forces the value
dev builds silently downgrade keyring/auto to file

findings.title: Traced: sandbox_mode, safe by default and settable from five places
findings.description: `sandbox_mode` decides how much of the machine model-generated commands can touch, making it the highest-consequence setting in the product. **Sources**: user, system, cloud and project `config.toml`; a `[profiles.<name>]` table or a v2 profile file; `-c sandbox_mode=...`; the `--sandbox/-s` flag; and indirectly `--approve-for-me` (which pushes `workspace-write`) and `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` (which bypasses the sandbox entirely). **Default**: `read-only` — the `#[default]` variant of the `SandboxMode` enum, so an unconfigured installation is in the **safest** of the three modes, which is the single most important default in the system and it is set correctly. **Coercion**: a closed three-variant kebab-case enum, so an unrecognised value fails to deserialize rather than falling through to a permissive mode. **Admin clamp**: `allowed_sandbox_modes` in `requirements.toml` lets an administrator remove `danger-full-access` from the menu entirely. The residual risk is not the default but the discoverability: `danger-full-access` disables sandboxing with one line in a TOML file that **no in-repo document mentions** — see `settings-surface/undocumented-settings`.

findings.title: 93 operator-settable keys in one schema, plus 36 admin constraints and 117 feature flags
findings.description: The primary operator-facing surface is the `ConfigToml` struct, which the build turns into a **93-key JSON Schema** — `codex-rs/core/config.schema.json`, 155 type definitions and roughly 490 nested properties, so the real settable surface is several hundred keys deep. These are all **tuning keys**, not specification keys: there is no input-document config here, every key changes how the program behaves on the same input. By area: **model and provider** (about 18 keys — `model`, `model_provider`, `model_providers`, reasoning effort and verbosity, context-window and compaction limits, `service_tier`); **sandbox and permissions** (about 10 — `sandbox_mode`, `sandbox_workspace_write`, `permissions`, `default_permissions`, `approval_policy`, `allow_login_shell`, `shell_environment_policy`); **auth and endpoints** (about 8 — the two credential-store keys, `openai_base_url`, `chatgpt_base_url`, the forced-login keys, MCP OAuth callback); **extensions** (about 10 — `mcp_servers`, `plugins`, `marketplaces`, `skills`, `hooks`, `apps`, `agents`, `goals`, `memories`); **UI and UX** (about 12 — `tui`, `file_opener`, `notify`, `notice`, reasoning visibility); **telemetry** (`otel`, `analytics`, `feedback`); and **9 `experimental_*` keys**. Two further surfaces sit alongside: **36 admin constraint keys** in `requirements.toml` and **117 feature flags** in the `[features]` table.

findings.title: 92 of 93 settings have no in-repo documentation, including every sandbox and auth key
findings.description: Grepping each of the 93 schema keys against `docs/` and `codex-rs/core/src/config/schema.md` finds **one key documented in the repository**: `log_dir`, in a single sentence of `docs/install.md`. The reason is structural rather than neglectful — **the configuration reference was moved off-repo**. `docs/config.md` is 15 lines whose substance is a link to `developers.openai.com/codex/config-reference`, and nine other files in `docs/` are 84-to-177-byte redirect stubs of the same shape, `authentication.md` and `sandbox.md` among them. So the settings are almost certainly documented *somewhere*; they are simply documented where **no CI check, no diff and no repo-local reader can see them**, which means schema drift against the published reference is undetectable from the code. Of the 92, about **25 are dangerous when wrong** and deserve naming: the sandbox and permission keys (`sandbox_mode`, `sandbox_workspace_write`, `permissions`, `default_permissions`, `approval_policy`, `allow_login_shell`, `shell_environment_policy`), the credential and login keys (`cli_auth_credentials_store`, `mcp_oauth_credentials_store`, `forced_login_method`, `forced_chatgpt_workspace_id`), the endpoint keys (`openai_base_url`, `chatgpt_base_url`, `model_provider`, `model_providers`, `mcp_servers`), and the telemetry keys (`otel`, `analytics`, `responses_api_metadata`). The sharpest case is `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"`, which **disables sandboxing entirely** from a config file that no shipped document describes.
findings.recommendation: Restore a generated, in-repo key reference — the 93-key `config.schema.json` already exists, so rendering it to Markdown in CI would give a repo-local document that cannot drift from the struct. Failing that, add a CI check that every schema key appears in the published reference, so drift is caught at build time rather than by a confused operator. Prioritise the 25 dangerous-when-wrong keys.

findings.title: Five retired keys are still accepted; four are silent no-ops and one fails fast
findings.description: Five keys remain in `ConfigToml` after the features behind them were removed, hidden from the generated schema with `#[schemars(skip)]` but **still accepted by the deserializer**. Four are **silent no-ops**: `js_repl_node_path` and `js_repl_node_module_dirs` (marked 'Deprecated: ignored'), `agents.job_max_runtime_seconds` ('Removed agent-job setting retained as a no-op for compatibility'), and the same `js_repl_node_path` inside `ConfigProfile`. An operator who set them keeps them in their config, sees no warning, and gets no behaviour. The fifth, `experimental_thread_store_endpoint`, is handled correctly and shows what the others should do: it is retained **specifically so the loader can reject it**, erroring with `is no longer supported; remove it from config.toml` rather than silently falling back to local persistence. Separately, two **renamed** keys are handled properly with real aliasing rather than deprecation: `no_memories_if_mcp_or_web_search` becomes `disable_on_external_context` and `agents.max_threads` becomes `max_concurrent_threads_per_session`, normalised during merge so the old spelling keeps working.
findings.recommendation: Give the four silent no-ops the treatment `experimental_thread_store_endpoint` already gets — either a startup warning naming the key or a hard error. Since they are hidden from the schema, `--strict-config` will not catch them either, so an operator has no way to discover the setting is dead.

findings.title: A typed Rust schema with a generated JSON Schema, not scattered lookups
findings.description: Configuration is represented as a **typed schema end to end**. `ConfigToml` and its 155 supporting types are ordinary serde structs with `JsonSchema` derives, so every key has a Rust type, and the build emits `codex-rs/core/config.schema.json` from them — a real generated artefact rather than a hand-maintained parallel document. Enums are **closed and kebab-cased** (`SandboxMode`, `AuthCredentialsStoreMode`, `WebSearchMode`), which is what gives the system its type-level validation: an unrecognised value for a closed enum cannot deserialize, so a typo in a mode name is caught at load. The typed layer sits **above** an untyped one: layers are merged as `toml::Value` and only deserialized into `ConfigToml` afterwards, which is what allows per-key origin tracking and per-key merging but also means **type errors surface only after merging**, attributed to the merged document rather than to the layer that introduced them. There are effectively **no ad-hoc lookups** — the config crate is the single owner, and the roughly 90 `unwrap_or` calls in `core/src/config/mod.rs` are default application, not independent reads.

findings.title: Defaults live in three places, consistent today but not single-sourced
findings.description: A default value for a given key can come from any of **three mechanisms**, and for several keys it comes from all three. First, `codex-rs/config/defaults.toml` — a 17-line file compiled into the binary with `include_str!` and pushed as the lowest layer, holding 14 values including `project_doc_max_bytes = 32768`, `file_opener = "vscode"` and `cli_auth_credentials_store = "file"`. Second, **serde defaults** on the struct — 29 `#[serde(default = ...)]` attributes with functions such as `default_project_doc_max_bytes()`. Third, **`unwrap_or` at the point of use** in `core/src/config/mod.rs`, about 90 of them, such as `cfg.project_doc_max_bytes.unwrap_or(AGENTS_MD_MAX_BYTES)`. I checked the overlapping keys and the values **agree** — `project_doc_max_bytes` routes to the same `DEFAULT_PROJECT_DOC_MAX_BYTES` constant in both the serde default and the `unwrap_or`, and `defaults.toml` states the same number literally. So this is redundancy rather than conflict. The cost is maintenance: changing a default correctly means finding all three sites, and the literal `32768` in `defaults.toml` is not derived from the constant, so nothing prevents them diverging in a future edit.
findings.recommendation: Derive the `defaults.toml` values from the same constants the serde defaults use, or drop the per-key `unwrap_or` fallbacks now that a packaged-defaults layer guarantees the key is present. findings.title: CLI override values fall back to a raw string when TOML parsing fails
findings.description: `-c key=value` parses the right-hand side as TOML so that `-c model=o3` works without quoting, and when that parse fails it **silently treats the text as a string literal** rather than reporting an error. For a string-typed key that is the convenience it was designed for. For a **typed** key it converts a syntax error into a type error one step later: `-c project_doc_max_bytes=32kb` becomes the string `"32kb"`, which then fails to deserialize into `usize` — so the operator does get an error, just one that describes the wrong problem. The riskier shape is a key whose type **is** a string but whose values are constrained, where a malformed override becomes a plausible-looking wrong value. Elsewhere coercion is well behaved: closed enums reject unknown variants outright, and the `SandboxMode` and credential-store enums are the ones that matter. Note also that a **typo'd override key** is not caught at all by default — `-c modle=o3` is discarded silently unless `--strict-config` is passed.
findings.recommendation: Report the TOML parse failure at debug level, or restrict the raw-string fallback to values that do not look like a failed literal (a bare `32kb` or `tru`). Today the fallback is indistinguishable from an intended string.

findings.title: Seven credential sources feed one resolution point
findings.description: Credentials reach Codex from **seven distinct sources**, all resolved in `load_auth` with an explicit precedence. First the **`CODEX_API_KEY` environment variable**, which outranks everything else. Then an **in-memory ephemeral store** for externally supplied ChatGPT tokens. Then **`CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN`**, classified at read time into either a personal access token or an agent-identity JWT. Then the **persisted store** — `$CODEX_HOME/auth.json` at mode `0600`, or the **OS keyring** under service name `Codex Auth`, with two keyring backends (a direct payload, or an age-encrypted local file whose passphrase lives in the keyring). Alongside these: **interactive ChatGPT login** via PKCE with a local callback server, which writes into the same `auth.json`; **AWS credentials** for Bedrock, delegated entirely to the AWS default chain rather than read by Codex; and **workload identity**, a federated token-file exchange driven by `OPENAI_FEDERATION_RULE_ID` and `OPENAI_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE`. `OPENAI_API_KEY` is notably **not** in the resolution chain — it is only a prefill for the onboarding screen, so it seeds `auth.json` rather than acting as a runtime credential.

findings.title: Keyring failure writes the credential to a plaintext file with only a warn log
findings.description: Both credential stores implement **`auto` mode as keyring-with-silent-file-fallback**. When the keyring save fails, `AutoAuthStorage` logs at `warn!` and writes the credential to `$CODEX_HOME/auth.json` instead; the MCP OAuth path does the same into `$CODEX_HOME/.credentials.json`. Nothing surfaces to the operator at the point of use — a `warn!` in a TUI session is not a prompt, and there is no configuration flag that says 'fail rather than downgrade' short of choosing `keyring` explicitly, which is a **different value the operator has to know exists**. This matters more for MCP than for CLI auth, because `cli_auth_credentials_store` defaults to `"file"` (already plaintext, so no downgrade occurs) while **`mcp_oauth_credentials_store` defaults to `"auto"`** — the fallback path is the shipped default for MCP OAuth tokens, and the code's own comment notes the resulting file is readable by any application running as the same user. There is a deliberate carve-out that shows the authors thought about this: a store *lock* failure is **not** treated as keyring-unavailable and does not fall back. That precision makes the remaining silence look like a choice rather than an oversight.
findings.recommendation: Surface the downgrade where the operator will see it — a startup warning in the same channel as the project-config denylist warnings, which already prove the mechanism exists. Better still, record in the credential file that it was written by fallback, so a later run can tell the operator their keyring configuration is not taking effect.

findings.title: Model providers configure their own credential env var, and may hold a token in plaintext
findings.description: `[model_providers.<name>]` lets an operator define a provider, and the credential plumbing is **part of that configuration**: `env_key` names the environment variable holding the API key, `env_key_instructions` supplies the message shown when it is missing, and `env_http_headers` maps header names to further environment variables. This makes the environment surface **user-extensible** — the set of credential-bearing variables Codex reads is not fixed by the code, so no static analysis of `env::var` call sites can enumerate it. The flow itself is clean: `api_key()` reads the named variable, rejects an empty or whitespace value, and returns a typed `EnvVarError` carrying the operator instructions rather than a bare failure. Alongside it sits `experimental_bearer_token`, which holds a **token literally in the config file**, and the field's own doc comment says its use is discouraged in favour of `env_key` for security reasons. That is the right warning in the right place — but it is a Rust doc comment, so an operator reading a config example never sees it, and the key is not in the project-config denylist.
findings.recommendation: Consider adding `experimental_bearer_token` and `model_providers` to the project-local denylist reasoning — `model_providers` is already denied, which covers the nested token, so the residual gap is only that a user-level config can carry a plaintext token with no warning at load. A startup warning when `experimental_bearer_token` is set would match how the denylist already warns.

findings.title: Best-effort regex redaction, including a pattern that catches config-shaped assignments
findings.description: The configuration layer redacts secrets before they reach logs and output using **four regexes**, and the module says of itself that it works 'on best effort basis'. Three match credential *shapes* — OpenAI keys (`sk-` plus 20+ characters), AWS access key ids (`AKIA` plus 16), and bearer tokens. The fourth is the one that matters for configuration: it matches **`api_key`/`token`/`secret`/`password` followed by `:` or `=` and a value**, which is precisely the shape of a TOML or env-var assignment, so a config file echoed into a log or an error message has its credential-bearing lines masked regardless of the key's own name. The limits are inherent to the approach: a provider whose key has no recognisable prefix and whose config key is not one of the four words passes through unredacted, and `experimental_bearer_token = "..."` is caught by the assignment pattern only because the key name contains `token`. Worth distinguishing from `thread_resume_redaction.rs`, which despite the name is a **payload-size measure** for two mobile clients and explicitly leaves persisted history unchanged — it is not a secrets control.

findings.title: No .env.example and no in-repo auth setup guide; the recipe lives in a crate README
findings.description: An operator setting Codex up for the first time gets **no dotenv scaffolding at all** — there is no `.env`, no `.env.example`, and no dotenv loader anywhere in the tree, which is consistent with the design (credentials come from a keyring, a key file, or an exported variable) but removes the usual discovery affordance. The in-repo guidance is thin: `docs/authentication.md` is **three lines redirecting to an external URL**, and neither credential-store key appears anywhere under `docs/`. The one concrete recipe that ships is in a crate README, showing `CODEX_API_KEY="$OPENAI_API_KEY"` for the exec-server. In practice there are three viable setup paths and an operator has to infer them from the code or the external site: run `codex login` for interactive PKCE, export `CODEX_API_KEY`, or export `OPENAI_API_KEY` and let the TUI onboarding screen detect and store it. That third path is the only one with a visible prompt — the onboarding screen says it detected the variable — which makes it the de facto documented route by accident rather than design.
findings.recommendation: Add a short in-repo `docs/authentication.md` section naming the three setup paths and the two credential-store keys. This is the highest-value single document to restore, because unlike tuning keys a credential misconfiguration blocks first use entirely.

findings.title: Unknown keys are silently dropped unless --strict-config is passed
findings.description: By default a key the schema does not recognise is **discarded without a word**. Serde ignores it, no warning is logged, and the operator's `modle = "gpt-5"` simply never takes effect. Strict rejection exists and is well built — `serde_ignored` plus `serde_path_to_error` produce `unknown configuration field \`<path>\`` with a **rustc-style caret diagnostic** pointing at the offending line and column, and it extends into the `[features]` table by checking each key against the known-feature registry. But it is reachable **only through the `--strict-config` CLI flag**, whose default is `false`; there is no config key and no environment variable that turns it on, so an operator cannot make strictness their standing preference — and a config-file setting could not do it anyway, since the strictness decision has to precede reading the file. The same silence applies to **`-c` overrides**: `-c modle=o3` is discarded by default, with its own dedicated message available only under strict mode. Several loader paths are also **hardcoded non-strict** regardless of the flag, including the local-executor reads and the default cloud-config path.
findings.recommendation: Add a warn-level middle ground: log unknown keys by name at startup even when strict mode is off. The machinery already collects them, so this is a matter of routing the collected paths to a warning instead of discarding them — and it would use the same startup-warning channel that project-config key stripping already uses.

findings.title: Malformed config aborts with a caret diagnostic, except in untrusted project directories
findings.description: A config file that will not parse as TOML is a **fatal error with an excellent message**. The loader converts the parse failure into a `ConfigError` carrying file, line and column, and the TUI restores the terminal, prints a **rustc-style rendering with a gutter, the source line and a caret underline**, and exits 1. This is the strongest part of the validation story: the operator learns exactly which character of which file is wrong. A **missing** file is not an error at all — it logs at info and contributes an empty layer, which is correct for a layered system where most layers are absent most of the time. There is **one exception worth knowing**: a malformed `.codex/config.toml` in an **untrusted** directory is not fatal. The loader substitutes an empty table and continues, and unlike the denylist-stripping path it does **not** push a startup warning, so the operator working in an untrusted checkout gets no signal that their project config is broken rather than merely disabled. The reasoning is defensible — an untrusted project's file contributes nothing anyway — but the silence conflates 'ignored because untrusted' with 'ignored because broken'.
findings.recommendation: Push a startup warning when an untrusted project config fails to parse, reusing the channel that already reports stripped denylist keys. The operator would then be able to distinguish a disabled layer from a broken one before they trust the directory.

findings.title: Types and enums checked at load; semantic checks deferred to first use
findings.description: Validation happens in **two waves at different times**. At load, everything the type system can express is checked: TOML syntax, field types, and closed-enum membership — so `sandbox_mode = "danger"` or `cli_auth_credentials_store = "kyring"` fails at startup with a spanned diagnostic. Beyond types, the load-time checks are **selective rather than systematic**: `validate_enabled_config_layers` checks the shell-environment-policy filter representation, permission-profile names are validated, and the multi-agent tool namespace is checked. Everything else is checked **when the subsystem first initialises**. The network proxy is the clearest case: `network.proxy_url`, `network.socks_url` and `network.allow_unix_sockets` are only parsed and range-checked when the proxy starts, where a non-absolute socket path or a zero port produces a contextual error. For a single-user interactive CLI this is a reasonable trade — the operator is present, sees the error, and fixes it. It matters more for the **headless `codex exec` path**, where a misconfigured proxy surfaces only once a session reaches the point of needing it.

findings.title: 117 feature flags in one registry with declared lifecycle stages
findings.description: Feature flags are a **first-class, centrally registered mechanism** rather than scattered booleans. A single `FEATURES` table declares every flag with an id, the `[features]` TOML key an operator writes, a **lifecycle stage**, and a default. The stages are meaningful: `Stable` (38 flags — shipped, the flag kept for ad-hoc disabling), `UnderDevelopment` (41 — not user-visible), `Experimental` (1 — surfaced in the `/experimental` menu with a name, description and announcement), `Deprecated` (3), and `Removed` (34). Flags are **config keys, not a remote service**: they come from the same layered `[features]` table as everything else, so an administrator can set them through `requirements.toml` and a user through their config file. The registry pays for itself in two places: strict-config validation checks `[features]` keys against it, and telemetry emits a `codex.feature.state` counter for every flag whose value differs from its default — deliberately **skipping `Removed` flags**, which is the one place the code acknowledges that removed flags still exist in the wild.

findings.title: 34 removed feature flags are still accepted as valid keys and do nothing
findings.description: Of the 117 registered flags, **34 are staged `Removed`** — the feature is gone and the branch is unreachable — yet they remain in the `FEATURES` table, and `feature_for_key` iterates the **whole table without filtering by stage**. findings.title: Effectively all settings require a restart; the only refresh is the cloud policy cache
findings.description: Codex has **no configuration reload mechanism** for its own files: no SIGHUP handler that rereads config, no watcher on `config.toml`, no `/reload` command. The layer stack is built once per session and the resulting `Config` is passed around by value, so changing `~/.codex/config.toml` mid-session has **no effect until the next launch**. The file-watching machinery that exists in the workspace watches **workspace files for the agent**, not configuration, and the `ConfigReloader` trait in the network proxy is implemented only by `StaticConfigReloader` and `StaticNetworkProxyReloader` — both of which return 'nothing changed' or refuse to reload, so the reload seam is declared but **not wired to any live source**. The single genuinely dynamic path is the **enterprise cloud bundle**, refreshed into its cache every 15 minutes, and even that takes effect at the next load rather than in the running session. What the product does provide instead is **per-session override**: `-c` flags and `--sandbox`/`--model` let an operator get a different effective configuration by starting a new session, which for a CLI is the idiomatic answer. The gap is only that nothing **documents** the restart requirement.

findings.title: A mature layered configuration system whose documentation left the repository
findings.description: Codex composes configuration from **nine explicitly ranked TOML layers** — packaged defaults, MDM, system, enterprise cloud, user, profile, project, session flags, and two legacy managed layers — folded by a recursive per-key merge that also records **which layer set each key**. Defaults come from three places (a compiled-in `defaults.toml`, serde attributes, and `unwrap_or` at point of use) that currently agree but are maintained by hand. Environment variables sit **outside** the stack as a parallel channel of 110 names, and CLI flags contribute one generic `-c key=value` plus about ten named settings. **How an operator finds out what they can set is the central weakness**: the surface is 93 schema keys, 36 admin constraint keys and 117 feature flags, and exactly **one key is documented in the repository** — the reference now lives behind a URL, so drift against the code is invisible to CI, to a diff, and to anyone reading the source. **The riskiest default is not dangerous** — the sandbox defaults to `read-only`, credentials to a `0600` file — but `mcp_oauth_credentials_store = "auto"` ships a **silent keyring-to-plaintext fallback** as the default path. **On bad input** the system is bimodal: a malformed file aborts with an excellent caret diagnostic, while an unrecognised key vanishes without a word unless the operator knew to pass `--strict-config`. Notable strengths worth preserving: the **project-config denylist**, which stops a checked-in file redirecting credentials; the numeric precedence order with per-key origins; and the feature registry with declared lifecycle stages. The three highest-leverage changes are documentation restoration, a warn-level unknown-key path, and making strict mode reject removed feature flags.

findings.title: Turn: one user input driven to completion; executed inside the engine as a Task
findings.description: A Turn is the unit of work inside a thread: it starts with user input (turn/start), runs the model/tool loop, and completes with status, timing and an optional error. Identity: UUIDv7 turn ids on the v2 Turn struct. Lifecycle: started by turn/start, redirected by turn/steer, stopped by turn/interrupt; at most one turn runs per thread at a time. findings.title: Plugin and Marketplace: installable packages and the catalogs they are resolved from
findings.description: A Plugin is an installable package that extends Codex with scripts, skills, hooks and MCP routing; its definition of record is PluginManifest ('parsed plugin metadata parameterized by its resource locator representation'), identified by a validated PluginId and loaded either from host paths or from authority-bound resolved packages. A Marketplace is a catalog plugins are added from: core-plugins recognizes marketplace manifests at .agents/plugins/marketplace.json and compatibility locations (.claude-plugin/, .cursor-plugin/), and the API exposes marketplace/add, marketplace/remove and marketplace/upgrade beside plugin/install, plugin/list, plugin/search and plugin/share. findings.title: The safety cluster: AskForApproval, SandboxPolicy, PermissionProfile, and Environment
findings.description: Four nouns govern what the agent may do. AskForApproval is the approval policy enum (untrusted, on-request, fine-grained categories) deciding when a human is asked before a command runs. SandboxPolicy 'determines execution restrictions for model shell commands' - the OS-level isolation mode. PermissionProfile is the canonical active-runtime-permissions value (managed sandbox construction, disabled, or externally enforced), with reserved built-in ids :read-only, :workspace and :danger-full-access; users select profiles by name (thread/start's permissions field). Environment is a thread's resolved execution attachment: EnvironmentConfig bundles a permission-profile snapshot, shell-environment policy, exec policy, MCP policy and network policy for wherever commands actually run - orbiting concepts (execpolicy rules, network sandbox, workspace roots) all hang off this cluster. Ownership: all defined in codex-protocol; enforced by the sandboxing/execpolicy/exec-server crates that security-design-scan covers.

findings.title: Four language contexts: protocol vocabulary, public API, engine runtime, persistence - with explicit translation
findings.description: The vocabulary is owned in four contexts. (1) codex-protocol is the canonical identity-and-engine-wire context: ThreadId, SessionId, TurnItem, Op/EventMsg, the permission vocabulary - the crate 68 others import (architecture-scan's codex-protocol-vocabulary finding). (2) app-server-protocol v2 owns the public names: Thread, Turn, ThreadItem and the resource/method grammar, governed by a written AGENTS.md rule (singular resource, thread/read style); it translates from context 1 via explicit mappers (v2_enum_from_core, event_mapping, item_builders) rather than sharing types blindly. (3) codex-core speaks an internal runtime dialect - Session, ActiveTurn, RunningTask, CodexThread - that never crosses the wire. (4) The persistence crates (history, rollout, state, thread-store) own RolloutItem/RolloutLine/SessionMeta. Concepts shared across contexts keep one canonical side: identity is always context 1's; public naming is context 2's. This is a deliberate context map, not drift - the drift findings cover where the translation leaks.

findings.title: 'Session' carries three meanings across public surfaces while 'Conversation' lingers; canonical term is Thread
findings.description: The Conversation-to-Thread rename that architecture-scan maps (evolution/conversation-to-thread-rename) has left 'session' bound to incompatible meanings on public surfaces. To the CLI, a session is one thread: 'Resume a previous interactive session', 'Archive a saved session'. To the v2 API, session_id groups a whole tree of threads, distinct from the thread id. To the engine, Session is the runtime object of a single loaded thread. Meanwhile 'Conversation' still leaks: the fork command's help says 'Conversation/session id (UUID)', ConversationPathResponseEvent is kept 'for backward compatibility' with a conversation_id field typed ThreadId, ResumedHistory.conversation_id likewise, and PermissionProfile's doc still says 'for a conversation'. The codebase's visible convergence target is Thread (v2 methods, ThreadId as the only durable handle), with SessionId being narrowed to the tree-grouping meaning - but until CLI help and engine naming follow, a newcomer reading 'session' cannot know which of the three referents is meant.

findings.recommendation: Adopt one glossary sentence repo-wide: 'a Thread is one conversation; a Session is the tree a root thread and its forks/sub-agents share'. findings.title: 'Turn' absorbed what protocol v1 called a 'Task'; the wire and engine internals still say task
findings.description: Protocol v1's documented model is Session -> Task -> Turn: a Task is 'Codex executing work in response to user input' and a Turn is 'one cycle of iteration in a Task' (one model request + tool execution). The v2 public API collapsed this: its Turn is the whole user-input-to-completion unit - v1's Task - and the inner model-request cycle no longer has a public name. The seams are visible on both sides: the v1 doc itself notes that EventMsg::TurnStarted/TurnComplete serialize as task_started/task_complete for wire compatibility, and inside codex-core the running turn is still an ActiveTurn holding a RunningTask (task: Option<RunningTask>). Canonical direction: Turn for the public unit, task surviving as engine-internal execution vocabulary and frozen wire tags. Reading old docs or wire dumps with the new vocabulary (or vice versa) silently shifts the meaning one level, so the stale v1 definition is the main trap for newcomers and log readers. Note 'task' also means a Codex Cloud work item in the cloud-tasks crates - a third, unrelated referent.

findings.recommendation: Add a short vocabulary note to protocol_v1.md (or its successor) stating the mapping explicitly: v1 Task = v2 Turn; v1 Turn = one model-request cycle, now unnamed publicly; wire tags task_* are frozen aliases. That one paragraph disarms the trap without any code churn.

findings.title: TurnItem and ThreadItem are the same concept under two names; 'item' spans four types in all
findings.description: The glossary item entry records the four-layer item family; the drift is that the two central layers name the identical concept differently: codex-protocol's TurnItem and app-server-protocol v2's ThreadItem carry the same variants (UserMessage, AgentMessage, Reasoning, CommandExecution, McpToolCall, ...) and are mechanically mapped into each other - one concept, two names, split exactly on the crate boundary. The names also disagree about ownership: the engine says items belong to turns (TurnItem), while the API type says they belong to threads (ThreadItem) even though the v2 Turn struct is what actually contains them ('Thread items currently included in this turn payload'). Add ResponseItem (model wire) and RolloutItem (persistence envelope) and 'item' requires a qualifier to be unambiguous anywhere in the codebase. This reads as a deliberate context translation rather than an accident - the mapping layer is explicit - but no comment states why the public name differs, so the alternative reading (an unfinished alignment) stays open.
