findings.title: 'Profile' is a homonym: config.toml preset profiles vs sandbox permission profiles
findings.description: Two unrelated load-bearing meanings share the word profile. ConfigProfile (codex-config) is a named bundle of common configuration options a user defines in config.toml and layers over the base config (the CLI's --profile / <name>.config.toml mechanism). PermissionProfile (codex-protocol) is the canonical runtime permissions value - sandbox construction mode plus filesystem/network policy - selected per thread via built-in ids like :read-only or named entries in the [profiles] permission tables of config requirements. Both are user-selectable by name, both live in configuration, and thread/start's field for the permission kind is even called permissions with a doc saying 'Named profile id' - so 'set the profile' is genuinely ambiguous in support conversations and config reviews. The API's choice to call the field permissions (not profile) suggests the visible canonical direction: permission profile is being spoken as 'permissions', leaving bare 'profile' to mean the config preset.

findings.title: Era 1 (2025-04 to 2025-08): the TypeScript CLI, with a Rust rewrite growing beside it

The era is a community burst followed by a lull: 157 commits in May, 44 in June with only 5 authors, 128 in July. The Rust CLI was declared the released product in July 2025 (`docs: update documentation to reflect Rust CLI release`). The era left behind the `codex-cli/` npm wrapper, the `codex-rs/execpolicy` and `mcp-types` crates, and the sandboxing work (Landlock/seccomp) that still frames the product.

Over the next eleven days a stream of `tui_app_server` fix commits removed the remaining core events and legacy auth handling, the feature was enabled by default, and on 2026-03-27 the **legacy TUI was removed** (856 files, 130858 lines). findings.title: Migration in progress: the core is being carved into crates, but still takes half of all activity

findings.title: Velocity: a high plateau, not acceleration, with a broadening team
findings.description: The 90-day comparison is flat: **2818 commits in the last 90 days versus 2856 in the previous 90**, after the April 2026 peak of 1060 commits in a month. Monthly volume has settled between 779 and 938 since May. Authors are still growing (195 active in 90 days versus 156), so the plateau is not a shrinking team but a steady one producing at the same rate with more hands, which typically means more reviewers and smaller commits. The project is neither accelerating nor decelerating; it is running at the highest sustained rate in its history.

findings.title: Work mix now: restructuring and hardening replace bug-fixing, and the messages stopped saying 'fix'
findings.description: The script's commit-theme classifier shows `fix` falling from 23% of commits in the older half of the last year to 12% in the recent half, `feature` from 30% to 25%, `refactor` rising from 4% to 6%, `security` from 1.6% to 3.6%, `test` from 1.9% to 4.4%, and `other` rising from 25% to 42%. Reading the recent messages, the `other` growth is largely a **house style change**: 2026 commit titles are imperative verbs without conventional prefixes (`Harden`, `Restrict`, `Isolate`, `Trace`, `Consolidate`), so the classifier under-counts fixes and refactors. Reading them, the recent quarter is dominated by **hardening and restructuring**: plugin isolation, Guardian approval routing, exec-server tracing, MCP process cleanup, and crate extractions, with feature work concentrated in extensions and plugins. Feature work has not stopped, so this is a healthy maturing mix rather than a fixes-only drift.

findings.title: Direction: from a terminal agent to an extensible agent platform, with the risks that implies
findings.description: The facts above point one way. Activity moved from the TUI to the app-server and core; the last quarter's births are all platform machinery (`ext/`, `core-plugins`, `codex-mcp`, `features`, `state`); the top contributor's recent work is the extension registry and Guardian; and the README now offers the CLI, an IDE integration, a desktop app and a cloud agent as peers. Codex is **turning into an agent platform** whose terminal UI is one client. The trajectory implies three risks already visible in the history: the core keeps absorbing half of all commits while being decomposed (lifecycle), one young crate is single-owner (people), and a deprecated crate still ships (lifecycle). None is acute today; the sustained 90-day velocity and broad ownership of the emerging areas are the strongest positive signals.

findings.title: Codex is a local coding agent with four product surfaces around one engine
findings.description: Codex is OpenAI's **coding agent that runs on the developer's machine**: it takes a natural-language task, reads and edits the working tree, runs commands inside an OS sandbox, and asks for approval when a policy requires it. It is for developers working in a terminal, an IDE or the Codex desktop app, individually or under enterprise-managed configuration. One engine (`codex-core`: turns, tools, sandbox, approvals, persistence) is reached through **four surfaces**: the interactive terminal UI (`codex`), the headless runner (`codex exec` and `codex review`, also driven by the TypeScript and Python SDKs), the JSON-RPC **app server** behind the IDE extension, the desktop app and remote control, and a deprecated MCP server (`codex mcp-server`). Feature families at a glance: the agent session (prompting, approvals, sandbox, compaction); session lifecycle (resume, fork, archive, delete, queue, rename); extending the agent (MCP servers, plugins and marketplaces, skills, AGENTS.md, lifecycle hooks); multi-agent work (subagents, side conversations, the shared agents daemon); Codex Cloud tasks; accounts and login; maintenance (`doctor`, `update`, `features`, `completion`); and import from Claude Code. It is deliberately not a hosted service: the README points cloud users to **Codex Web** at chatgpt.com/codex, and this repository ships only the local binary, its SDKs and the protocol bindings. The software is obtained via an install script, npm (`@openai/codex`), Homebrew or GitHub release archives.

evidence.snippet: Codex CLI is a coding agent from OpenAI that runs locally on your computer.

evidence.note: root usage: bare prompt starts the TUI, subcommands select other surfaces

evidence.snippet: If you are looking for the cloud-based agent from OpenAI, Codex Web, go to chatgpt.com/codex.

attributes.audience: developers; enterprise admins via managed config

findings.title: The engine's capability set is defined by the tools it offers the model
findings.description: What Codex can *do* to a machine is exactly the tool list the engine registers for the model, so the tool registry is the most honest capability inventory. The first-party tools are: running commands (`shell_command`, and the unified-exec pair `exec_command`/`write_stdin` for long-running processes), editing files (`apply_patch`), planning (`update_plan`), asking the user a question (`request_user_input`), asking for more permissions (`request_permissions`), viewing images (`view_image`), web search (hosted `WebSearch` tool), calling MCP tools and reading MCP resources, requesting plugin installs, opening a fresh context window, and the multi-agent tools (`spawn_agent`, `send_input`, `wait_agent`, `close_agent`). Everything else a user experiences (review, compaction, cloud tasks) is orchestration around these tools. Which tools are present in a given turn depends on feature flags (for example `multi_agent`, `code_mode`) and on the model family, so the exact count varies per session; about **18 first-party tool names** are registered in the handler specs.

findings.title: CLI: 30 top-level subcommands (31 on macOS/Windows), 3 hidden, plus 2 hidden debug subcommands
findings.description: The `codex` binary is a clap multitool: with no subcommand the options are forwarded to the interactive TUI; otherwise one of **30 subcommands** in the `Subcommand` enum runs (`app` is compiled only on macOS and Windows, making 31 there). Visible: `agents`, `exec` (alias `e`), `review`, `login`, `logout`, `mcp`, `plugin`, `mcp-server`, `app-server`, `remote-control`, `app`, `completion`, `update`, `doctor`, `sandbox`, `debug`, `apply` (alias `a`), `resume`, `queue`, `archive`, `delete`, `migrate-rollouts`, `unarchive`, `fork`, `cloud` (alias `cloud-tasks`), `exec-server`, `features`. Hidden with `#[clap(hide = true)]`: `execpolicy`, `responses-api-proxy`, `stdio-to-uds`; inside `debug`: `trace-reduce` and `clear-memories`. Marked `[experimental]` in help: `app-server`, `remote-control`, `cloud`, `exec-server`. Global options that flow into every subcommand: `-c key=value` config overrides, `--enable`/`--disable <feature>` (validated against the feature registry), `--remote <ws://...|unix://>` to attach the TUI to a remote app server, and `--profile` for a v2 config profile. One-line behaviour for entries not covered by a feature finding: `completion` prints a shell completion script; `sandbox` runs an arbitrary command under the host sandbox (Seatbelt, Landlock or the Windows sandbox); `apply` git-applies the latest diff produced by a Codex agent task; `debug models`/`prompt-input`/`app-server send-message-v2` dump the model catalog, the model-visible prompt and drive the app server for diagnostics; `exec-server` runs the standalone sandboxed executor or registers it as a remote environment; `migrate-rollouts` inspects or migrates legacy session files into paginated thread history. In-repo help is the only documentation for this set: user docs redirect to developers.openai.com.

Visibility is decided per command: `/sandbox-add-read-dir` only on Windows, `/copy` not on Android, `/app` only on macOS and Windows, `/rollout` and `/test-approval` only in debug builds. findings.title: App server: 153 client-request methods (148 v2), 9 server requests, 75 notifications over stdio, unix socket or websocket
findings.description: `codex app-server` exposes the engine as JSON-RPC to IDEs, the desktop app and the SDKs; the same protocol is used in-process by the TUI. The request table is generated by the `client_request_definitions!` macro in `app-server-protocol`: **153 client-to-server methods**, of which 148 use the versioned v2 `family/verb` naming (`thread/start`, `turn/start`, `turn/steer`, `review/start`, `plugin/install`, `fs/readFile`, `command/exec`, `remoteControl/pairing/start`, `account/login/start`, ...) and 5 remain v1-era camelCase (`initialize`, `getConversationSummary`, `gitDiffToRemote`, `getAuthStatus`, `fuzzyFileSearch`). The server initiates **9 requests** back to the client (command and file-change approvals, permission and tool-call requests, MCP elicitation, token refresh, attestation, current time) and emits **75 notifications** (thread, turn and item lifecycle). Families by count: thread lifecycle and queue, projects and thread sections, plugins and marketplaces, skills and hooks, file system, realtime audio, MCP servers, accounts and usage, config and requirements, Windows sandbox, remote control, external-agent import, process and command execution. 59 method or field definitions carry an `#[experimental(...)]` marker and are omitted from generated TypeScript bindings unless `--experimental` is passed to `codex app-server generate-ts`. Transports: `stdio://` (default), `unix://`, `ws://IP:PORT` with bearer-token auth, or `off`; the app server can also run as a managed daemon (`codex app-server daemon start|stop|restart|bootstrap`).

findings.title: Configuration surface: a nine-layer config stack, requirements.toml, AGENTS.md, .rules, skills and hook declarations
findings.description: Behaviour is shaped by files more than by flags. `config.toml` is resolved through a **layer stack** whose precedence is fixed in `ConfigLayerSource`: packaged defaults, MDM-managed preferences, a system file, an enterprise cloud bundle, the user file (optionally with a named profile), the project's `.codex` folder, and session flags (`-c`, `--enable/--disable`); two legacy managed-config sources are still read. `requirements.toml` (system or MDM) pins what users may change and is the only place `allow_managed_hooks_only` works. Instruction files: `AGENTS.md` and a local `AGENTS.override.md` are discovered from the project root; skills are folders declared by a `SKILL.md` with frontmatter; plugins ship `hooks/hooks.json`; execpolicy `.rules` files classify commands. Configuration keys are consumed by the features that name them (`features.*`, `model_providers`, `mcp_servers`, `analytics.enabled`, `otel`, `hooks.state`); the schema is generated into `core/config.schema.json`. `/debug-config` in the TUI shows the resolved layers and requirement sources; `codex features list` shows the effective flag state.

findings.title: Interactive session: the TUI agent loop with approvals and sandbox
findings.description: Entry points: `codex [PROMPT]`, `codex resume`, `codex fork`, or `codex --remote ws://...` to attach to a remote app server. The user types a task (with `@file` mentions, `/ide` context, images); the engine runs a turn: the model calls tools, each command execution or patch passes the approval policy and then runs in the OS sandbox. Approval policy defaults to `on-request` (the model decides when to ask) with `untrusted`, `never` and fine-grained variants; the sandbox default is read-only, changed via `/permissions`, `--sandbox` or `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`. Outputs: streamed agent messages, diffs, command output cells; the transcript is persisted as a rollout after every item. On exit the CLI prints token usage and a `codex resume <id>` hint. Fails with a fatal message (exit code 1) when the engine reports an unrecoverable error; refuses to start outside a Git repository unless `--skip-git-repo-check`. Data owned: the terminal state file for `/theme`, `/keymap`, `/statusline` and `/title` preferences in config.

findings.title: `codex exec`: non-interactive runs with JSONL events, output schemas and ephemeral mode
findings.description: Entry point: `codex exec [PROMPT]` (alias `e`), with `exec resume` and `exec fork` to continue existing sessions; the SDKs and CI pipelines drive this surface. Inputs: the prompt as an argument or stdin (`-`), images, `--output-schema <json-schema>` to constrain the final message, `--last-message-file` to write the final answer, `-c` overrides. Behaviour: runs a full agent turn without a UI, approvals resolved by policy only. Output: human-readable event log by default; with `--json`, stdout is strict JSONL, one event per line. Switches: `--ephemeral` runs without persisting session files; `--ignore-user-config` skips `config.toml`; `--ignore-rules` skips execpolicy files; `--skip-git-repo-check` allows running outside a repository. Fails when the working directory is not a Git repository (unless skipped) or when the output does not match the schema.

findings.title: Code review: `codex review` and `/review` review uncommitted changes, a branch diff or a commit
findings.description: Entry points: `codex review` (a thin wrapper that runs `codex exec review`), `codex exec review`, `/review` in the TUI, and `review/start` on the app server. Inputs: `--uncommitted` (staged, unstaged and untracked changes), `--base <branch>`, `--commit <sha>` with optional `--commit-title`, and a custom instruction prompt (or stdin). Behaviour: builds a `ReviewRequest` for the chosen target, runs a dedicated review turn with the review prompt, and prints a summary hint describing what was reviewed. Output: findings as agent messages; in exec mode the same JSONL stream as any run. Fails when the target cannot be resolved (unknown branch or commit).

findings.title: Session lifecycle: resume, fork, archive, unarchive, delete, rename, queue and migrate
findings.description: Entry points: `codex resume|fork [SESSION_ID|name] [--last] [--all] [--include-non-interactive]`, `codex archive|unarchive|delete <SESSION>`, `codex queue <SESSION> <MESSAGE>`, `codex migrate-rollouts`, the TUI commands `/resume`, `/fork`, `/archive`, `/delete`, `/rename`, `/new`, and the `thread/*` API family (`thread/resume`, `thread/fork`, `thread/archive`, `thread/delete`, `thread/name/set`, `thread/queue/*`, `thread/list`, `thread/search`). Behaviour: `resume` opens a picker of sessions for the current directory (`--all` lifts the filter) and replays the rollout into a new turn; `fork` copies the thread into a new id; `archive` moves the rollout to `archived_sessions`; `delete` removes it and requires confirmation unless `--force` with a UUID; `queue` appends a message to a running session's queue; `migrate-rollouts` moves legacy session files into paginated thread history. Output: the TUI, or a one-line result for the CLI commands. Fails with `No sessions yet` in the picker when nothing was recorded, and `--force requires a session UUID` for named deletes.

findings.title: Context compaction: `/compact` and automatic summarisation when the context window fills
findings.description: Entry points: `/compact` in the TUI, `thread/compact/start` on the app server, and the engine's inline auto-compaction task that fires mid-turn when the context limit is approached. Behaviour: replaces the conversation history with a model-written summary; manual and pre-turn compaction inject the initial context again, mid-turn compaction keeps the summary as the last item because the model is trained to expect it there. Output: a compaction checkpoint recorded in the rollout; the user sees a notice and continues in the same thread. Related hooks: `PreCompact` and `PostCompact` lifecycle events fire around it.

findings.title: MCP client: configure external MCP servers whose tools and resources the agent can call
findings.description: Entry points: `codex mcp list|get|add|remove|login|logout`, `/mcp` (with `verbose`) in the TUI, `config/mcpServer/reload`, `mcpServerStatus/list`, `mcpServer/tool/call`, `mcpServer/resource/read` and `mcpServer/oauth/login` on the app server, and the `mcp_servers` table in `config.toml`. Inputs: a stdio launcher (command, args, env) or a streamable-HTTP URL with an optional bearer-token env var and OAuth client settings (`auto`, `cimd`, `dcr` registration strategies). Behaviour: each configured server is started or connected at session start; its tools are exposed to the model as `mcp__<server>__<tool>` function tools and its resources via `list_mcp_resources`/`read_mcp_resource`; tool calls pass the approval layer (auto-approved in Auto mode based on the server's annotations). Output: server status and tool lists in `/mcp` and `codex mcp list --json`. Fails per server: an unreachable server is reported and skipped, the session continues without its tools.

Inputs: a marketplace source (local path, `owner/repo[@ref]`, HTTPS or SSH Git URL, optional sparse-checkout paths) and a plugin reference `PLUGIN@MARKETPLACE`. Behaviour: marketplaces are snapshotted into the plugin cache; installing a plugin records it in config and materialises its skills, MCP server declarations, hooks (`hooks/hooks.json`) and app connectors; `upgrade` refreshes Git snapshots; the model can also ask to install one via the `request_plugin_install` tool. findings.title: Skills and AGENTS.md: project and user instructions that shape how the agent works

findings.title: Multi-agent: subagents, side conversations and the shared agents daemon
findings.description: Entry points: the model's `spawn_agent`, `send_input`, `wait_agent` and `close_agent` tools; `/subagents` to switch between a session's subagents; `/side` or `/btw` for an ephemeral fork side conversation; `codex agents` and `/agents` to browse every agent session on the shared local app-server daemon. Behaviour: a subagent is a child thread with its own turn loop and a role; the parent waits on or steers it; side conversations fork the thread and are discarded after. `codex agents` attaches to the daemon and refuses invocation-specific overrides (`-c`, `--model`, `--sandbox` ...) because shared sessions cannot carry per-invocation configuration; it is unavailable under workload identity and needs `--remote` on non-Unix platforms. Flags: `multi_agent` (stable, on), `multi_agent_v2` (stable, off by default).

findings.title: Workflow: first run to first completed task
findings.description: 1. Install via the install script, npm or Homebrew (README) and run `codex`. 2. Sign in: the TUI offers ChatGPT OAuth or an API key (feature `login-and-accounts`); nothing else works until credentials exist in `auth.json` or the keyring. 3. Open a Git repository: outside one the CLI refuses unless `--skip-git-repo-check`; the project trust level picks the approval default. 4. Optionally `/init` to create `AGENTS.md` (feature `skills-and-agents-md`). 5. Type a task; approve commands or patches as prompted (feature `interactive-agent-session`); state left behind is a rollout under `sessions/`, a row in the state database and `history.jsonl`. 6. Exit; the CLI prints token usage and `codex resume <id>` (feature `session-lifecycle`). Exceptional path: an unrecoverable engine error exits with code 1 and a session id for later resume.

Run `codex exec --json [--output-schema schema.json] [--ephemeral] "task"` or the SDK's equivalent (feature `headless-exec`); approvals are decided by policy, typically `--full-auto` or `--sandbox workspace-write`. 3. Consume the JSONL event stream or `--last-message-file`; with a schema the final message is validated JSON. 4. For reviews, `codex exec review --base main` in the pull-request job (feature `code-review`). 5. Optionally `codex exec resume <id> "follow-up"` to continue the same thread later. State left behind: a rollout unless `--ephemeral`; nothing else touches the repository except the agent's own edits. findings.title: Workflow: resuming, forking and cleaning up sessions
findings.description: 1. `codex resume` shows the picker for the current directory (`--all` for every directory, `--last` to skip the picker); `codex resume <id-or-name>` goes straight in (feature `session-lifecycle`). 2. To try an alternative without losing the original, `codex fork <id>` or `/fork` creates a new thread id from the same history. 3. When the context fills, `/compact` (or automatic compaction) summarises and continues (feature `context-compaction`). 4. Finished work: `codex archive <id>` moves the rollout to `archived_sessions`; `codex unarchive` reverses it; `codex delete <id>` removes it after confirmation. 5. Legacy session files from older versions are converted with `codex migrate-rollouts` before they show in paginated history. State: the rollout file and the SQLite state row move together; `history.jsonl` keeps prompt history across sessions. Exceptional path: `--force` deletion is only accepted for UUIDs so a name cannot delete the wrong session.

findings.title: Local state under $CODEX_HOME: config, credentials, sessions, state database, memories, shell snapshots, logs
findings.description: Everything Codex keeps lives under one directory (`CODEX_HOME`, default `~/.codex`). `config.toml` and `<profile>.config.toml`: user configuration (owner: configuration surface). `auth.json`: OAuth tokens or API key unless the keyring store mode is selected (owner: login). `sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/*.jsonl` and `archived_sessions/`: one rollout file per thread, one line per item (owner: session lifecycle); mirrored into `state_5.sqlite`, the SQLx-managed state database that also holds thread metadata, queues, projects and the local log database. `memories/`: generated memory files when the `memories` feature is enabled; `codex debug clear-memories` wipes them. `shell_snapshots/`: captured shell environments used to run commands (flag `shell_snapshot`). `log/`: the opt-in TUI log file; plugin caches and marketplace snapshots also live here. Lifecycle: rollouts persist until archived or deleted; `--ephemeral` skips them entirely; the state database is recreated on corruption by the recovery module.

findings.title: Data that leaves the machine: model requests, analytics metrics, feedback uploads, cloud tasks
findings.description: Model requests: every turn sends the prompt, instruction files, tool outputs and file contents the agent read to the configured provider (OpenAI by default; Bedrock, Ollama or LM Studio when configured). Analytics: in release builds with `analytics.enabled` true the OTel metrics exporter pushes to Statsig at `ab.chatgpt.com`; the TUI defaults analytics on, `codex app-server` defaults it off unless `--analytics-default-enabled` (the IDE passes it); `[analytics] enabled = false` opts out everywhere. Logs and traces are exported only when `otel` is configured; user prompts are redacted in logs by default. Feedback: `/feedback` uploads a Sentry envelope with a redacted in-memory log ring only when the user submits it. Cloud tasks: `codex cloud` sends task prompts and receives diffs from the ChatGPT backend. MCP servers and hooks receive tool arguments and event payloads by design.

findings.title: Model providers: OpenAI (ChatGPT or API key) by default, Amazon Bedrock, Ollama and LM Studio built in
findings.description: The built-in provider catalog contains `openai`, `amazon-bedrock`, `amazon-bedrock-runtime`, `ollama` and `lmstudio`; users add their own under `model_providers` in `config.toml` and select one with `--model`/`--oss` or per profile. Enables: running against ChatGPT plan quotas or an API key, AWS-hosted models (`account/bedrock/setup` walks through credentials), and fully local models over the Responses wire API on the Ollama or LM Studio port. When the provider is unreachable the turn fails with a provider error and the TUI's error classifier maps known messages to user guidance; there is no offline mode.

findings.title: Desktop app and IDE: `codex app`, `/app`, `/ide` and the app-server daemon
findings.description: The IDE extension and the desktop app are separate products that talk to this binary through the app server. `codex app [PATH]` (macOS and Windows only) opens the workspace in the desktop app and downloads the installer when it is missing; `/app` hands the current session over to it. `/ide` pulls the current selection and open files from a connected IDE into the prompt. `codex app-server daemon bootstrap` installs durable daemon management for SSH-driven use, and `codex app-server proxy` relays stdio to the control socket. When no app or IDE is connected these commands are inert: `/ide` adds nothing and `codex app` falls back to the installer download.

findings.title: 117 feature flags: 41 under development, 34 removed-but-accepted, only 1 in the /experimental menu
findings.description: The `FEATURES` registry in `codex-features` is the central switchboard: **117 entries** with stages `Stable` (38), `UnderDevelopment` (41), `Removed` (34), `Deprecated` (3) and `Experimental` (1). Any key, including under-development ones such as `code_mode`, `realtime_conversation`, `guardianv2` and `unified_exec_zsh_fork`, can be flipped by a user with `--enable <key>`, `codex features enable <key>` or `features.<key>` in config; the only guard is that the key must exist. The `/experimental` menu in the TUI lists only flags whose stage is `Experimental`, which today is just `network_proxy`, so the menu under-represents what the registry exposes. 34 removed keys are still parsed so old configs do not break; 3 deprecated keys (`web_search_request`, `web_search_cached`, one more) map to the newer `web_search` mode. Stable-but-off defaults worth knowing: `memories`, `multi_agent_v2`. Intent is clear from the stage doc comments, so this is filed as `low`: the gap is that no in-repo document explains the stages to users beyond `codex features list`.

evidence.note: menu filters on the Experimental stage

findings.recommendation: Document the stage vocabulary next to `codex features list` output and consider warning when an `UnderDevelopment` flag is enabled from the CLI.

findings.title: In-repo user docs are redirect stubs; the README leads with install and sign-in only
findings.description: `docs/getting-started.md`, `config.md`, `exec.md`, `slash_commands.md`, `sandbox.md`, `skills.md`, `agents_md.md`, `authentication.md`, `execpolicy.md` and `example-config.md` are three-line files pointing at developers.openai.com. `AGENTS.md` instructs contributors not to add user-facing documentation to `docs/`, so this is deliberate. The consequence for a reader of the repository: the functional surface described in this scan (30 subcommands, 58 slash commands, 153 API methods, 117 flags) is documented in-repo only through clap help strings, the slash-command `description()` table and the `codex-rs/docs` protocol notes, one of which (`protocol_v1.md`) warns that the code may not match it. Not a defect, but a due-diligence reader must treat help text as the manual.

findings.title: `/debug-m-drop` and `/debug-m-update` show in the release popup labelled `DO NOT USE`
findings.description: The `SlashCommand` enum ends with two debugging commands, `MemoryDrop` (`/debug-m-drop`) and `MemoryUpdate` (`/debug-m-update`), whose popup description is literally `DO NOT USE`. Unlike `/rollout` and `/test-approval`, they are not gated on `debug_assertions` in `is_visible()`, so they appear in release builds' popup for every user. The behaviour they trigger belongs to the memory pipeline that is off by default; a user who runs them without memories enabled gets a no-op or an error rather than harm, so severity is `low`.

findings.title: Memories: a stable feature that is off by default and reachable only via config or /memories
findings.description: The `memories` flag is `Stable` with `default_enabled: false`; the pipeline writes generated memories under `$CODEX_HOME/memories` and injects them into later sessions. It is switchable through `/memories` in the TUI, `thread/memoryMode/set` and `memory/reset` on the app server, and `features.memories` in config, and it is described in-repo only by the crate README. findings.title: Realtime voice conversation: six API methods shipped behind an under-development flag
findings.description: The app server registers `thread/realtime/start`, `appendAudio`, `appendText`, `appendSpeech`, `stop` and `listVoices`, and the engine has a realtime conversation path, but the `realtime_conversation` flag is `UnderDevelopment` and off by default. A client that discovers the methods from the generated schema (they are experimental-marked) can enable the flag with `--enable realtime_conversation` and reach unfinished behaviour; nothing in-repo describes the feature. Filed as `low` because the stage is explicit and the methods are marked experimental; confidence `likely` because the gating point was not traced into the handler.

findings.title: Eight environment-definition files, no provisioning IaC
findings.description: A direct filesystem glob (not the Sokrates index, which excludes `.github/`) finds **8 infrastructure files** and they are all *environment definitions*, never provisioning code. Three Dockerfiles: `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` (the arm64 contributor image), `.devcontainer/Dockerfile.secure` (the customer-oriented profile) and `.github/workflows/Dockerfile.bazel`. Two devcontainer manifests: `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` and `.devcontainer/devcontainer.secure.json`. Three Nix files: `flake.nix`, `flake.lock` and `codex-rs/default.nix`. There is **no Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, CDK, Kubernetes manifest, Helm chart, Kustomize overlay, Ansible playbook, docker-compose file, serverless config or Vagrantfile anywhere in the tree** — every one of those globs returns zero. This is the correct shape for the artifact: Codex is a CLI distributed as signed binaries and npm packages, so it has environments to *develop in*, not environments to *provision*. `tech-stack-scan` already records that Docker and Nix are in use; this scanner reads what those files declare.

findings.title: Nothing this repository runs could be rebuilt from it, and it does not need to be
findings.description: Asked the load-bearing question — *if this repository were the only thing left, what could be rebuilt?* — the answer is: **the developer environment, completely; the delivery infrastructure, not at all**. The release pipeline mutates named infrastructure that no file here declares. `publish_r2_release.py` writes into a Cloudflare R2 bucket hard-coded as `releases` under prefix `codex`; nothing creates that bucket, its lifecycle rules, or its public-read policy. Four GitHub deployment environments are referenced by name — `codex-r2-publisher`, `issue-triage`, `pypi` and `dev-website-vercel-deploy` — with their protection rules, reviewers and secrets living in GitHub settings, not in code. The full CI/release matrix requests **self-hosted runner groups by name** (`${{ github.event.repository.name }}-runners`, `…-linux-x64-xl`); no code here provisions those machines. The Azure Key Vault used for macOS and Windows code signing, the npm and PyPI registries, the WinGet repository, the Vercel project behind `developers.openai.com`, and the ChatGPT backend the CLI talks to are all consumed by name and declared nowhere. Nothing here builds or publishes any of the three container images either — `Dockerfile.bazel` in particular is referenced by **no workflow at all** (see `resources/container-images`). Crucially, **this team is not the owner of most of what is missing**: npm, PyPI, WinGet and the ChatGPT backend belong to other parties or other repositories, so their absence is a boundary, not a gap. The genuinely OpenAI-owned pieces that only exist as GitHub and Cloudflare console state are the R2 bucket, the four environments and the self-hosted runner fleet — those would have to be recreated from memory or from a private repository. Per the severity rule this stays `info`: a CLI that consumes hosted infrastructure is not its owner, and `cicd-scan` already owns the question of when these steps run.

evidence.note: the R2 bucket is a hard-coded name; nothing in the repo declares it

findings.title: Three single-stage images, all Ubuntu 24.04, none of them built by anything here
findings.description: All three Dockerfiles are **single-stage** — the script counts 3 `FROM` lines across 3 files — and all three land on Ubuntu 24.04. `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` is the contributor image: `ubuntu:24.04`, apt build deps plus musl and clang, then `USER ubuntu` before installing Rust into the user's home, `WORKDIR /workspace`, no `ENTRYPOINT`, no `CMD`, no `EXPOSE`, no `HEALTHCHECK` — it is a shell to work in, not a service. `.devcontainer/Dockerfile.secure` starts from `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu-24.04`, adds the firewall toolchain (`iptables`, `ipset`, `dnsutils`, `aggregate`), installs bubblewrap and marks it setuid (`chmod u+s /usr/bin/bwrap`), installs a lockfile-pinned Codex CLI, then drops to `USER vscode`. `.github/workflows/Dockerfile.bazel` is `ubuntu:24.04` plus dotslash, `USER ubuntu`. **Every image runs as a non-root user in its final stage** — `ubuntu`, `vscode`, `ubuntu` respectively — which is the single strongest declared property in this repository's infrastructure. The notable gap is that **nothing in the repository builds or publishes any of them**. A comment in `Dockerfile.bazel` says it was pushed by hand to a personal Docker Hub account, `docker.io/mbolin491/codex-bazel:latest`, with a `TODO` to move somewhere proper — and no workflow references the file or that image, so it is effectively dead weight whose only consumer would be someone running the buildx line in the comment. Separately, two CI jobs run *inside* stock images that no Dockerfile here produces: `rust-release-zsh.yml` sets `image: ubuntu:24.04` and `image: arm64v8/ubuntu:24.04` as job containers, installing build prerequisites as root at job time.

evidence.note: the CI image is hand-pushed to a personal registry namespace and referenced by no workflow

findings.title: Two devcontainer profiles that differ by an entire security model
findings.description: The two devcontainer manifests are not staging-and-production variants of one environment; they are **two different threat models** sharing a folder, and `.devcontainer/README.md` names the split: `devcontainer.json` is 'for working on this repository', `devcontainer.secure.json` is 'for running Codex inside a project container'. The contributor profile is 31 lines: build the local Dockerfile with context `..`, force `--platform=linux/arm64`, one dotslash feature, two env values (`RUST_BACKTRACE`, `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`), `remoteUser: ubuntu`. No mounts, no capabilities, no lifecycle scripts. The secure profile adds essentially everything else: 4 build args, 9 `runArgs` granting capabilities and unconfining seccomp/AppArmor, `init: true`, 7 named volume and bind mounts, **10 `containerEnv` values plus a `remoteEnv` that forwards the host's `OPENAI_API_KEY` into the container**, and two lifecycle hooks (`postCreateCommand` runs `post_install.py`, `postStartCommand` runs `post_start.sh`, which installs the iptables/ipset egress allowlist). The interesting property is the **egress allowlist as declared configuration**: `OPENAI_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` names 14 hosts (OpenAI API and auth, GitHub and its content CDNs, crates.io, static.rust-lang.org, npm, PyPI) and `init-firewall.sh` default-denies IPv6 outright so the allowlist cannot be bypassed over AAAA. Two things are worth flagging as declaration quality rather than risk. First, `containerEnv` sets **`CODEX_UNSAFE_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX: 1`, a variable that no code in the repository reads** — a grep of the entire tree finds exactly one occurrence, this line. It is either renamed-away or aspirational, and a reader would reasonably believe it disables Codex's sandbox when it does nothing. Second, the README documents a real residual hole in the profile's own words: the firewall does not filter DNS, so 'code from an untrusted repository can exfiltrate data through DNS'. That honesty is unusual and worth preserving. The `remoteEnv` API-key forward is the mechanism only; `configuration-scan` and `security-scan` own the credential itself.
findings.recommendation: Delete `CODEX_UNSAFE_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX` from `devcontainer.secure.json`, or restore the code that reads it. A security-relevant environment variable that no longer has a reader is worse than none, because it advertises a control that is not there.

evidence.note: the only occurrence of this name anywhere in the tree; no code reads it
host API key forwarded into the container by the manifest

evidence.snippet: The firewall does not apply its domain allowlist to DNS traffic, so code from an untrusted repository can exfiltrate data through DNS. This devcontainer does not provide secure DNS resolution. Use it only with trusted repositories. To mitigate DNS exfiltration, implement your own DNS filtering and restrict outbound DNS traffic to the filtered resolver; this does not make untrusted repositories safe because they can still exfiltrate data through allowed HTTPS destinations.
evidence.note: the profile documents its own residual exfiltration channel

findings.title: Nix flake pins its inputs by revision but its Rust toolchain by 'latest'
findings.description: The Nix flake is the third developer-environment mechanism and pins differently from the containers, so it gets its own finding. `flake.nix` declares two inputs — `nixpkgs` from the **`nixos-unstable` rolling channel** and `oxalica/rust-overlay` — across four systems (x86_64/aarch64 for Linux and Darwin). A rolling channel would be unreproducible on its own, but `flake.lock` pins both to exact commits (`nixpkgs` at `bfc1b8a…`, `rust-overlay` at `a1d32c9…`), so a checkout builds the same closure until someone runs `nix flake update`. The residual looseness is *inside* the pinned snapshot: both the package build and the dev shell take `pkgs.rust-bin.stable.latest`, so the Rust version is whatever the locked nixpkgs/rust-overlay pair happens to consider latest — **not the `1.95.0` that `Dockerfile.secure` pins, and not whatever `rust-toolchain.toml` pins for Cargo builds**. Three developer environments in this repository therefore agree on almost everything except the compiler version. `codex-rs/default.nix` is the actual derivation: `cargoLock.lockFile = ./Cargo.lock`, `doCheck = false`, and a `postPatch` that rewrites the placeholder `version = "0.0.0"` — the same version-stamping asymmetry `cicd-scan` found in the release flow, handled here explicitly.
findings.recommendation: Pin the Nix toolchain to the same version the other two environments use — read `rust-toolchain.toml` from the flake (`rust-bin.fromRustupToolchainFile`) instead of `stable.latest`, so all three developer paths compile with one compiler.

evidence.note: rolling channel as input, held steady only by flake.lock
toolchain resolved as 'latest' rather than the pinned 1.95.0
Rust dependencies are lockfile-pinned in the derivation

findings.title: The secure profile trades container isolation for an egress firewall, deliberately and in writing
findings.description: `devcontainer.secure.json` grants **seven Linux capabilities and unconfines both seccomp and AppArmor** in nine `runArgs` lines: `SYS_ADMIN`, `SYS_CHROOT`, `SETUID`, `SETGID`, `SYS_PTRACE`, `NET_ADMIN`, `NET_RAW`, plus `--security-opt=seccomp=unconfined` and `--security-opt=apparmor=unconfined`. Read naively this is the most alarming declaration in the repository — `SYS_ADMIN` with seccomp off is close to container escape. Read in context it is the opposite of careless. `.devcontainer/README.md` explains each grant: the profile 'disables Docker's outer seccomp and AppArmor profiles so bubblewrap can construct Codex's inner sandbox' and 'requires `NET_ADMIN` and `NET_RAW` so the firewall can be installed at startup'. The design is a **deliberate swap of outer isolation for inner isolation**: Docker's generic profile is relaxed so that Codex's own bubblewrap sandbox — the Linux backend `architecture-scan` documents, using `--unshare-user --unshare-net` — can build its namespaces as a non-root user, which is why `Dockerfile.secure` also marks bubblewrap setuid (`chmod u+s /usr/bin/bwrap`). The egress allowlist then constrains what the whole container can reach. Three things keep this at `low` rather than `medium`. The container is developer-facing and never deployed anywhere. The relaxation is confined to the *secure* profile — the default contributor profile has zero `runArgs` beyond `--platform`. And the reasoning is documented next to the declaration rather than discovered by a reader. The genuine residual is that these grants are unconditional: a developer who sets `CODEX_ENABLE_FIREWALL=0` (which `post-start.sh` honours, exiting early with 'Firewall mode: permissive') gets the relaxed container **without** the compensating egress control, and nothing in the manifest prevents that combination. The `vscode` user also has passwordless sudo from the Microsoft base image, which `post_install.py` and `post-start.sh` both rely on — so the non-root `USER vscode` is a smaller boundary than it looks.
findings.recommendation: Make the compensating control non-optional: have `post-start.sh` fail rather than warn when `CODEX_ENABLE_FIREWALL` is not `1`, so the capability grants and the egress allowlist can never be separated. Consider dropping `SYS_PTRACE` unless a debugger genuinely needs it in this profile — it is the one grant the README does not justify.

evidence.note: bubblewrap made setuid so the inner sandbox works for a non-root user

findings.title: Every image reference is a mutable tag; nothing is pinned by digest
findings.description: **Zero of the five image references in the repository are pinned by digest.** Three are base images in Dockerfiles: `ubuntu:24.04` twice and `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu-24.04` once. Two are CI job containers in `rust-release-zsh.yml`: `ubuntu:24.04` and `arm64v8/ubuntu:24.04`. All five are version tags rather than `:latest`, which is the better half of the spectrum — `ubuntu:24.04` moves only as the 24.04 LTS point releases advance — but a tag is still a mutable pointer the publisher can repoint, and none of these is verified by digest or signature at pull time. The contrast with the rest of this repository's supply-chain posture is stark and worth stating plainly: `cicd-scan` found **195 of 195** third-party GitHub Actions pinned to full commit SHAs; pnpm enforces a 7-day `minimumReleaseAge` and `blockExoticSubdeps`; uv sets a 7-day `exclude-newer`; Cargo dependencies are lockfile-pinned and audited by `cargo-deny`. Container images are the one dependency class that escaped that discipline entirely. This stays `low` rather than `medium` under the 'nothing publishes or deploys the artifact' rule: no workflow builds or pushes any of the three images, so the mutable base tags only affect developer machines and the two zsh-build CI jobs. **If the Bazel image were ever wired into CI as its `TODO` intends, this would become `medium`** — a repointed base tag would then silently change what builds release artifacts.
findings.recommendation: Pin the two `ubuntu:24.04` bases and the two zsh job containers by digest (`ubuntu:24.04@sha256:…`) with a renovate-style bot to advance them, matching the SHA-pinning rule already applied to every GitHub Action. The devcontainer base can follow the same pattern.

evidence.note: Microsoft-published base on a mutable tag
CI job container built by no Dockerfile here, also unpinned

findings.title: Three curl-pipe-shell installers and a :latest devcontainer feature inside otherwise locked-down builds
findings.description: Four places pull executable content from the network into an image without verifying it, in a repository that verifies almost everything else. Both devcontainer Dockerfiles install Rust with `curl -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh` — the canonical rustup bootstrap, TLS-protected but with no signature or checksum, and the `.secure` variant at least pins the resulting toolchain to `1.95.0`. `Dockerfile.secure` additionally pipes NodeSource's setup script straight into bash (`curl -fsSL "https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_${NODE_MAJOR}.x" | bash -`), which adds an apt repository and its signing key to the image on the strength of that one TLS connection. Both devcontainer manifests pull `ghcr.io/facebook/devcontainers/features/dotslash:latest` — **an explicitly mutable `:latest` tag on a third-party feature that executes at container build time**, the loosest reference in the repository. `Dockerfile.bazel` is the counter-example that shows the team knows how: it fetches dotslash from a **pinned release URL** (`v0.5.8`), not a rolling tag. The bright spot is the Codex CLI install path in `Dockerfile.secure`, which is genuinely well-provenanced: a dedicated `.devcontainer/codex-install/` boundary with its own lockfile, `corepack pnpm install --prod --frozen-lockfile`, a `pnpm-workspace.yaml` carrying `minimumReleaseAge: 10080` and `blockExoticSubdeps`, and a build-time assertion that the lockfile's `@openai/codex` version equals the `CODEX_NPM_VERSION` build arg. That is the standard the curl-pipes fall short of. Developer-scope keeps this `low`; the `:latest` feature is the piece most worth fixing because it is the only reference here that can change without anyone editing a file.
findings.recommendation: Pin the dotslash devcontainer feature to a released version instead of `:latest` in both manifests — it is a one-word change that removes the only silently-mutable dependency in the developer environments. For the shell installers, download to a file, verify a published checksum, then execute, as `Dockerfile.bazel` already does for dotslash.

evidence.note: third-party build-time feature on a mutable :latest tag
remote script piped to bash, adding an apt repo and key
the same tool fetched from a pinned release URL - the pattern the others should follow

findings.title: No secret reaches a build, but the whole repository is the build context with no .dockerignore
findings.description: The build-secret surface is clean and the build-context surface is not. Six `ARG`s exist across the two devcontainer Dockerfiles and **every one is a non-sensitive build parameter**: `DEBIAN_FRONTEND`, `TZ`, `NODE_MAJOR`, `RUST_TOOLCHAIN`, `CODEX_NPM_VERSION`. No credential is passed as a build arg, no `--mount=type=secret` is needed, and no `COPY` brings a key into an image — `Dockerfile.secure` copies only three named install files and three named scripts, never the tree. The context, however, is wide open. **There is no `.dockerignore` anywhere in the repository**, and both devcontainer manifests set `"context": ".."`, so the Docker daemon receives the entire checkout — roughly **61 MB across 6,400 files** in a clean clone, with `MODULE.bazel.lock` (1.5 MB), `.github/codex-cli-splash.png` (0.8 MB), a TUI test fixture (0.8 MB) and two app-server JSON schemas (1.2 MB together) as the largest items. Because nothing does a `COPY . .`, none of that reaches an image layer — the cost is transfer time on every rebuild, plus the fact that anything a developer happens to leave in their working tree (`.env` files, `personal/`, a `~/.codex` copy) is handed to the daemon. `.gitignore` covers those for git but a build context ignores `.gitignore` entirely. The README's manual `docker build ./.devcontainer` uses the small folder as context instead and is unaffected, which means **the two documented ways to build the same image disagree about the context** — a reader following the README sees none of this. This is `info`: no secret is exposed and no image is published, so it is a fact about the build, not a risk.

evidence.note: build context is the repository root; no .dockerignore exists to filter it
representative build arg - a version, not a credential
the documented manual build uses the .devcontainer folder as context, unlike the manifests

findings.title: Posture: complete developer environments, zero provisioning code, and one dependency class left out of an otherwise excellent supply chain
findings.description: **What could be rebuilt from this repository: the way Codex is developed. What could not: anything it is delivered through.** Three developer-environment mechanisms — a contributor devcontainer, a firewalled 'secure' devcontainer, and a Nix flake — are declared completely enough that a new contributor on Linux, macOS, x86 or arm can reproduce a working toolchain from a clean clone. That is the whole of the infrastructure code: **there is no Terraform, no Kubernetes, no Helm, no compose file, no CloudFormation, no Ansible anywhere in the tree**, and for a CLI shipped as signed binaries that is the right answer rather than a gap. The delivery side is entirely console state: a Cloudflare R2 bucket named `releases` in a Python script, four GitHub deployment environments, a self-hosted runner fleet requested by label, an Azure Key Vault for code signing, and registries owned by other parties. Most of that is not this team's to own, so `coverage` rates it `info` — but the R2 bucket, the environments and the runner group are OpenAI's and exist only as clicks. **Strongest declared property**: every one of the three images runs as a non-root user in its final stage, and the secure profile's relaxations are justified line by line in a README that also admits the residual DNS exfiltration channel it cannot close. Infrastructure that documents its own weaknesses is rarer than infrastructure that has none. **Weakest declared property**: pinning of pulled content. Five image references, none by digest; two devcontainer features on `:latest`; three `curl | sh` installers. This sits inside a repository where 195 of 195 GitHub Actions are SHA-pinned, pnpm enforces a release-age floor, and `cargo-deny` audits every crate — containers are simply the class that the discipline never reached. The three highest-leverage changes, in order: pin `ghcr.io/facebook/devcontainers/features/dotslash:latest` to a version in both manifests (`hardening/build-provenance` — the only reference here that can change with nobody editing a file); pin the Ubuntu bases and the two zsh CI job containers by digest (`hardening/image-pinning`); and delete the dead `CODEX_UNSAFE_ALLOW_NO_SANDBOX` variable that advertises a control the code no longer has (`environments/dev-environment`). One piece of housekeeping worth its own line: `.github/workflows/Dockerfile.bazel` is referenced by no workflow and carries a `TODO` about a personal Docker Hub account — either wire it up properly or remove it, because a build file nothing builds will rot silently.

evidence.note: the developer-environment story, which is the whole of this repository's IaC

findings.title: Modularity: weak - a DAG with a god crate on top and a vocabulary crate that ripples into every layer
findings.description: System grade **weak**. Sokrates extracted no component dependencies for this Rust workspace, so fan-in/fan-out and cycles come from architecture-scan's manifest graph rather than from `metric:` data; confidence is lowered accordingly. Driver 1: the manifest graph is acyclic in production builds, but `codex-core` depends on 61 of 133 crates and is depended on by 23, so the compile-time seam around the engine constrains almost nothing and most changes rebuild the whole engine. Driver 2: change impact travels through the protocol crate rather than through imports - 4389 of the 10000 co-change pairs Sokrates kept cross component boundaries (metric:temporal_coupling), and the four strongest cross-component pairs all have `codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs` on one side (141 shared commits with the TUI, 110 with app-server, 100 with the MCP server, 90 with core). Driver 3: the ext/* extension seam holds in one direction only - the traits are clean but ten of twelve extensions still link `core`. What keeps this off `poor`: the TUI genuinely does not link `core`, and no production cycle exists. Component grades sit in `attributes.components`: the protocol crate is `poor` because every field added there reaches 68 dependents at once; `auth`, `code-mode`, `sdk` and `repo tooling` are `strong` leaves with one or zero co-change partners.

findings.description: Sokrates' temporal coupling shows the protocol crate as the hub of shotgun surgery: `protocol.rs` co-changed 141 times with `tui/src/chatwidget.rs`, 110 with `app-server/src/bespoke_event_handling.rs`, 100 with `mcp-server/src/codex_tool_runner.rs` and 90 with `core/src/session/mod.rs` (metric:temporal_coupling). Reading tempers the top pair: since the March 2026 rewrite the TUI consumes `app-server-protocol` notifications and `chatwidget.rs` contains a single `EventMsg` reference, so the 141 shared commits mostly predate the current architecture; the live ripple for an `EventMsg` change today is `protocol.rs` -> `bespoke_event_handling.rs` -> the v2 `ServerNotification` enum -> the TUI's `app_server_events.rs`, plus `codex_tool_runner.rs` in the deprecated MCP server. findings.title: Reusability: adequate - 24 real leaf utility crates, but the vocabulary crate everyone reuses drags the proxy and policy engine with it
findings.description: System grade **adequate**. Driver 1 (positive): the workspace is deliberately split into small crates, and most of them are libraries in fact - 17 of the 24 `codex-rs/utils/*` crates depend on no other workspace crate or only on sibling utils, and `codex-protocol`, `app-server-protocol`, `apply-patch`, `execpolicy` and the SDKs each have more than one consumer. Driver 2 (negative): the most reused asset is trapped - `codex-protocol` (68 dependents) depends on `codex-network-proxy`, `codex-execpolicy` and `codex-http-client`, so nobody can reuse the vocabulary without compiling a TLS proxy; details in `reusability/trapped-protocol`. Driver 3: reuse by copy is small in volume - 302 of the 10000 duplicate blocks Sokrates kept span components, 12.9 percent duplication overall (metric:duplication) - but the pairs that exist are the hand-written parsers and fixtures a shared crate should own (`reusability/copy-instead-of-reuse`). Two further utilities point back at the product: `utils/oss` links `codex-core` and `utils/plugins` links `codex-exec-server`, which makes them engine adapters wearing a utils path. Component grades: `protocol` and `core` are `weak` (trapped or unreusable by design), `persistence`, `exec-server`, `model backends`, `configuration`, `auth`, `code-mode` and `sdk` are `strong` as crates with a manifest, a narrow API and external consumers.

findings.title: codex-protocol is the workspace's most reused asset and it cannot be reused without the proxy and the policy engine
findings.description: `codex-protocol` is the serde vocabulary 68 of 133 crates depend on and the one crate an external integrator would want on its own. Its manifest makes that impossible: it pulls `codex-network-proxy` (an HTTP and SOCKS5 proxy with a TLS stack), `codex-execpolicy` (the Starlark rule engine) and `codex-http-client`. architecture-scan documents the inversion; the maintainability cost is that the vocabulary crate has the **poorest modularity grade** in the workspace (every field added reaches every layer, and its four strongest co-change partners sit in four different components) while being the thinnest-tested one (testing-scan: ratio 0.08 path-based). The fix is mechanical and bounded - move `RequirementsExecPolicy`, `EnvironmentNetworkPolicy` and the `HttpError` wrapper behind a small trait or into a `protocol-policy` crate - which is why this earns `medium` rather than `low`.

Between `protocol/src/permissions.rs` and `windows-sandbox-rs/src/resolved_permissions.rs` the script counts 586 duplicated lines in 29-line blocks of `FileSystemSandboxEntry` construction, the reuse-by-copy signal between the vocabulary and the sandbox backend. Volume is low for the workspace (302 cross-component blocks), so this is a `low` finding with two concrete targets rather than a systemic one.

findings.title: Analysability: weak - the code is well named and the contributor guide is real, but the files a newcomer needs are huge, module docs are rare in the engine, and user docs live off-site
findings.description: System grade **weak**. Driver 1: size - 38 percent of main LOC sits in files over 1000 lines and 61 percent in files over 500 (metric:unit_size, script from files.json); the three files a typical change needs, `core/src/config/mod.rs` (3837 LOC), `protocol/src/protocol.rs` (3057) and `app-server/src/bespoke_event_handling.rs` (3937), are each a day's reading. Sokrates inflates this somewhat because it counts inline `#[cfg(test)]` modules (140k LOC per testing-scan) as main code, but the three files above are production code. Driver 2: documentation - the top-level `docs/` pages are three-line redirects by policy, the one substantive protocol document describes the v1 model that domain-language-scan shows is a generation behind, and the doc footprint of 32k lines (45 doc lines per kLOC, script) is mostly `README.md` per crate plus the 322-line `AGENTS.md`, which is the genuinely useful map. A grep of `//!` crate and module docs across the 2130 main Rust files (a reading count, not a Sokrates metric) finds them in 63 percent of TUI files but 9 percent of core and 7 percent of app-server files. Driver 3: naming and generations - `session` carries three meanings, `Conversation*` aliases survive as `#[deprecated]` re-exports in `core/src/lib.rs`, and v1 and v2 API modules, `compact_remote` and `compact_remote_v2`, `guardian` and `guardian-v2` all compile side by side, so a reader cannot tell the live path from the legacy one without git. What keeps this off `poor`: names inside the code are precise, hotspot units read as rule-per-branch logic (risk-synthesis), and `AGENTS.md` states the layering rules in plain words. findings.title: Modifiability: adequate - low logical complexity and a strong configuration surface, offset by three merge-magnet files and 33 percent single-owner files
findings.description: System grade **adequate**. Driver 1 (positive): logical complexity is low - only 2 percent of unit LOC sits in high or very-high McCabe units (script, on Sokrates' capped 10000-unit export), and risk-synthesis found the flagged units to be rule-per-branch validators rather than tangled logic. Driver 2 (positive): behaviour is configured, not hardcoded - a 117-entry feature-flag registry, a nine-layer config stack and generic `-c key=value` overrides mean many product changes are a flag flip (`modifiability/configurability`). Driver 3 (negative): change concentrates in a few central files that everyone edits - `core/src/config/mod.rs` with 81 contributors and 515 commits, `core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs`, `app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs` with 43 contributors (metric:commits, metric:contributors); `modifiability/hotspot-cluster-core-engine` covers the cluster. Driver 4: ownership - 33 percent of main files have a single contributor (metric:contributor_share, script), rising to 57 percent in persistence and 66 percent in code-mode, though project-level bus factor is healthy and the named single-owner areas are peripheral. Driver 5: duplication at 12.9 percent (metric:duplication) is mostly within components (302 of 10000 blocks cross them). Fix-vs-feature share is 18 percent fix, 25 percent feature, 5 percent refactor over all 9546 first lines (script keyword classification, 53 percent unclassified because 2026 titles use bare imperatives) - the script cannot split this per component, so the fix-heavy-areas driver is a data gap; evolution-scan reads the same messages as fixes falling from 23 to 12 percent. findings.title: Testability: adequate - the design's seams sit at process and provider boundaries, and the parts behind them are tested for real; the sandbox and the vocabulary are the exceptions
findings.description: System grade **adequate**. Driver 1 (positive): the design's seams are where the architecture puts its boundaries - `ExecBackend` in exec-server, `TimeProvider` and `AttestationProvider` in core, `AuthProvider` in codex-api, the JSON-RPC process boundaries - and testing-scan shows the engine is exercised through them with only the model faked (`wiremock` at `/v1/responses`), giving core a 2.16 test ratio and app-server 1.23. Driver 2 (negative): the same boundaries that make the engine testable make its lower layers hard to test in isolation: the sandboxing and policy component sits at 0.26 and its OS-level tests are platform-gated and self-skipping, and the protocol crate at 0.08 path-based is guarded only by serde round-trips, so a renamed variant is caught downstream by snapshots (both `weak`). Driver 3: global state is modest for 97k LOC of engine - 31 `static`/`OnceLock`/`LazyLock` sites in core, mostly caches and templates - but one is a test-mode global (`testability/global-state`), and 54 env mutations in tests need `serial_test`. Driver 4, rolled up by reference: 1320 `skip_if_*` macro sites report pass when they skip and nextest retries every test once, so a green run proves less than it appears to (testing-scan). Component grades follow testing-scan's ratios where the design does not contradict them: `core`, `app-server`, `extensibility`, `exec-server`, `auth`, `code-mode`, `sdk` are `strong`; `protocol`, `sandboxing`, `repo tooling` are `weak`.

findings.title: Global state in the engine: a test-mode switch baked into ThreadManager and process-wide caches
findings.description: Global mutable state is limited but two shapes work against isolation. `thread_manager.rs` carries `FORCE_TEST_THREAD_MANAGER_BEHAVIOR`, a process-wide `AtomicBool` that changes production code paths when tests set it - a test hook inside the object under test rather than an injected collaborator, and one that leaks between tests in the same binary. `connectors.rs` keeps `ACCESSIBLE_CONNECTORS_CACHE` as a `LazyLock<Mutex<Option<..>>>`, so connector availability is memoised per process and tests that need a different answer must reset or serialise. These are the patterns behind the 54 environment mutations and 25 `serial_test` files testing-scan counts; the engine's other statics are message templates and model presets. `low`: contained, named, and the integration harness already works around them.

findings.title: Maintainability posture: modularity weak, reusability adequate, analysability weak, modifiability adequate, testability adequate; the core engine costs the most; trajectory improving slowly
findings.description: **Modularity weak**: no production cycles and a TUI that cannot bypass the API, but a 61-crate-fan-out engine and a vocabulary crate whose changes ripple into four components. **Reusability adequate**: dozens of real leaf crates, one trapped crate (`protocol`) and a handful of copied parsers. **Analysability weak**: precise names and a good `AGENTS.md`, but 38 percent of main LOC in files over 1000 lines, few module docs in the engine, off-site user docs and two generations of API compiled side by side. **Modifiability adequate**: complexity is low and behaviour is configurable, but three engine files are merge magnets with 40-80 contributors each and a third of files have one owner. **Testability adequate**: seams at the right boundaries and an integration suite that runs the engine for real, with the sandbox and the vocabulary thin and a green run that can hide skips. The **costliest component is the core engine**: weak or poor on four of five sub-characteristics, 46 percent of recent commits, and the place the repo's own guidance says not to grow. **Trajectory: improving slowly** - evolution-scan shows a deliberate extraction programme (config, models, http-client, ext/* crates), a flat high-velocity plateau with a broadening team, and fix-share falling; the counter-signal is that core's share of activity has not dropped. Highest-leverage changes: cut the service-crate edges out of `codex-protocol` (`reusability/trapped-protocol`), break up the core config and tool-registry cluster along the extension seam (`modifiability/hotspot-cluster-core-engine`), and generate the v2 notification projection instead of hand-mirroring `EventMsg` (`modularity/cross-component-cochange`). Data gaps: Sokrates extracted no component dependencies for this Rust workspace, its unit, duplicate and co-change exports are capped at 10000 entries, and the commit-mix could not be split per component.

findings.title: Endpoint inventory: one model API by default, plus login, updates, telemetry and opt-in local or remote peers
findings.description: Codex is **both a client and a server**: it calls a model provider over HTTPS and serves JSON-RPC to front ends. On the default path the only outbound endpoint a turn needs is the **model API**: `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex` when signed in with ChatGPT, `https://api.openai.com/v1` when an API key is used, chosen by auth mode in `to_api_provider`. Around it sit auxiliary outbound endpoints: the ChatGPT backend for login token exchange, model catalog, cloud tasks and product analytics; `api.github.com` and the npm registry for the TUI update check; `ab.chatgpt.com` for Statsig metrics in release builds; Sentry only when the user submits feedback. Opt-in endpoints: Amazon Bedrock (`bedrock-mantle.us-east-1.api.aws`), local Ollama (`localhost:11434`) or LM Studio servers, user-configured MCP servers over streamable HTTP, and a remote-control relay on `chatgpt.com`. Inbound: the app-server listens on stdio by default and optionally on a unix socket or a WebSocket port; sign-in opens a short-lived loopback HTTP callback; the managed network proxy listens on loopback for sandboxed children. The full table is in `attributes`; siblings own what each integration does and the auth policy.

findings.title: Listeners: stdio by default; every TCP listener is loopback-only unless explicitly authenticated
findings.description: The app-server's `--listen` defaults to `stdio://`; `unix://` and `ws://IP:PORT` are opt-in. The WebSocket transport **refuses a non-loopback bind without auth**: `is_unauthenticated_non_loopback_listener` errors out unless `--ws-auth capability-token` or `signed-bearer-token` is given, and it exposes `/readyz` and `/healthz` routes. A unix control socket (`app-server-control.sock`) is created with restricted permissions for the daemon and IDE clients. The OAuth sign-in callback binds `127.0.0.1:1455` (fallback port if taken) but advertises `http://localhost:<port>/auth/callback`, so a browser resolving `localhost` to `::1` first must fall back to IPv4. The managed network proxy defaults to `127.0.0.1:3128` (HTTP) and `:8081` (SOCKS5) and **clamps any non-loopback bind back to 127.0.0.1** unless an override setting is set, logging it as DANGEROUS. Auth and trust for these listeners are security-design's domain.

findings.title: Model API: base URL chosen by auth mode, WebSocket transport preferred with session-scoped fallback to HTTPS
findings.description: The model endpoint is resolved per provider in `to_api_provider`: an explicit `base_url` wins, otherwise ChatGPT-family auth modes get the Codex backend and everything else gets `api.openai.com/v1`. Providers with `supports_websockets` open a **Responses-over-WebSocket** connection lazily and reuse it across turns, sending the beta header `responses_websockets=2026-02-06`; the connection attempt is bounded by `DEFAULT_WEBSOCKET_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s). Once retries are exhausted on WebSocket the session flips `disable_websockets` and uses HTTPS + SSE for the rest of the session (the policy is reliability's finding). Bedrock cannot combine with WebSockets (`validate` rejects it), so it is always HTTPS + SSE with SigV4. Request bodies to the Responses API can be **zstd-compressed**.

findings.title: Streaming as used: SSE with a per-event idle timeout, terminal events decide success, WebSocket reuses incremental payloads
findings.description: Model responses arrive as an SSE stream parsed by `codex-client::sse_stream`, which wraps every `stream.next()` in `tokio::time::timeout(idle_timeout)`; the default is `DEFAULT_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` (300 s), per provider via `stream_idle_timeout_ms`. The stream ends on `response.completed` (carrying token usage) or `response.failed`, which is turned into an `ApiError::Stream` and fed to the retry logic; a dropped connection without a terminal event is an idle timeout, not silent success. Over WebSocket the session keeps the last full request so following turns can send **incremental request payloads**; request compression is `zstd` when enabled. Ollama model pulls use the same streamed-response pattern until a success event or the server closes. The app-server side is JSON-RPC framed per transport (architecture owns the seam).

evidence.note: per-event idle timeout on the SSE reader

findings.title: MCP as used: stdio child processes and streamable-HTTP transports (plain, OAuth, access-token) through the shared HTTP client
findings.description: The `rmcp-client` crate wraps the `rmcp` SDK with three streamable-HTTP variants: `StreamableHttp`, `StreamableHttpWithOAuth` and `StreamableHttpWithAccessTokenOnly`, plus stdio for child-process servers. HTTP MCP traffic goes through a `StreamableHttpClientAdapter` over the workspace `HttpClient`, so proxy and CA handling match the model client; OAuth for MCP servers has its own token store and refresh transaction (the largest auth-header footprint in the count script). Startup and per-call timeouts for MCP servers are reliability's finding. Codex also serves MCP itself (`codex mcp-server`, deprecated) over stdio.

findings.title: One HttpClientFactory per config; clients are pooled per resolved proxy route (16 routes) and legacy builders are deprecated
findings.description: Product traffic is meant to enter through `HttpClientFactory::build_client` (fixed destination) or `RouteAwareClientPool` (varying URLs and redirects). The pool **reuses one reqwest client per resolved route** (`MAX_CACHED_ROUTES` = 16) so PAC or system-proxy decisions and connection reuse line up per destination; redirects are re-resolved hop by hop with sensitive headers stripped. A rustls sub-cache retries an origin with rustls when the platform TLS backend fails on a protocol-version error. Older entry points (`build_with_transport_default_proxy`, `*_with_custom_ca_fallback`) are `#[deprecated]` and documented as legacy-only, so **construction is converging but not uniform**: the doctor, Ollama client and analytics client build their own pools with their own connect or request timeouts. Cookies are kept only for the ChatGPT Cloudflare cookie store.

findings.title: No connect or total timeout on the default client; streams rely on the idle timeout, unary backend calls rely on the OS
findings.description: `HttpClientBuilder::default` sets `connect_timeout: None` and never sets a total request timeout; `connect_timeout` limits only connection establishment when a caller opts in. The model stream is protected by the 300 s idle timeout and WebSocket connects by 15 s (reliability's verdict). Unary calls on the ChatGPT backend (`backend-client`: models catalog, cloud tasks, usage) and the login token refresh construct `RouteAwareClientPool` **without a timeout**, so a black-holed TCP connect waits for the OS timeout (typically 60-130 s) before the retry/backoff sees an error. Where timeouts exist they are local: doctor probes 8 s, Ollama `OLLAMA_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT` on connect, analytics 10 s per post. Mitigation: every turn is interruptible and the calls are on an interactive path, so this is a slow failure, not a hang.

findings.recommendation: Give `HttpClientBuilder::default` a connect timeout (10-15 s, matching the WebSocket connect bound) and apply a per-request total timeout on unary backend calls, so unreachable hosts fail into the existing backoff instead of the OS connect timeout.

findings.title: TLS: platform roots plus an optional custom CA bundle from CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE or SSL_CERT_FILE; rustls fallback on Windows; no verification bypass
findings.description: Verification uses the platform native roots (`rustls_native_certs::load_native_certs`, errors logged but not fatal) with optional extra roots from `CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE`, falling back to `SSL_CERT_FILE`; empty values are unset, and the Codex-specific variable wins. The reqwest client uses the transport default TLS backend unless the builder selects rustls; a **schannel protocol-version error** on Windows triggers a one-off retry through rustls for that origin. Custom-CA parse errors fail construction on the modern path and fall back to system roots on the deprecated legacy path with a warning event. WebSocket connects share the same rustls config (`build_rustls_client_config_with_custom_ca`), including TLS-to-proxy. No `danger_accept_invalid_certs` or equivalent exists (security-scan's sweep); the count script's single `verify=False` hit is a **post-publish verification flag** in the R2 release script, not TLS. OTLP exporters add mutual TLS (observability's finding). `codex doctor` checks that the CA env vars point at readable files.
