findings.title: Proxy env vars work everywhere; PAC and system proxy exist but are behind an under-development feature flag
findings.description: Two proxy paths exist. With the default `OutboundProxyPolicy::ReqwestDefault`, reqwest and tokio-tungstenite read `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`ALL_PROXY`/`NO_PROXY` themselves. With `RespectSystemProxy` the `outbound_proxy` module resolves per request URL: platform PAC/WinHTTP or macOS SystemConfiguration lookups (serialised through a permit and cached), then env variables by scheme kind, then direct; `ws`/`wss` are mapped to their HTTP equivalents so one policy applies. That richer path is gated on `Feature::RespectSystemProxy`, whose stage is `UnderDevelopment`, so **corporate PAC-only networks do not work out of the box**; the doctor detects the situation and tells the user to ask an administrator to run `codex features enable respect_system_proxy`. Authenticated proxies are recognised (`407` maps to a `ProxyAuthenticationRequired` failure class) but the count script found no credential-broker for the outbound path beyond URL-embedded credentials. The inbound managed proxy for sandboxed children is a separate mechanism (security-design's egress finding).

evidence.snippet: "A macOS system proxy is configured but unused. If your organization requires it, ask your administrator whether to enable the under-development feature with `codex features enable respect_system_proxy`."

findings.recommendation: Promote `respect_system_proxy` past under-development (or default it on where a PAC/system proxy is detected and no env proxy is set); until then document the flag in the networking docs so enterprise users find it before the doctor does.

findings.title: Every request identifies itself: originator/version (OS arch) terminal user-agent, plus session-id, thread-id and subagent headers
findings.description: `get_codex_user_agent` builds `<originator>/<version> (<os> <os-version>; <arch>) <terminal>` from `os_info` and terminal detection, with an optional suffix and header-value sanitisation; the default originator is `codex_cli_rs`, overridable per process and per thread (`originator` header) for IDE and desktop front ends. Model requests add `session-id`, `thread-id`, `x-client-request-id` and, for sub-agents, `x-openai-subagent`. This is more than most CLIs send and is worth knowing when reading data-in-transit: the **OS version, architecture and terminal program** ride on every call, including update checks.

findings.title: Endpoints come from config.toml, not env vars: per-provider base_url, chatgpt_base_url, --listen; headers and keys come from env
findings.description: Precedence for the model endpoint is `model_providers.<id>.base_url` (config.toml) then the auth-mode default; there is **no `OPENAI_BASE_URL`-style environment override** in the Rust code (the count script's endpoint env hits are test servers, sample skills and the workload-identity token URL). Environment is used for secrets and headers instead: `env_key` names the API-key variable and `env_http_headers` maps header names to variables. The ChatGPT backend for login, models and cloud tasks is `chatgpt_base_url`; the remote-control relay URL is validated to `chatgpt.com`, `chatgpt-staging.com` or `localhost`. Inbound transports are flags: `--listen stdio://|unix://|ws://IP:PORT`, `--ws-auth`; the managed proxy ports are `network.proxy_url`/`socks_url`. Retry counts and timeouts are per provider (`request_max_retries`, `stream_max_retries`, `stream_idle_timeout_ms`, `websocket_connect_timeout_ms`). Enterprise requirement layers can pin some of these (security-design's managed-requirements finding).

findings.title: Self-hosting the model is a config change; ChatGPT-account features, update checks, Statsig and Sentry are pinned to OpenAI hosts
findings.description: An **air-gapped or self-hosted deployment is feasible for the model path**: any OpenAI-compatible Responses endpoint (Ollama, LM Studio, a gateway) can be the provider with `wire_api = "responses"`; the legacy chat wire API was removed. What cannot be repointed: the remote-control relay (host allowlist `chatgpt.com`/`chatgpt-staging.com`/`localhost`), the update check (`api.github.com` and the npm registry), the Statsig metrics endpoint and the Sentry DSN. In a blocked network these produce warnings or silent skips rather than failures: the update check is background and cached, metrics are lossy, feedback is manual. ChatGPT-login-only features (cloud tasks, plan quotas, models catalog) follow `chatgpt_base_url` and so can be pointed at a proxy but need the real backend behind it.

findings.title: Startup tolerates no network: the model catalog is fetched only if uncached, the update check is background, local providers are probed once
findings.description: Session start refreshes the model catalog with `RefreshStrategy::OnlineIfUncached` for root sessions and `Offline` for sub-agents; the catalog is cached in `models_cache.json` and bundled defaults exist, so a first run without network still gets a model list but a **cold first run** will attempt the fetch. The TUI update check reads the cache first and refreshes in a background task only when the last check is older than 20 h, explicitly so startup is not blocked. The Ollama/LM Studio providers **probe the server on construction** (`probe_server` with a connect timeout) and fail fast with a readable error if the daemon is not running. The first turn is the real network dependency: nothing is prefetched that would let a turn run offline.

findings.title: codex doctor is the only connectivity check: probes with an 8 s budget and classifies failures (TLS, proxy auth, PAC, timeout)
findings.description: There is no runtime connectivity check or offline mode; a turn simply fails after the retry budget with a provider error that the TUI classifier maps to guidance (functionality and reliability say the same). Diagnosis lives in `codex doctor`: the network check prints which proxy env vars are set, the macOS system proxy mode (PAC/manual/direct), whether `respect_system_proxy` and the managed proxy are on, and whether the CA env vars point at readable files. Probes run through the same route-aware pool with an **8 s budget** (5 s for PAC resolution plus 3 s HTTP) and map `RouteFailureClass` into plain sentences such as `TLS handshake or certificate validation failed` or `proxy authentication required (HTTP 407)`. findings.title: What crosses the wire per turn: prompt, instruction files and read file contents to the provider, tagged with session, thread, OS and terminal identity
findings.description: Functionality and security-design already list what leaves the machine as policy; the map here adds the envelope. Each model request carries the conversation input (user text, `AGENTS.md` and skill instructions, tool outputs including file contents the agent read, bounded per tool call) as a Responses API body, optionally zstd-compressed, with `session-id`, `thread-id`, `originator` and a user-agent naming OS version, architecture and terminal. Over WebSocket, later turns send incremental payloads rather than the full history. The ChatGPT backend additionally receives login tokens, analytics events (a bounded lossy queue) and cloud-task prompts; the update check sends only the user-agent; Sentry receives a redacted log ring only when the user submits feedback. Inbound trust: SSE events are deserialised into typed structs and the model's tool calls are treated as untrusted by the orchestrator (security-design's boundary map).

findings.title: Connectivity posture: one configurable model endpoint over HTTPS/SSE or WebSocket, loopback-only listeners, strong TLS and env-proxy story, weak PAC and timeout defaults, no offline mode
findings.description: **Endpoint map**: by default Codex talks to one host, `chatgpt.com` (ChatGPT login) or `api.openai.com` (API key), plus background `api.github.com` update checks and `ab.chatgpt.com` metrics in release builds; Bedrock, local Ollama/LM Studio, HTTP MCP servers and the remote-control relay are opt-in. **Listeners** are stdio by default and every TCP listener is loopback-only unless authenticated. **Strongest handling**: the route-aware client pool with per-route reuse, custom CA via `CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE`/`SSL_CERT_FILE` on top of platform roots, a rustls fallback for Windows TLS quirks, and a doctor that names TLS, proxy and PAC failures. **Weakest**: system/PAC proxy support is behind an under-development flag, and the default HTTP client has no connect or total timeout, so unreachable backends fail via the OS rather than by design. **Offline**: startup works, the first turn does not; there is no cached or degraded mode, only clear errors. **Deployability**: proxies via env vars yes, PAC after enabling a flag, air-gapped only with a self-hosted Responses-compatible provider and without ChatGPT-account features. Highest-leverage changes: `finding:network-scan/connection-management/proxy-support`, `finding:network-scan/connection-management/timeouts`, and documenting the endpoint table from `finding:network-scan/topology/endpoints` for enterprise allowlists.

findings.title: Panic hooks restore the terminal and forward panics to tracing without swallowing default reports
findings.description: The TUI installs chained panic hooks: one restores the terminal and re-emits the panic through tracing::error! before delegating to the previous (color-eyre) hook so users still get a full backtrace, and a second in tui.rs restores the terminal on panic while explicitly ignoring restore errors. Telemetry initialization itself is wrapped in catch_unwind in both the TUI and exec entry points, so a panicking OTel provider degrades to 'no telemetry' instead of crashing the app - the observer cannot take down the observed.

findings.title: Sentry is used only for user-initiated feedback envelopes; no automatic crash reporting
findings.description: There is no sentry::init call anywhere in the workspace - the Sentry SDK is used purely as an envelope builder/uploader inside the feedback crate. findings.title: Metrics default to a Statsig exporter: OTLP-HTTP to ab.chatgpt.com with an embedded client key, release builds only
findings.description: While log and trace exporters default to None, otel.metrics_exporter defaults to Statsig, which resolves to an OTLP-HTTP/JSON push to https://ab.chatgpt.com/otlp/v1/metrics authenticated with a client API key embedded in the source. The default is disabled in debug builds and gated at runtime on analytics_enabled (the TUI passes default_analytics_enabled=true), so a stock release install with analytics on sends usage/performance metrics to OpenAI by default. Mitigations are real: only sanitized low-cardinality metric data is sent (no prompts or log content), and a curated STATSIG_DISABLED_METRICS list keeps token-usage, API-call and tool-call metrics off the built-in route while still delivering them to any user-configured OTLP exporter. Worth flagging because 'metrics on by default to the vendor' is a posture users and enterprises will want to know about and how to opt out of (analytics_enabled=false or metrics_exporter='none').

findings.title: Blind spots: a default install is nearly dark locally, and the SDK/JS surfaces emit nothing
findings.description: Several failure modes are invisible today. (1) A default install gives the local user almost no signals: file logging requires configuring log_dir, exec's stderr filter is 'error', and the metrics that do flow by default go to OpenAI's Statsig endpoint - not anywhere the user can see - so 'why is my Codex slow/failing' is answerable only via opt-in logs, the SQLite log db, or codex doctor. (2) Crash visibility is consent-bound: with no automatic crash reporter, panics that users do not report leave no operator-side trace. (3) The TypeScript SDK sources contain no logging or telemetry calls at all, and the thin npm/python wrappers likewise emit nothing, so integrations built on the SDKs are dark unless the spawned Rust binary's telemetry is configured. (4) Anything OpenAI might want to alert on fleet-wide beyond the curated Statsig metric slice (e.g. API error rates, which are on the disabled list) is structurally unavailable from the default pipeline.

findings.title: Cost scales per turn with history items, sampling steps and tool calls, not with repository size
findings.description: Codex is an **interactive agent runtime**: the unit of work is a turn, and a turn is a loop of sampling steps. Each step sends the whole conversation history to the model, streams the response back, dispatches the tool calls it contains and loops until the model stops calling tools. The scaling factors are therefore **history items × sampling steps per turn** (the prompt is rebuilt from the full history every step), **stream events per step** (one channel send and one JSON parse each), **tool calls per step** (one spawned task each, gated for parallelism) and **rollout lines per session** (one JSONL append per persisted item). Startup scales with the number of configured MCP servers and AGENTS.md ancestor directories; session listing scales with the number of rollout files in `CODEX_HOME/sessions`. Nothing scales with repository size except the on-demand fuzzy file search. The static reading below covers the engine turn path (`codex-core`), the model client, the rollout writer and reader, the TUI render path and the MCP startup path; no profiler was run.

evidence.note: turn loop: one iteration per sampling step
stream loop: one iteration per response event
tool results drained in order before the next step

findings.title: Main loop: turn -> sampling step -> streamed response -> gated tool tasks -> drain -> next step
findings.description: The turn loop in `run_turn` drains pending user input, captures a fresh `StepContext` (tool router, MCP binding, environment) and rebuilds the prompt from the full history. `try_run_sampling_request` then consumes the response stream event by event; each `OutputItemDone` that is a tool call becomes a spawned task pushed into a `FuturesOrdered`, and `drain_in_flight` waits for all of them before the step ends. The loop repeats until a step produces no tool calls. Per-step work is all **O(history)** and per-event work is **O(1)** plus one channel hop, so the latency budget of a turn is dominated by network round trips and tool execution, not by engine CPU.

evidence.note: prompt rebuilt from full history each step

findings.title: Currency is per-turn latency (time to first token, tool dispatch wait) and a memory footprint bounded by the context window
findings.description: For an interactive runtime the currency is **latency**, and the code measures the part it cares about: `record_turn_ttft_metric` stamps time-to-first-token on every stream event, and tool calls carry a timing guard that separates dispatch wait from execution. The TUI renders at a fixed **120 Hz cap** (`MIN_FRAME_INTERVAL` 8.33 ms), so render cost matters only when a frame exceeds that budget. **Memory** is a secondary currency: the in-memory history is bounded by auto-compaction against the model context window, and tool output is capped, so steady-state RSS is proportional to the context window plus the TUI transcript. **Startup time** matters once per session (MCP server spawn, AGENTS.md discovery, websocket prewarm). Throughput is not a concern: one session runs one turn at a time.

findings.title: Every sampling step clones, normalizes and re-estimates the entire conversation history
findings.description: Each iteration of the turn loop calls `sess.clone_history()` and `for_prompt`, which does `Arc::unwrap_or_clone(self.items)` - a **deep copy of every `ResponseItem`** in the history (the `Arc` is shared with session state, so the clone is never elided) - then runs four normalization passes over the copy. Independently, `get_total_token_usage` and `estimate_token_count` iterate all items to sum byte-based token estimates, and they are called at least once per step for the auto-compaction check plus from compaction paths. Cost is **O(history items × sampling steps)** per turn, with each item carrying its full text payload (tool outputs up to the truncation policy). History is bounded by the context window (roughly hundreds of items, a few hundred KB), so this is a linear pass with a large constant rather than a super-linear path; a 20-step agentic turn copies the transcript 20 times. Static reading only; not measured.
findings.recommendation: Keep a running token estimate updated in `record_items` instead of re-summing all items, and build the prompt from a borrowed or `Arc`-shared normalized snapshot that is invalidated on `history_version` change rather than deep-cloning per step.

findings.title: Tool router and MCP tool exposure are rebuilt for every sampling step, not once per turn
findings.description: `capture_step_context` runs inside the turn loop, and it calls `built_tools`, which assembles the tool registry, applies the MCP exposure policy over all MCP tools, resolves tool-suggest candidates and builds the model-visible specs. For a turn with N sampling steps this is N full rebuilds of a structure that changes rarely within a turn (it exists per step so mid-turn MCP refreshes and plugin selection are picked up). Cost is **O(tools × steps)**; with a few dozen tools it is small, with many MCP servers exposing hundreds of tools with schemas capped at 512 KiB per namespace it becomes real allocation churn per step. Static reading; the design trade-off (freshness per step) is deliberate.
findings.recommendation: Cache the built `ToolRouter` keyed on the MCP binding generation and selected-plugin snapshot so consecutive steps without a refresh reuse it.

findings.title: Hook matchers compile their regex on every hook event evaluation
findings.description: `matches_matcher` in the hooks engine calls `regex::Regex::new(matcher)` each time a hook's matcher is tested against an input, so a regex matcher is compiled once per hook × per event (tool call, turn start, ...). The pattern is validated at config load, but the compiled form is not kept. Off the model round-trip path and with small hook counts the cost is microseconds per event; it only matters with many regex matchers and many tool calls. The other non-static `Regex::new` sites in the workspace are one-shot (config validation, seatbelt log parsing, search-term escaping) or already behind `LazyLock`/`OnceLock` (markdown link suffixes, SSE rate-limit parsing).

evidence.note: validated at load, compiled form discarded

findings.recommendation: Compile the matcher once when the hook config is loaded and store the `Regex` alongside the hook definition.

findings.title: Well-chosen structures on the hot path: prefix-diffed websocket requests, ordered tool futures, hashed MCP call lookup
findings.description: The model client keeps the last request and diffs the new input against it item by item so a reused websocket sends **only the incremental items** (`get_incremental_items`), a linear prefix compare that avoids resending the whole history; the equality check clones both items only when they differ on metadata. Tool results are collected in a `FuturesOrdered` so completion order does not reorder the transcript. MCP tool dispatch looks calls up in a `HashMap` keyed by (server, tool) - correct choice, though each lookup allocates two `String`s for the key. Thread listing sorts lightweight candidates rather than parsed items. Nothing on the per-turn path is a linear search inside a loop over the same collection.

evidence.note: clone only on the metadata-mismatch branch

findings.title: Rollouts are read line by line; listing reads only the first 10 records per file and scans indexes from the end in 64 KiB chunks
findings.description: Resume (`load_rollout_items`) streams the JSONL transcript through an async line reader and parses one `serde_json::Value` per line, so memory during resume is one line plus the accumulated items rather than the whole file. Session listing calls `read_head_summary` with `HEAD_RECORD_LIMIT` 10 so each candidate file costs one small read, and the session-name index is scanned from the end with a `ReverseJsonlScanner` in 64 KiB chunks on a blocking thread. Compressed (zstd) rollouts are decoded through `spawn_blocking`. Model responses are parsed per SSE event with `serde_json::from_str`. These are the streaming choices one wants; the only whole-input read on a per-turn path is the `Value` round trip per rollout line (parse to `Value`, inspect, then deserialize), which doubles parse work on resume of long transcripts.

findings.title: The rollout writer is a single background task that writes one line per item and flushes after every batch
findings.description: Persistence goes through an mpsc channel to one `rollout_writer` task, which appends items to `pending_items` and calls `flush_if_materialized` on every `AddItems` command. `write_pending_items_once` then serializes and writes **one line per item** through an unbuffered `tokio::fs::File` and flushes once per batch - so a step that persists k items costs k write syscalls plus one flush, and per-turn persistence is serialized behind that single task. The transcript is never fsynced (reliability-scan owns that trade-off). For interactive turns this is a handful of small writes per step; it becomes visible only when many items land at once (large tool outputs are truncated first, so line size is bounded by the truncation policy). Deliberately streaming rather than build-then-write.

findings.title: Engine memory is the compaction-bounded history; TUI memory is an unbounded transcript of rendered cells
findings.description: The engine holds the conversation as `Arc<Vec<ResponseItemEnvelope>>` inside session state; it grows per step until `context_window_token_status` triggers auto-compaction, so peak engine memory is **proportional to the model context window** (plus the per-step deep copy described under `repeated-work-prompt-build`). The TUI keeps every history cell for the session in `transcript_cells: Vec<Arc<dyn HistoryCell>>`; markdown cells keep their raw source plus a one-entry render cache of wrapped lines for the current width, so TUI memory grows **linearly with session length** and is never trimmed - a very long session accumulates every rendered message and tool output cell. The model stream is buffered by a bounded channel of 1,600 events; the mapping task additionally keeps `items_added` (a clone of every output item) for websocket reuse and trace recording, duplicating one response's items in memory for the life of the step.

evidence.note: second copy of each output item

findings.title: Parallel where it pays: gated concurrent tool tasks, JoinSet MCP startup, 256-wide AGENTS.md probes, prewarmed websocket, threaded file search
findings.description: Tool calls run as spawned tasks admitted through a `RwLock` gate: tools that declare parallel support take the read lock and run concurrently; the response stream keeps being consumed while they run. MCP servers are started in a `JoinSet` with a `LazyWhenCached` policy that reuses cached tool lists instead of blocking startup. AGENTS.md discovery probes ancestor directories with `buffered(256)`. Session startup schedules a prewarm that preconnects the websocket and warms auth so the first turn skips connection setup. The fuzzy file search runs a walker thread feeding a `nucleo` matcher on 2 threads. Rollout compression runs at most 2 blocking jobs. These are the deliberate optimizations a re-run should diff against.

evidence.note: parallel tools share the read lock

findings.title: Serial by design: non-parallel tools take a write lock that drains all other tools, and each step waits for every tool before sampling again
findings.description: Any tool that does not declare parallel support acquires the **write side** of the parallel-execution `RwLock`, which waits for all in-flight parallel tools to finish and blocks new ones until it completes - one slow shell command serializes the step. After the stream ends, `drain_in_flight` awaits every tool result in order before the next sampling request is sent, so the step latency is the **max of tool latencies plus the model round trip**, never overlapped with the next request (the Responses API requires the outputs first, so this is inherent). Persistence is a single writer task. The scaling factor is tool calls per step × tool latency; for shell-heavy turns the write-locked shell tool is the bottleneck, which is a correctness choice (sandbox and cwd state) rather than an oversight.

evidence.note: all tools drained before the next step

findings.recommendation: Mark read-only tools (file read, grep-like, list) as parallel-capable where they are not already, so a shell command does not exclude them; the drain-before-next-step is protocol-bound and should stay.

findings.title: Blocking work is moved off the runtime with spawn_blocking; the remaining std locks on the hot path are short and uncontended
findings.description: Filesystem-heavy work is consistently wrapped: zstd materialization and decoding of rollouts, the reverse session-index scans, plugin store install/uninstall and Windows sandbox setup all use `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`. No `block_on` or `block_in_place` exists in `codex-core`, the rollout crate or the TUI event loop. `std::sync::Mutex` is used for tiny flags in the websocket session (`connection_reused`) and the TUI render cache; the session state itself is a `tokio::sync::Mutex` taken briefly for history clones and token estimates. Grep counted 72 `spawn_blocking`/`block_on` sites workspace-wide outside tests, none of which is a blocking call inside an async hot path.

evidence.note: short std lock on the client

findings.title: Session state is one tokio Mutex taken on every step for history clone, token estimate and compaction checks
findings.description: `Session.state` guards the history, token info and turn bookkeeping. Per step it is locked for `clone_history` (deep copy under the lock), for `get_total_token_usage` (full-item iteration under the lock) and again by event handlers that record items. Because one session runs one turn at a time, contention is between the turn task and app-server request handlers reading state, not between turns; the cost is the critical-section length, which is proportional to history size. Not a serialization point today; flagged so the deep copy under the lock is not forgotten when multi-agent sub-sessions share a process.

findings.title: Caches that exist: reused websocket with incremental input, lazy MCP tool lists, one-width markdown render cache, streaming prefix cache, static regexes
findings.description: The model client caches the last request and its response items so a reused websocket sends only new items. The MCP connection manager reuses previously started servers and cached tool lists under `LazyWhenCached`. The TUI caches each finalized markdown cell's rendered lines for the current width, theme and palette (single entry, replaced on change) and the streaming controller caches the rendered line count of the stable prefix so table detection does not re-render the prefix per delta. Regexes on render and SSE paths are `LazyLock`/`OnceLock`. The one intentional non-cache: `finalize_remaining` re-renders the whole message from raw source once at the end of each stream so the transcript is canonical. Missing caches are the prompt snapshot and tool router described under `algorithms-and-data`.

evidence.note: render cache hit (still clones the lines)

caches: markdown render cache (1 entry per cell)

findings.title: Listing sessions by updated_at re-walks and re-sorts the whole rollout tree on every page
findings.description: When the SQLite state DB is unavailable and the filesystem fallback is used with `ThreadSortKey::UpdatedAt`, `traverse_directories_for_paths_updated` collects **every rollout file** under `sessions/` (one `metadata` call each), sorts all candidates, then skips to the cursor - so page k costs a full walk and O(N log N) sort again, capped at `MAX_SCAN_FILES` 10,000. The created_at sort avoids this because directory names encode the date and the walk breaks once the page fills. The primary path (state DB) has covering indexes on `(archived, cwd, updated_at_ms DESC, id DESC)`, so this only bites users without the index. Per-page cost is bounded by the 10k cap; with thousands of sessions the resume picker's fallback path is the slowest I/O in the TUI.

evidence.snippet: CREATE INDEX idx_threads_archived_cwd_updated_at_ms ON threads(archived, cwd, updated_at_ms DESC, id DESC);

findings.recommendation: Cache the sorted candidate list for the duration of a listing session (cursor carries a generation) or rely on the state DB and drop updated_at sorting from the filesystem fallback.

findings.title: Cost caps are pervasive: output bytes and delta counts per exec, token budgets for compaction, MCP spec bytes, listing scan cap, bounded channels
findings.description: Shell output is retained up to `DEFAULT_OUTPUT_BYTES_CAP` with `append_capped`, read in 8 KiB chunks, and live deltas are capped at 10,000 per call while the reader keeps draining to EOF to avoid back-pressure on the child. Compaction has explicit token budgets (20k for the compacted user message, 64k retained budget in remote v2). MCP namespaces are capped at 512 KiB of description, executed tool-call args at 8 KiB with 256 pending. Session listing stops at 10,000 files; the response stream channel holds 1,600 events; realtime context has per-section token budgets. These caps mean no single tool call, model response or session directory can dominate memory. There is no sampling and no skip-if-over-N switch because there is no batch stage to skip.

findings.title: No bound on the TUI transcript or on total in-flight tool tasks per step
findings.description: Two growth paths have no cap: the TUI `transcript_cells` vector (every cell of the session, with its rendered lines) and the number of tool tasks spawned per step (one per tool call in the response; the model decides how many). The engine-side history is bounded by compaction and each tool's output is bounded, so both are linear in session length and in model behaviour respectively, not in input size. The exec delta cap and the pending executed-tool-calls cap show the pattern the codebase uses elsewhere; a transcript cap (or off-screen cell eviction) is the one missing sibling.
findings.recommendation: Evict or collapse cells beyond a configurable transcript length in very long sessions; keep the raw source so scroll-back can re-render on demand.

findings.title: Posture: a latency-bound runtime whose engine work is linear in history per step; the plausible bottlenecks are per-step transcript copies, serialized non-parallel tools and the filesystem listing fallback
findings.description: Codex's cost rides on **history items × sampling steps** and **tool latency per step**, and its engine does nothing super-linear on that path: the stream is consumed event by event, tool calls run as concurrent tasks, persistence is a single streaming writer, outputs are capped and history is compacted. Ranked likely bottlenecks, static reading only: (1) `algorithms-and-data/repeated-work-prompt-build` - the full transcript is deep-copied, normalized and token-estimated every step; (2) `concurrency/serial-stages` - a non-parallel tool takes the exclusive gate and every step waits for all tools before the next request; (3) `algorithms-and-data/repeated-work-step-context` - the tool router and MCP exposure are rebuilt per step; (4) `caching-and-reuse/recomputation-thread-listing` - the updated_at filesystem fallback walks and sorts all sessions per page; (5) `limits-and-safeguards/missing-limits` - the TUI transcript grows without bound. What grows without bound: TUI transcript cells (session length). Where parallelism would pay: marking read-only tools parallel-capable. Highest-leverage changes: a version-keyed prompt snapshot and running token estimate, parallel-capable read-only tools, and a cached tool router per MCP generation. Nothing found justifies `medium` or above; the runtime's dominant latency is the model round trip, which the code cannot shorten.

findings.title: One central error type (`CodexErr`) with a classified taxonomy
findings.description: Almost every fallible path in `codex-core` and its frontends returns `codex_protocol::error::Result<T>`, whose error is the `CodexErr` struct wrapping a `CodexErrorDetails` enum. The enum is a **classified taxonomy**, not a bag of strings: transient stream failures (`Stream`, `ConnectionFailed`, `ServerOverloaded`), hard limits (`ContextWindowExceeded`, `UsageLimitReached`, `QuotaExceeded`), lifecycle outcomes (`TurnAborted`, `Interrupted`, `InternalAgentDied`), sandbox failures (`SandboxErr` with `Denied`, `Timeout`, `Signal`) and a `Fatal(String)` escape. Every variant carries a **user-facing message** via `thiserror`, and the wrapper carries an optional `retry_delay` so a server-supplied `Retry-After` travels with the error to the retry loop. `From` conversions absorb `io::Error`, `serde_json::Error`, `JoinError` and Landlock errors, so `?` works everywhere without losing the category. A `strum` discriminant (`CodexErrKind`) gives analytics a payload-free category. Sub-crates outside core (`rmcp-client`, `core-plugins`) use `anyhow` or their own `thiserror` enums and convert at the core boundary.

evidence.note: the variant the retry loop treats as transient
task panics/cancellations convert into the same type

findings.title: Workspace lint denies `expect`/`unwrap` outside tests
findings.description: The Cargo workspace sets `expect_used = "deny"` in `[workspace.lints.clippy]` and `clippy.toml` grants `allow-unwrap-in-tests` / `allow-expect-in-tests`, so the **error model is enforced by the linter** rather than by convention. The effect is visible in the counts: after excluding `#[cfg(test)]` modules, `*_tests.rs`, `tests/` and `*_tests/` directories, the 700k-line workspace has only **55 `.unwrap()` and 40 `.expect("..")` call sites**, and `codex-core` itself has none. `panic!` (175) and `unreachable!` (95) remain available and are used for invariant checks, mostly in Windows PTY/sandbox code and TUI rendering. `result_large_err` is raised to 256 bytes to keep rich error payloads. The raw grep count without the test filter is 8,300+ `.expect(` hits, which is why it must be filtered.

findings.title: Residual `unwrap` on locks in the TUI onboarding screen
findings.description: The few `unwrap` sites that survive the lint are concentrated: **29 of the 95** non-test `unwrap`/`expect` sites are in `tui/src/onboarding/auth.rs`, where a `std::sync::RwLock` around `sign_in_state` is read and written with `.unwrap()`. A poisoned lock (a panic while holding the write guard) would turn the next key press into a second panic in the TUI. The rest are small groups in Windows ConPTY code, `fuzzy_file_search` and `file_search`. None sits on the turn loop or persistence path, so the consequence is a crash of the onboarding/login screen, not of a running session. The `unwrap`/`expect` counts in `stats` use the rule: exclude `#[cfg(test)]` modules, `*_tests.rs`, `tests.rs`, `tests/` and `*_tests/` directories.
findings.recommendation: Replace the `RwLock` unwraps in `onboarding/auth.rs` with the `unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner)` convention already used in `rmcp-client` and `rollout-trace`, or a `parking_lot` lock that cannot poison.

findings.title: Lock poisoning is recovered with `PoisonError::into_inner`, not propagated
findings.description: Where `std::sync::Mutex` guards shared state on the failure-critical paths (`rollout-trace` writer, `rmcp-client` transport routing, the rollout writer task handle) the code uses `lock().unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner)`. The convention means a **panic in one holder does not cascade**: the next holder proceeds with whatever state the lock had. The `rollout-trace` writer documents the reason (losing diagnostic events in exactly the session being debugged). The `rmcp-client/src/auth_status.rs` recorder is the one place in that crate that still uses `.expect("...should not be poisoned")`, but it is test-support code. Most other shared state uses `tokio::sync::Mutex`, which cannot poison; `await_holding_lock` is denied at the workspace level, so guards are not held across awaits.

findings.title: Resume skips unparseable rollout lines and continues with a partial transcript
findings.description: `RolloutRecorder::load_rollout_items` reads the JSONL transcript line by line; a line that fails `serde_json::from_str` is logged at `warn` and **skipped**, with a `parse_errors` counter returned to the caller. The user resumes with a transcript that is silently missing the affected turns - a truncated last line (the tail-loss case in the writer finding) is the common cause, and there the behaviour is desirable, but the same path hides any corruption in the middle of the file. Because the count is returned, callers can surface it; the TUI resume path does not currently show it to the user.

evidence.snippet: warn!("failed to parse line as JSON: {line:?}, error: {e}");

findings.recommendation: Surface `parse_errors > 0` to the user on resume (a one-line warning that N transcript entries were unreadable), and distinguish a truncated final line from corruption elsewhere in the file.

findings.title: Headless `codex exec` exits non-zero after any turn error
findings.description: The headless runner threads an `error_seen` flag through its event loop: an `Error` event, a failed server request or an unexpected stream end sets it, and after final output is printed the process ends with `std::process::exit(1)`. Startup failures (exec-policy load errors, login restrictions, an unreadable output schema) also exit 1 with a message on stderr. This is the **success-after-failure check passing**: CI and the TypeScript/Python SDKs (which shell out to `codex exec`) can rely on the exit status. The TUI equivalent is `ExitReason::Fatal`, printed with `ERROR:` and the session id for resume, followed by `exit(1)`.

findings.title: A panic inside a turn task is never joined; the client waits for a turn that will not complete
findings.description: Every turn (`RegularTask`, `CompactTask`, `ReviewTask`, user shell commands) runs in its own `tokio::spawn` inside `Session::start_task`. **Errors** are contained well: the task body calls `on_task_finished`, which maps a `CodexErr` to an `Error` event and a turn-error lifecycle, and `TurnAborted` to the abort lifecycle. **Panics** are not: the `JoinHandle` is stored as an `AbortOnDropHandle` in `RunningTask` and is only ever `abort()`ed or `detach()`ed, never awaited, and the `done.notify_waiters()` at the end of the task body is skipped when the body unwinds. The session loop keeps running (nothing else dies), but `active_turn` stays occupied and no `TurnComplete`/`Error` event is emitted, so a TUI or app-server client sees a turn that never finishes until the user submits something else (`spawn_task` first calls `abort_all_tasks(Replaced)`). `unwrap`/`expect` are lint-denied in core, so the practical triggers are `panic!`/`unreachable!`/indexing/arithmetic bugs and third-party panics. Compare the tool-call boundary, which does convert a `JoinError` into a `Fatal` error.

evidence.note: only reached when run() returns normally
the handle is detached or aborted, never awaited

findings.recommendation: Observe the join result: wrap the task body in `AssertUnwindSafe(..).catch_unwind()` (as the remote-control websocket task already does) or await the handle in `on_task_finished`'s caller, and on `JoinError::is_panic()` emit an `Error` event with `CodexErrorDetails::Fatal`, clear `active_turn` and notify `done`, so the client sees a failed turn instead of a hung one.

findings.title: Each tool call is a spawned task; failures become model-visible outputs, panics become a fatal turn
findings.description: `ToolCallRuntime::handle_tool_call_with_source` spawns one `AbortOnDropHandle` task per tool call, gated by a read/write lock that lets parallel-safe tools overlap and serialises the rest. The result is partitioned in three ways: a normal tool error becomes a `FunctionCallOutput` with `success: false` that the **model sees and can react to**; `FunctionCallError::Fatal` ends the turn with `CodexErr::Fatal`; and a `JoinError` (the task panicked or was cancelled) is converted to `Fatal("tool task failed to receive")`, so a panicking tool handler ends the turn with an error rather than hanging it. Cancellation via the turn's `CancellationToken` aborts the task, or waits for runtime teardown when the tool asked for it, and reports `aborted by user` back to the model. Blast radius of one failing tool: that turn, on that thread.

findings.title: Shell commands run in a child process group with timeout, kill escalation, drain timeout and output cap
findings.description: `core/src/exec.rs` bounds everything the model's shell commands can do to the agent: a per-call timeout (default `DEFAULT_EXEC_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000`) after which the whole **process group** is killed and a synthetic exit status 128+64 is reported with `timed_out: true`; on user cancellation the group gets `SIGTERM`, a 50 ms grace period, then `SIGKILL`; `Ctrl-C` on the CLI kills the group too. The stdout/stderr reader tasks are awaited with a 2 s `IO_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS` so grandchildren that inherited the pipes cannot hang the agent, and retained output is capped at 1 MiB (`DEFAULT_OUTPUT_BYTES_CAP`) so a runaway command cannot OOM the process. Long-running `unified_exec` sessions are tracked by a manager that `terminate_all_processes` on session shutdown. Sandbox denials surface as `SandboxErr::Denied` with the captured output, distinct from timeouts and signals. What this boundary does not do: a child that ignores `SIGKILL` semantics (e.g. in uninterruptible I/O) still blocks `child.wait()`.

evidence.snippet: pub const IO_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS: u64 = 2_000; // 2 s should be plenty for local pipes

findings.title: MCP servers are bounded by a 30 s startup timeout and a 300 s tool-call timeout
findings.description: Every MCP server (stdio child process or streamable-HTTP endpoint) is started under `DEFAULT_STARTUP_TIMEOUT` (30 s) and each `tools/call` under `DEFAULT_TOOL_TIMEOUT` (300 s), both overridable per server via `startup_timeout_sec` / `tool_timeout_sec` in `config.toml`; the startup timeout message tells the user exactly which key to raise. A server that dies or hangs therefore costs at most one tool call, which returns an error to the model, and a server that fails to start is reported and skipped rather than blocking the session. Resource and pagination listings use the same tool timeout (`DEFAULT_MCP_PAGINATION_TIMEOUT` 30 s per page). Retries on streamable-HTTP transports are limited to a classified set of initialize/HTTP-status errors and bounded by the same deadline (`sleep_with_retry_deadline`).

findings.title: Death of a thread's session loop surfaces as `InternalAgentDied`, not a process crash
findings.description: Each thread has one long-lived `submission_loop` task. Callers reach it only through an `mpsc` channel and `oneshot` replies, and both failure modes are mapped: a closed channel becomes `CodexErr::InternalAgentDied`, a dropped reply becomes the same. The termination future (`session_loop_termination_from_handle`) does `let _ = handle.await`, so a **panic in the loop is swallowed at join time** and observed only through `InternalAgentDied` on the next call. Multi-agent code (`agent/control.rs`, `interrupt_agent.rs`) explicitly treats `InternalAgentDied` like `ThreadNotFound`, so a dead sub-agent thread does not take down its parent. In the app-server, one thread's loop dying leaves other threads and connections running; the process-level panic reaches stderr via the chained panic hook.

findings.title: Explicit panic boundaries exist only at the remote-control websocket, code-mode callbacks and the TUI terminal
findings.description: Three places catch panics deliberately. The app-server remote-control websocket task is wrapped in `catch_unwind`, logs `panicked` with connection identifiers, then `resume_unwind`s - so the boundary is for **diagnostics**, not survival. The code-mode (V8) runtime and gRPC session callbacks use `catch_unwind` around delegate callbacks so a panicking host callback does not unwind through the FFI boundary. The TUI installs a panic hook that restores the terminal before chaining to the default hook, so a crash leaves a usable shell and a backtrace. Elsewhere Codex relies on tokio's per-task panic isolation: a panic ends the task, and whether anyone notices depends on whether the `JoinHandle` is awaited (see the turn-task and session-loop findings). No process-level supervisor or restart exists; the app-server daemon is restarted by its client, not by itself.

evidence.note: panic hook restores the terminal before the default hook runs

findings.title: Model streams and remote-control sockets retry with bounded exponential backoff, jitter and transport fallback
findings.description: Outgoing calls have one shared backoff (`util::backoff`: 200 ms x 2^attempt, +/-10 % jitter) and per-subsystem bounds. **Model requests**: `stream_max_retries` defaults to 5 and `request_max_retries` to 4 (per provider, configurable); a server `Retry-After` overrides the computed delay; when retries are exhausted on WebSocket the client falls back to HTTPS and resets the counter; an opt-in feature (`UnboundedConnectionRetries`) retries connection failures forever at 5 s doubling to a 60 s cap, excluded for internal sessions and Bedrock. The SSE reader enforces a per-event idle timeout (`DEFAULT_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` 300 s), so a stalled stream becomes a retryable `Stream` error rather than a hang. Retries re-send the same request; there is no side effect between attempts, so the retry is idempotent. **Remote control**: reconnects with the same backoff capped at 30 s and reset after the cap, 10 s ping / 60 s pong timeout, 30 s connect timeout. Compaction requests use the idle timeout times a multiplier. The user sees `Reconnecting... n/max` warnings after the first attempt.

findings.title: Guardian review fails closed on a 90 s timeout and trips a per-turn circuit breaker after 3 denials
findings.description: The optional model-based guardian that reviews risky actions is designed to **fail closed**: a timeout (`GUARDIAN_REVIEW_TIMEOUT` = 90 s), a review-session failure or malformed output all block the action, with timeouts reported separately from denials. A `GuardianRejectionCircuitBreaker` counts denials per turn and interrupts the turn after `MAX_CONSECUTIVE_GUARDIAN_DENIALS_PER_TURN` (3) consecutive or a windowed number of recent denials, so a model that keeps proposing blocked actions does not loop indefinitely. The breaker state is cleared at the start of each turn. This is the only circuit breaker in the codebase; there is none in front of the model provider or MCP servers.

evidence.snippet: //! 3. Fail closed on timeout, execution failure, or malformed output.

findings.title: Designed fallbacks: SQLite index to filesystem scan, WebSocket to HTTPS, compaction model downshift
findings.description: Three reduced modes are deliberate. **Thread listing** first asks the SQLite state DB and, if that fails or disagrees, falls back to scanning the rollout files on disk, recording a `record_fallback("list_threads", "db_error")` metric - the JSONL files remain the source of truth and the DB is an index. **Transport**: after stream retries are exhausted on WebSockets the client switches to HTTPS for the rest of the session with a visible warning. **Compaction**: `should_retry_with_current_model` classifies which compaction errors (invalid request, context window, usage limits, overload, internal server error, retry limit) justify retrying with a different model, and the fallback is recorded for analytics. There is no offline mode - without the model provider a turn fails after the retry budget - and no alternate provider is tried automatically; provider choice is configuration.

evidence.snippet: // If SQLite listing still fails, return the filesystem page rather than failing the list.
message: format!("Falling back from WebSockets to HTTPS transport. {err:#}"),

findings.title: Transcript writer buffers unwritten items and retries, but never fsyncs; a crash loses the unflushed tail
findings.description: The per-thread transcript (`rollout-*.jsonl`) is owned by one background writer task fed through a bounded channel. Items stay in `pending_items` until a write succeeds; on an I/O error the writer drops its file handle, logs once per distinct error, **reopens and retries once** per barrier (`persist`/`flush`/`shutdown`), and keeps the unwritten suffix for the next barrier. A terminal task failure is remembered so later API calls get the real error instead of a channel error. Every turn ends with `flush_rollout`, and a failure produces a user-visible warning (`Failed to save the conversation transcript; Codex will continue retrying`). Each line is `write_all` + `flush()` (a `tokio::fs::File` flush pushes to the OS, it is not `sync_all`), and `open_rollout_for_append` repairs a missing trailing newline on resume, so the only loss mode is the **tail since the last OS writeback** on power loss or kernel crash; a process crash loses at most what is still in `pending_items`. Files are append-only JSONL, so there is no torn-rewrite risk, and `load_rollout_items` tolerates a partial last line.

evidence.snippet: warn!("failed to {operation} rollout writer; reopening and retrying: {first_err}");
warn!("failed to flush rollout before completing turn: {err}");

findings.recommendation: Acceptable for a local transcript; if durability across power loss matters, add `sync_data()` at the `Shutdown` barrier and after each user turn rather than per line.

findings.title: Config, caches and plugin installs use temp-file + rename; SQLite runs WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`
findings.description: Persistent state other than the transcript is written **atomically**: `codex_utils_path::write_atomically` (NamedTempFile in the target directory + `persist`) is used for config-style files (6 call sites); plugin installs stage into a directory and `rename` it into place with a backup-and-rollback sequence in `core-plugins/src/store.rs`; the shell snapshot is written to a temp path, validated, then renamed, and removed on validation failure; the installation id is the one file written with `sync_all`. The state database (`state`) opens with `journal_mode=WAL`, `synchronous=NORMAL`, a 5 s `busy_timeout` and a pool of 5 - WAL+NORMAL is durable across process crashes and can lose the last transactions on power loss, which is acceptable because the DB is an index over the JSONL files. Connectors and plugin catalogs cache with `let _ = write_atomically(..)`, accepting a failed cache write silently.

findings.title: Shutdown cancels the turn, reaps child processes and MCP servers in a fixed order; interruption waits 100 ms
findings.description: `shutdown_session_runtime` runs a fixed sequence: abort the startup prewarm, shut down the realtime conversation, `abort_all_tasks(Interrupted)`, shut down hooks, drain async hook results, `terminate_all_processes` in the unified-exec manager, shut down code-mode, then the rollout writer's `Shutdown` barrier (which keeps the writer alive if draining fails so it can be retried). Interrupting a turn cancels its `CancellationToken`, waits up to `GRACEFULL_INTERRUPTION_TIMEOUT_MS` (100 ms) for the task to acknowledge, then `abort()`s the tokio task and calls the task's `abort` hook; child processes get the TERM/50 ms/KILL sequence from the exec finding. Cancellation is propagated through child tokens from session to turn to tool call. The app-server tracks per-connection cleanup in a `JoinSet` and logs, rather than propagates, a cleanup task failure. Nothing here covers `SIGTERM`/`SIGHUP` to the process itself - only `Ctrl-C` is handled explicitly (in the exec child loop), so an external kill of the TUI relies on the OS to reap children and on the append-only transcript for state.

findings.title: Reliability posture: errors are modelled and contained per turn; the remaining gaps are unobserved panics and unsynced transcript tails
findings.description: Codex is an interactive agent runtime whose failure theory is **per-turn containment**: one thread, one session loop, one spawned task per turn, one spawned task per tool call, one child process group per shell command, one MCP server per plugin. Per failure source: **network/model** - bounded retries (5 stream / 4 request) with jittered backoff, 300 s idle timeout, WebSocket-to-HTTPS fallback, then an `Error` event that ends the turn; blast radius is the turn. **Child processes** - 10 s default timeout, group kill, 2 s drain, 1 MiB output cap; blast radius is the tool call. **MCP servers** - 30 s startup / 300 s call timeouts; blast radius is the call. **Disk** - append-only transcript with buffered retry, atomic rename for everything else, SQLite as a rebuildable index with filesystem fallback; a crash loses at most the unflushed tail. **Own bugs** - `unwrap`/`expect` are lint-denied and tool-task panics become a fatal turn error, but a panic inside the turn task itself is never joined and leaves the client waiting, and a panic in the session loop is only visible as `InternalAgentDied` on the next call. The strongest mechanisms are the classified `CodexErr` taxonomy, the tool-call boundary, the exec process-group handling and the guardian's fail-closed circuit breaker. Highest-leverage changes: observe turn-task panics (`finding:reliability-scan/isolation/turn-task-panic-never-observed`), surface skipped transcript lines on resume (`finding:reliability-scan/handling/rollout-resume-skips-malformed-lines`), and remove the remaining lock `unwrap`s in the TUI onboarding screen (`finding:reliability-scan/handling/unwrap-residue-tui-onboarding`). Coverage: the Rust workspace was read; the TypeScript and Python SDKs were skimmed only - they wrap `codex exec` and inherit its exit-code contract.

findings.title: app-server thread request processor is the top churn x complexity hotspot
findings.description: thread_processor.rs implements the JSON-RPC 'thread/*' API surface of the app server: thread create/resume/fork/list/revert, dynamic tool validation, pagination cursors, and persisted resume settings, all in one 5,161-LOC file (plus embedded test modules from line 5798). It is the highest-scoring hotspot: 131 commits total, 48 in the last 90 days, 43 contributors (metric:hotspot_score, metric:commits_90d). The flagged units are validation gauntlets - validate_dynamic_tools (McCabe 23) checks name/namespace rules against Responses API constraints, collect_resume_override_mismatches (McCabe 23) compares each resume override field against the active config snapshot. Their complexity is essential rule-per-branch logic and individually readable; the risk is the container: every thread-related protocol change lands in this one file touched by 43 people, so unrelated features collide here and reviewers must hold a 5k-line context.
findings.recommendation: Continue the split already started with persisted_resume_settings/thread_enrichment: move self-contained request families (revert, sections, pagination + cursor codec, dynamic-tool validation) into sibling modules so a typical change touches a few hundred lines instead of a 5k-line file.

findings.title: Plugin manager cache-refresh coalescing is hand-rolled concurrent state logic (McCabe 32)
findings.description: core-plugins/src/manager.rs (2,985 LOC, 77 commits, 37 in 90 days, 22 contributors) is the plugin subsystem's central manager: marketplaces, curated/non-curated caches, remote plugins, git upgrades. The worst unit, schedule_non_curated_plugin_cache_refresh (McCabe 32, 157 LOC), builds a refresh request and then, inside a poisoned-lock-tolerant write block, applies four interleaved rules to decide whether to escalate the mode to ForceReinstall, deduplicate against the pending request, or skip entirely - including a three-way structural comparison against last_refreshed with special-casing for git_mode Manual vs Automatic. The paired worker loop run_non_curated_plugin_cache_refresh_loop re-reads state and loops until requested==request. This is accidental complexity: a bespoke coalescing job queue expressed as nested boolean conditions over shared mutable state, exactly the kind of code where a subtle predicate change causes missed or duplicated refreshes, and it is being edited weekly.

evidence.note: nested dedup predicate over shared state

findings.recommendation: Extract the request-coalescing decision (given current state + incoming request, return Skip / Replace / Escalate) into a pure function on a small state struct and unit-test its rule table; keep the lock handling and thread spawn as a thin shell around it.

findings.title: TUI slash-command dispatcher: one 294-line match arm per command (McCabe 39)
findings.description: slash_dispatch.rs routes parsed slash commands to chat-widget behavior. dispatch_prepared_command_with_args (McCabe 39, 294 LOC) is a single match over SlashCommand where each arm mixes argument parsing, usage-error messages, telemetry, and event emission inline - /plan alone embeds byte-range fixups for prefixed text elements. Sokrates shows the growth pattern: 59 commits, 21 in the last 90 days, 15 contributors, because every new slash command or argument form adds an arm here. The companion guard slash_command_blocked_by_active_task (McCabe 11 in 12 lines) is a dense boolean expression encoding per-command availability rules. The complexity is structural, not algorithmic: the dispatcher works, but it taxes every command addition and makes per-command behavior hard to test in isolation.
findings.recommendation: Move per-command argument parsing and usage strings into small handler functions (or a table keyed by SlashCommand carrying parse + execute + availability), leaving the match as a one-line-per-command jump table; fold the availability predicate into the same per-command declaration.

findings.title: Tool registry assembly accretes a feature-flag branch per tool
findings.description: core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs decides which tools a turn exposes to the model. add_core_utility_tools (McCabe 19, 95 LOC) is a run of conditional registry.add calls, each gated on some combination of feature flags, config fields, model_info.experimental_supported_tools string matching, session source, and environment mode; register_code_mode_executors (McCabe 14) and apply_mcp_tool_exposure_policy (McCabe 10) follow the same shape. With 121 commits (42 in 90 days, 24 contributors - metric:commits_90d), this file is where every new tool and every tool-gating experiment lands. The complexity is essential in the sense that the product genuinely has this many conditional tools, but the gating vocabulary is inconsistent (Feature enum vs config booleans vs substring checks on experimental_supported_tools), which makes it easy to gate a new tool subtly differently from intent.

evidence.note: string-typed tool gating alongside Feature-enum gating

findings.recommendation: Normalize the gating vocabulary: represent each tool's availability as data (tool id -> required feature / config predicate) so registration is a loop over declarations, and replace raw substring checks on experimental_supported_tools with named helpers.

findings.title: Schema export generator: flagged complexity lives in guard tests and a small lexer - acceptable
findings.description: app-server-protocol/src/export.rs generates the TypeScript/JSON schema bindings for the app-server protocol (its output carries a GENERATED CODE header). The top-ranked unit by McCabe (50) is generated_ts_optional_nullable_fields_only_in_params - a #[test] that sweeps the generated fixture tree and asserts invariants like '?: T | null' appearing only in *Params types; long, but linear assertion lists whose failure mode is a precise CI error, not a runtime bug. The next units are ScanState::observe (McCabe 15), a compact hand-rolled lexer tracking strings/comments/bracket depth in generated TS, and build_schema_bundle (16), mechanical ref-rewriting. 53 commits (14 in 90 days) simply track protocol evolution. Examined and found acceptable: the complexity is proportionate to what the file does and is fenced by strong guard tests; no action needed.

evidence.note: McCabe-50 unit is a guard test

evidence.snippet: pub(crate) const GENERATED_TS_HEADER: &str = "// GENERATED CODE! DO NOT MODIFY BY HAND!\n\n";
evidence.note: file's role: codegen for protocol bindings

findings.title: core config/mod.rs: low per-unit complexity but the repo's biggest merge magnet
findings.description: core/src/config/mod.rs is the most-committed file in the shortlist by far: 515 commits all-time, 57 in the last 90 days, 81 distinct contributors (metric:commits_90d, metric:contributors), across 3,837 LOC. Reading shows why: it is the funnel where every feature's configuration gets resolved - the flagged units (resolve_rollout_budget_config, validate_multi_agent_v2_tool_namespace, resolve_permission_config_syntax, all McCabe 9) are well-shaped, self-contained resolver/validator functions with clear error messages. Per-unit complexity is fine; the risk is the container's centrality: with a new resolver appended per feature, 81 contributors editing one file guarantees merge conflicts, and the file's sheer size hides which config surface belongs to which subsystem.

evidence.note: representative per-feature resolver appended to the central file

findings.recommendation: Adopt a rule that per-feature resolve_*/validate_* functions live in the owning feature's module (config/rollout_budget.rs etc.) with mod.rs only orchestrating; migrate opportunistically as functions are next touched to bleed off the merge pressure.

findings.title: TUI classifies remote plugin errors by substring-matching message text (McCabe 29)
findings.description: tui/src/app/background_requests.rs handles async fetches for the TUI (plugin catalogs, MCP inventory). Its dominant unit, plugin_remote_section_error_next_step (McCabe 29 in 37 lines), chooses the user-facing 'next step' hint by lowercasing the error string and probing it with a dozen substring chains like err.contains("authentication required") || err.contains("not signed in"), with ordering subtleties (the catch-all 'request'/'status' branch precedes the more specific 'disabled by admin' checks, making some later branches unreachable in practice). This couples UI guidance to the exact wording of errors produced elsewhere; a reworded server or client error silently degrades the hint. The file is active (39 commits, 22 in 90 days, 18 contributors), so the pattern will keep accreting branches.

evidence.note: guidance keyed to error message wording

findings.recommendation: Have the plugin/remote layer return a typed error kind (enum) alongside the message and match on that in the TUI; keep the substring fallback only for legacy paths, and reorder so specific checks precede the broad 'request'/'status' catch-all.

findings.title: ConfigRequirements TryFrom is a 383-line manual conversion that every new requirement must thread through
findings.description: config/src/config_requirements.rs (4,001 LOC, 56 commits, 23 in 90 days, 25 contributors) defines the managed-requirements model. Its centerpiece, impl TryFrom<ConfigRequirementsWithSources> for ConfigRequirements::try_from (383 LOC, McCabe 22), exhaustively destructures a ~40-field struct - explicitly discarding some fields with `field: _` - then validates and re-assembles each requirement inline (model-slug validation, MCP server requirement checks, nested plugin requirements). The exhaustive destructure is a deliberate safety net (adding a field forces this function to be revisited), but the price is that all validation for unrelated requirement families is interleaved in one giant function, and at 23 commits per quarter people pay that price often.
findings.recommendation: Keep the exhaustive destructure, but delegate each requirement family to a named helper (convert_auto_review(...), convert_mcp_servers(...)) so try_from reads as a table of one-liners and family validation is testable in isolation.

findings.title: /debug-config renderer repeats a stanza per requirement field
findings.description: tui/src/debug_config.rs renders the /debug-config diagnostic view. render_debug_config_lines (250 LOC, McCabe 29) walks the config layer stack and then emits one copy-pasted stanza per requirement field - 'if let Some(x) = requirements.x.as_ref() { requirement_lines.push(requirement_line("x", ...)) }' repeated for sqlite_home, log_dir, model_catalog_json, check_for_update_on_startup, allow_login_shell, feedback, and so on. The churn (70 commits, 22 in 90 days, 23 contributors) is mechanical fallout from the requirements surface growing in config_requirements.rs: every new requirement needs a matching stanza here, or the debug view silently omits it. Low direct risk (it is a diagnostics screen), but it is a standing shotgun-edit partner to the requirements model and an easy place for drift.

evidence.note: first of many copy-pasted per-field stanzas

findings.recommendation: Drive the view from data: a slice of (label, extractor) pairs - or a small macro over the requirements struct - so adding a requirement adds one table row, and a unit test can assert every requirements field has a renderer.

findings.title: resume_picker.rs is the largest TUI file, but over half is tests and the render code is sound
findings.description: tui/src/resume_picker.rs is nominally the biggest shortlisted file (6,298 LOC, 103 commits, 27 in 90 days, 31 contributors), implementing the session-resume picker: filtering, pagination, expansion, density modes. Reading tempers the number: the #[cfg(test)] module starts at line 3438, so roughly 45% is production code. The flagged units are unproblematic - render_list (McCabe 17) is careful but straightforward viewport math with saturating arithmetic for the more-above/more-below chrome; footer_hint_lines and matches_query (McCabe 12 each) are similar. The real cost is navigational: picker state, rendering, query matching, and pagination all share one file, so the module would benefit from a split, but nothing here is fragile.
