findings.recommendation: When next touched substantially, split into a resume_picker/ module (state, render, query, pagination) and move the test module alongside; no urgent action.

findings.title: Project-level bus factor is healthy: top contributor holds 15% of commits
findings.description: Contribution is well spread for a project of this size: 581 contributors total, with the top committer at 1,442 commits (15% share, last commit 2026-08-20), the second at 10% (last active 2026-07-30), and the next three at 5-6% each, all active within the last month (metric:contributors, sokrates contributors.json). No single person's departure would strand the codebase as a whole; concentration risk is local (see the single-owner findings) rather than global. This is contextual information derived from the Sokrates contributor metrics, so it carries no file evidence.

findings.title: External-agent migration subsystem is effectively single-owner
findings.description: The feature that imports sessions, skills, and plugins from other coding agents spans at least three single-contributor files across two crates: app-server/src/external_agent_migration/protocol.rs (349 LOC, 5 commits, all in the last 90 days), external-agent-migration/src/detect/sessions/connectors_cla.rs (213 LOC, heuristic detection of connector usage in foreign session files, McCabe 13), and external-agent-migration/src/service_tests/plugins/marketplaces.rs (718 LOC of tests, updated 2026-08-20). One person wrote and maintains the whole area (metric:contributors). The code itself is clean - protocol.rs is mechanical core-to-protocol type mapping - but migration logic encodes hard-won knowledge about competitors' on-disk formats that is documented nowhere else. The owner is still active (latest commit 2026-08-20), which keeps this at medium rather than high; it should not ship a major migration wave with a bus factor of one.
findings.recommendation: Route the next few migration changes through a second reviewer as deliberate knowledge transfer, and add a short doc of the foreign-format assumptions (which files are read, which keys matter) next to the detect/ module.

findings.title: Security-sensitive workload-identity token exchange has one contributor
findings.description: workload-identity/src/exchange.rs (287 LOC, 4 commits, all within the last 90 days, single contributor) implements OAuth JWT-bearer token exchange for workload identity: it caches short-lived access tokens in memory, retries transient failures, and enforces token-URL hygiene in validate_token_url (McCabe 9) - rejecting URLs with credentials/query/fragment and allowing http only for loopback hosts. This is exactly the kind of code where the security reasoning behind each check matters more than the code itself, and today that reasoning lives with one person (metric:contributors). The file was updated 2026-08-15, so the owner is active; the concern is continuity and review depth for future changes, not current quality - the checks read carefully considered.
findings.recommendation: Add a second maintainer for the workload-identity crate and require security-aware review on changes to validate_token_url and the caching/retry logic; a brief threat-model comment block would preserve the intent behind each rejection rule.

findings.title: Release mirroring to Cloudflare R2 depends on a single-owner script
findings.description: .github/scripts/publish_r2_release.py (467 LOC, one contributor, 5 commits) mirrors GitHub releases to Cloudflare R2: it verifies checksums, writes versioned release.json metadata, advances the latest/prerelease channel pointers, and updates the mutable install.sh/install.ps1 bootstrap aliases. Its main() (147 LOC, McCabe 21) and get_release_metadata (McCabe 18) concentrate the orchestration. The module docstring is genuinely good documentation of the flow, which softens the risk, and the script is release tooling rather than product code - but it sits on the distribution path (what 'codex install' fetches), and only one person has ever touched it (metric:contributors).

evidence.snippet: """Mirror a Codex GitHub Release to Cloudflare R2.

findings.recommendation: Have a second release engineer run one release end-to-end with this script and note any tribal steps in the docstring; consider splitting channel-pointer advancement out of main() so a partial failure's blast radius is obvious.

findings.title: Assorted peripheral single-owner files: small, simple, owners active
findings.description: The remaining single-contributor files the selection surfaced are small, low-complexity, and recently maintained: the Python SDK facade sdk/python/src/openai_codex/api.py (676 LOC but max McCabe 5 - a thin typed wrapper whose class Codex mostly delegates), path rendering in utils/path-uri/src/api_path_string.rs (282 LOC, Windows-path edge cases, McCabe 10), and TUI leaf modules chatwidget/usage.rs and app/thread_goal_actions.rs (max McCabe 2-3). All were updated between 2026-07 and 2026-08, so their owners are active (metric:contributors). Individually none justifies action; collectively they are ordinary for a 581-contributor codebase where leaf features start with one author. Worth revisiting only if an owner goes quiet - the Windows path-encoding rules in api_path_string.rs would be the first to become archaeology.

evidence.note: thin SDK facade, single owner, low complexity
Windows path edge-case logic, single owner

findings.recommendation: No immediate action; fold these into normal review rotation and prioritize a co-reviewer for api_path_string.rs if its owner becomes inactive.

findings.title: protocol EnvironmentConfig co-changes 100% with core validation and selection code
findings.description: codex-rs/protocol/src/environment.rs changed in the same commit as codex-rs/core/src/environment_selection.rs in 8 of its 8 commits (ratio 1.0), and nearly as often with core/src/session/environment.rs (6/8) and session/session.rs (7/8) (metric:temporal_coupling). Reading explains the ripple: the protocol file defines EnvironmentConfig / EnvironmentConfigState as plain data, while all semantics live in core - session/environment.rs hand-validates each field (rejecting network_policy with 'not supported yet', capping capability roots, forbidding exec-policy allow rules) and environment_selection.rs (1,777 LOC) plumbs ownership via EnvironmentConfigOrigin. So every field added to the protocol struct forces coordinated edits in at least two core files. This is a deliberate protocol/implementation split for an in-flight feature (the struct doc comments even state which restrictions core will reject), so the boundary is not wrong - but while the feature is under construction, changes here are shotgun edits across a crate boundary with validation far from the type it guards.

evidence.note: protocol data type at the center of the coupling
field-by-field semantics maintained in core, far from the type

findings.recommendation: While the environment-attachment feature stabilizes, keep a single validation entry point (validate_environment_config) as the required companion to any protocol field addition - a checklist comment on the struct pointing at it would prevent missed edits; once stable, consider moving structural invariants (max roots, no allow rules) onto constructors in the protocol crate so only policy checks remain in core.

findings.title: codex-mcp connection_manager couplings are one type split across files - cohesive by design
findings.description: Three flagged pairs sit inside codex-rs/codex-mcp: connection_manager.rs with required.rs (ratio 1.0) and tool_catalog.rs (0.76), and binding.rs with tool_catalog.rs (0.78) (metric:temporal_coupling). Reading shows connection_manager.rs declares required.rs, tool_catalog.rs, startup.rs, and resources.rs as #[path] submodules that hold impl blocks of the same McpConnectionSet type - so 'files that change together' here is literally one component whose source is split for readability. tool_catalog.rs imports McpBinding/PreparedMcpCall from binding.rs, the call-preparation seam of the same subsystem. Examined and found acceptable: the co-change is what a well-factored multi-file module looks like in commit data, not a leaky boundary. No boundary change is warranted.

evidence.note: coupled files are submodules of one type
tool_catalog is part of the same McpConnectionSet impl

findings.title: ext/skills loader facade forces three-file edits for each new loader capability
findings.description: codex-rs/ext/skills/src/loader/mod.rs co-changed with lib.rs and with host_service.rs in 7 of its 10 commits (ratio 0.7 each) (metric:temporal_coupling). The mechanism is visible in the code: loader/mod.rs is a facade that re-exports selected pub(crate) items from its submodules (discovery, host, host_merge, ...) plus a block of shared limit constants, lib.rs re-exports the crate's public API from those internals, and host_service.rs is the primary consumer of the loader entry points. Each new loader capability therefore edits the submodule, the loader facade's use lines, and usually lib.rs or the host service - mechanical but reliable three-file commits. The layering itself is sound (limits and names are defined once); the friction is modest and mostly inherent to keeping a narrow public API over a deep module tree.

evidence.note: facade re-export layer that grows with each capability
second re-export layer coupled to the same changes

findings.recommendation: Acceptable as-is; if the churn grows, collapse one hop - either let host_service import loader submodules directly or re-export loader items wholesale (pub use loader::host_merge::*) so a new entry point is declared in one place.

findings.title: Authentication: OAuth PKCE to ChatGPT, API key from environment, plus two machine-identity flows
findings.description: Codex authenticates the **user**, never the model. The interactive path is **OAuth with PKCE**: a 64-byte verifier and a 32-byte `state` nonce are generated per login, the callback is served on loopback, and the resulting access/refresh/id tokens are refreshed through `refresh_token_endpoint`. The headless path reads `CODEX_API_KEY` first and `OPENAI_API_KEY` second from the environment. Two machine flows sit beside them: `workload-identity` exchanges a file-backed assertion for ChatGPT auth, and `agent-identity` signs with ed25519 and validates RS256 JWTs against a fetched JWK set. There is no local password, no session cookie, and no role model; identity is whichever credential the process could load, so the security of the token store (`secrets/at-rest`) is the whole story.

evidence.note: PKCE verifier from the process CSPRNG
agent identity JWT validated against JWKS

findings.title: Authorization: the exec policy decides Allow / Prompt / Forbidden per command, with the sandbox as the fallback wall
findings.description: There are no users or roles; the subject being authorized is the **model's proposed action**. `core/src/exec_policy.rs` is the enforcement point for commands: a dangerous-command heuristic match (forced `rm`, PowerShell URL launches, and so on) or a Windows filesystem restriction without a sandbox backend yields `Forbidden` under `AskForApproval::Never` and `Prompt` otherwise, before any policy rule is consulted. Unmatched commands under `Never` are **allowed outright, relying on the sandbox**; under `OnRequest` (the protocol default) they are allowed when the filesystem sandbox is restricted and only prompt when the command asks to escalate out of it; `UnlessTrusted` prompts for everything not explicitly allowed. Patches have their own gate: `assess_patch_safety` auto-approves only when every path normalizes into a writable root **and** a platform sandbox exists, otherwise it asks or rejects. Project `trust_level` selects which of these profiles applies. The design is a policy layer in front of a structural layer; when the structural layer is absent (Windows default, see architecture-scan), the policy layer alone stands.

evidence.note: dangerous command under Never is refused, not prompted
unmatched command under Never: allowed, sandbox is the wall

findings.title: Approval flow: four human-or-model gates, one of them a fail-closed model reviewer
findings.description: Consent is collected at four distinct gates. **Command approval** comes from the exec-policy `Prompt` decision and is answered by the user through the TUI or an app-server client. **Patch approval** is the `SafetyCheck::AskUser` branch of `assess_patch_safety`. **MCP tool approval** renders a per-tool elicitation with connector and parameter metadata and can persist a decision for the session or always. The optional **guardian** replaces the human for policies routed to it: a second model reviews the compact transcript plus the requested action and any timeout (`GUARDIAN_REVIEW_TIMEOUT`), review failure or malformed verdict **blocks** the action, with a circuit breaker after repeated denials. Approvals can be pre-granted through `execpolicy` allow rules and amended at runtime (`add_prefix_rule`). What the flow does not do is record an audit trail of grants beyond the session rollout; reliability-scan covers the breaker.

evidence.note: auto-approve only when a sandbox backend exists
which approval policies the guardian answers

findings.title: Managed overrides: requirements.toml / MDM can pin approval policies; the hook-trust bypass is loud but available
findings.description: Enterprise control sits in `config_requirements.rs`: a system `requirements.toml` or MDM managed preferences deliver `allowed_approval_policies` and constrained values with their source, and the resolved `approval_policy` is a `ConstrainedWithSource` so a user-layer value outside the allowed set is rejected rather than merged. This is the mechanism that makes the `dangerously_*` escape hatches architecture-scan lists governable. The one hatch that is not covered by requirements is `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`: it is honored from any layer and only produces a startup warning. Hooks from managed layers are implicitly trusted (`HookTrustStatus::Managed`), so an MDM-delivered hook runs without the hash check that user hooks face.

evidence.note: resolved value carries its constraint source

evidence.snippet: "`--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` is enabled. Enabled hooks may run without review for this invocation."

findings.title: App-server listener auth: non-loopback WebSocket refuses to start without a token; capability token compared in constant time
findings.description: The app-server is the surface other programs use to drive Codex, so its listener auth is the closest thing to a service boundary. `stdio://` and the unix control socket (mode `0600`, directory `0700`) rely on OS identity. The WebSocket transport **refuses to bind a non-loopback address unless `--ws-auth` is set**; loopback binds may run unauthenticated by design. `capability-token` mode stores only the SHA-256 of the token and compares with `constant_time_eq_32`; `signed-bearer-token` mode verifies an HS256 JWT with a shared secret of enforced minimum length, disables the library's `exp`/`nbf` checks and re-implements them with a configurable clock skew, then checks issuer and audience. Remote control adds enrollment and segment limits on top. The design gap is deliberate: an unauthenticated loopback WebSocket trusts every local process, which is the same trust the unix socket grants only to the same user.

evidence.snippet: "refusing to start non-loopback websocket listener {bind_address} without auth; configure `--ws-auth capability-token` or `--ws-auth signed-bearer-token`"

findings.title: Secrets at rest: keyring first, 0600 files as fallback, age-encrypted store for managed secrets
findings.description: Three stores, one pattern. **User auth** (`auth.json`) is written with `OpenOptions::mode(0o600)` and truncate-in-place (storage-scan covers the durability side) or, in `Keyring`/`Auto` store mode, into the OS keyring under service `Codex Auth` with an account derived from `sha256(codex_home)`. **MCP OAuth tokens** go to the keyring and fall back to `CODEX_HOME/.credentials.json` created with mode `0o600`, with a test that re-asserts the mode under a permissive umask. **Managed secrets** (`local.age`, `codex_auth.age`, `mcp_oauth.age`) are `age` scrypt-encrypted with a generated high-entropy passphrase that lives only in the keyring. Nothing is stored in plaintext outside the home directory, no secret is written relative to the project, and the keyring is the default where available. On Windows the `mode(0o600)` branches are `cfg(unix)` only, so the file fallbacks rely on the profile ACL there.

evidence.note: age passphrase generated and kept in the keyring

findings.title: In memory and on the way out: regex redaction and a credential broker, but process hardening only guards the API proxy
findings.description: The design keeps real credentials away from the model and from logs in three ways. `redact_secrets` (OpenAI key, AWS key id, `Bearer` tokens, `token=`/`password=` assignments) is applied to every command string the app-server emits and to memory summaries before they are persisted. The network proxy's **credential broker** hands sandboxed commands a `dummy_value` per provider and swaps in the `real_value` only inside the proxy, so a command that prints its environment leaks nothing usable. `responses-api-proxy` is the component built to hold the API key on behalf of an untrusted client; it zeroizes the key buffer and calls `pre_main_hardening` (ptrace deny, non-dumpable, `LD_PRELOAD`/`DYLD_*` stripped). The drift is that this hardening is **only** linked into `responses-api-proxy` and the Linux sandbox proxy lifecycle: the main `codex` binary, which holds the OAuth access and refresh tokens as plain `String`s and the keyring passphrase in memory, does not call it and uses no zeroization. Architecture-scan's description of hardening as running before `main` applies to the proxy binary, not the agent. Same-user ptrace and core dumps of the agent are therefore not defended, which is the norm for CLI tools and why this stays low.

evidence.note: real credential substituted only inside the proxy
the only binary that calls the hardening entry point

findings.recommendation: Decide whether the agent process should get the same `pre_main_hardening` (at least `disable_process_dumping`) as the proxy, and wrap the in-memory token and passphrase types in `zeroize`/`SecretString` so accidental `Debug` output and freed heap do not carry them; if the asymmetry is intentional, say so in `process-hardening`'s docs.

findings.title: Model-run commands inherit the user's full environment by default, including *KEY*, *SECRET* and *TOKEN* variables
findings.description: `ShellEnvironmentPolicy` is the mechanism that decides what environment a model-proposed command sees. Its default is `inherit: All` with `ignore_default_excludes: true`, so the documented default exclude patterns `*KEY*`, `*SECRET*` and `*TOKEN*` are **not applied unless the user opts in**; `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, cloud credentials and anything else in the shell reach the untrusted command. The safe mode exists and is one config line (`ignore_default_excludes = false`, or `include_only`), and the doc comment on the struct states the default plainly, so this is a deliberate trade-off (developer tooling expects its env), not an oversight. What stands between the inherited secret and the network is the sandbox's outbound cut-off, so exfiltration needs an approved network-enabled command, `network_access = true`, or a proxy allow-list; the credential broker only protects secrets when the managed proxy is on. In the common `OnRequest` plus `WorkspaceWrite` configuration a prompt-injected command can still read the secrets and write them into the workspace, which the next `git push` carries out.

evidence.note: the filter that is skipped by default
config layer keeps the open default

findings.recommendation: Flip the default to `ignore_default_excludes = false` for sandboxed (non-`DangerFullAccess`) runs, or at least apply the default excludes whenever the approval policy is `Never`; let users re-add specific variables with `set`/`include_only`. Surface the current default in `codex doctor` so operators can see which secrets a model command would inherit.

attributes.mitigation: sandbox network cut-off; credential broker only with managed proxy

findings.title: Secrets in the tree: clean - 13 credential-shaped hits are all fixtures, redaction test vectors or test key material
findings.description: The sweep covered `sk-`, `sk-proj-`, `ghp_`, `AKIA`, `xox*`, `BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY` and long literals near auth words across the whole tree except vendored code, lockfiles and git exports. Every hit was read: the `sk-proj-`/`ghp_` strings are inputs to the credential-broker and redaction tests, the `sk-` literals in `item_builders_tests`, `login.rs` and `memories` are masking test vectors, and the three PEM blocks are `TEST_AGENT_IDENTITY_RSA_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM` constants used to exercise the agent-identity signer. No real API key, OAuth secret, signing key or telemetry write key is committed.

evidence.note: test-only key inside a cfg(test) module

findings.title: Published identifiers: OAuth client id, Statsig client key and Sentry DSN are intentionally shipped
findings.description: Three literals look like secrets and are not. `CLIENT_ID = "app_EMoamEEZ73f0CkXaXp7hrann"` is the public OAuth client id of the CLI (overridable through `CODEX_APP_SERVER_LOGIN_CLIENT_ID`); PKCE makes the client public by design. `STATSIG_API_KEY` is a `client-` scoped write key sent as a header with metrics, and `SENTRY_DSN` is the ingest address used only when a user submits feedback. All three are meant to be embedded in a distributed binary; what they permit is writing telemetry or starting a login, not reading anything. They are listed so a future sweep does not re-flag them.

findings.title: Validation posture: typed serde at every wire boundary, lenient parsing of model tool arguments, shell wrappers unwrapped before policy
findings.description: All five doors architecture-scan mapped are parsed through serde into typed protocol structs (JSON-RPC v2, MCP, the exec-server protocol, rollout JSONL), so malformed input fails at deserialization rather than deep in the engine. Model output is the exception by design: tool-call `arguments` are parsed with `serde_json::from_str(...).unwrap_or_else(|_| Value::String(...))`, so non-JSON arguments become a string and are still forwarded to the handler, which then does its own typed parse. For commands, the policy layer does not trust the outer argv: `exec_policy.rs` carries a table of shell wrappers (`bash -c`, `sh -lc`, `powershell -Command`, `python -c`, ...) and lowers the inner command before matching rules and dangerous heuristics, which closes the obvious `bash -c "rm -rf"` bypass. Canonicalization of paths is done without touching the filesystem in `safety.rs` (see `injection/path`). No input path was found that reaches a sink without a parser in front of it.

evidence.note: shell wrapper table used to inspect inner commands

findings.title: Archive extraction: zip-slip is covered in the curated-plugin zipball, but the zip path lacks the size cap and link refusal its tar sibling has
findings.description: The only archive Codex extracts from a network source is the curated plugins repository, fetched as a GitHub zipball. `extract_zipball_to_dir` rejects any entry whose `enclosed_name()` is `None` (absolute paths and `..` components), drops the zipball's synthetic top-level directory, rebuilds the relative path from `Normal` components only, and writes into a staging directory before the result is swapped in. Unix mode bits from the archive are applied to extracted files, so a zip can mark plugin scripts executable, which is required for hooks and is acceptable given the source (see `third-party-trust/plugins-and-extensions`). The sibling tar extractor in `plugin_bundle_archive.rs` is stricter: it refuses hard links and symlinks and enforces a total extracted-size cap, while the zip path applies the archive's mode bits verbatim and has no decompression limit, so a zip bomb in the curated repository would be decompressed to disk without a ceiling. The two extractors should share one hardening level. Plugin and marketplace ids are validated against a character allow-list with an explicit traversal rejection before they become path segments.

evidence.note: the tar sibling's link refusal, absent on the zip path

findings.recommendation: Route the zipball through the same entry filter as the tar extractor: cap total extracted bytes, mask mode bits to `0o755`/`0o644`, and reject symlink entries; or extract with the tar code path by requesting a tarball from GitHub instead.

findings.title: Parser limits: remote-control segments capped at 150 KiB / 100 MiB, MITM bodies at 4 KiB, command output at 1 MiB
findings.description: Where untrusted bytes stream in, sizes are bounded. Remote-control WebSocket frames are segmented with `REMOTE_CONTROL_SEGMENT_MAX_BYTES` and a reassembly cap of `REMOTE_CONTROL_REASSEMBLED_MAX_BYTES`, and enrollment responses are truncated at 4 KiB before they are logged. The network proxy's MITM hook only buffers `MITM_MAX_BODY_BYTES` of a body. Command output retained for the model is capped at 1 MiB with a 2 s drain timeout (reliability-scan). What has no explicit limit is the stdio JSON-RPC line reader and MCP tool results, both of which come from processes the user launched; performance-scan lists the remaining unbounded inputs.

findings.title: Command construction: the model's command is the intended shell sink; config-owned helper commands are the only other `sh -c` callers
findings.description: There is no hidden command-injection path because command execution is the product. Model-proposed commands are wrapped as `<shell> -c <command>` by `Shell::derive_exec_args` and then pass through exec-policy, dangerous-command heuristics, the approval gate and the OS sandbox; the untrusted string is the argument, never spliced into a format string. Beyond that path, `sh -c` appears in two places, both fed from **user-authored configuration**: the MCP `http_headers` helper command (with a comment acknowledging the shell convention) and hook `command` handlers via the hooks command runner. On Windows both use `raw_arg(format!(r#""{command}""#))`, which would be quote-injectable if the command came from an untrusted source; it comes from config files the same user controls, and hooks from other layers are hash-trusted first. Windows-specific dangerous-command heuristics exist for PowerShell and `cmd` URL launches. Verdict: no injection, one documented convention.

evidence.note: model command as a single shell argument

findings.title: SQL: clean - every query is a static string with bound parameters, and clippy forbids bypassing the sqlite shim
findings.description: All SQLite access in `codex-state` (and the thread store, log db, memories, queue) uses `sqlx::query`/`query_as` with literal SQL and `.bind()` for values; no `format!` builds a `SELECT`/`INSERT`/`WHERE` fragment anywhere outside tests. `clippy.toml` disallows `sqlx::Pool::connect` and its variants so connections cannot be opened outside the shim that sets pragmas and paths. The data in these databases is the user's own session history, so even a hypothetical injection would be self-inflicted; the clean pattern is still worth recording.

evidence.snippet: { path = "sqlx::Pool::connect", reason = "Create SQLite pools through codex-state's sqlite shim." },

findings.title: Path construction from model output: patch targets are normalized against writable roots without touching the filesystem
findings.description: Model-supplied paths reach the filesystem through `apply_patch` and through the sandboxed command. For patches, `is_write_patch_constrained_to_writable_paths` resolves each target against `cwd`, normalizes `.` and `..` purely lexically (so a non-existent file is still checked) and requires every target to lie under a writable root; a full-disk policy short-circuits to allowed. The code comments that hard links could still point outside the roots, which is why an auto-approved patch is still applied **inside the sandbox** rather than trusted on the path check alone - the check-then-use gap is closed by the second layer, not by the check. Symlink following during the patch write itself is delegated to the OS sandbox rules. Commands see paths only as argv, constrained by Seatbelt/Landlock/bwrap rules architecture-scan describes.

findings.title: Algorithms fit their jobs: SHA-256 digests, HS256/RS256 JWTs, age scrypt at rest, ed25519 signatures, CSPRNG nonces
findings.description: Every primitive matches its role. **Integrity/lookup**: SHA-256 for the capability-token digest, the keyring account key and the age passphrase cache hash; SHA-1 appears only through `gix` for git object ids. **Identity**: HS256 with a length-checked shared secret for app-server bearer tokens, RS256 against a fetched JWK set for agent identity, ed25519 (`ed25519-dalek`) for agent signing, `crypto_box` sealed boxes and Noise (`clatter`, with ML-KEM options) for channels. **At rest**: `age` scrypt with a generated passphrase. **Randomness**: `rand::rng()` (rand 0.9's OS-seeded ChaCha generator) fills the 64-byte PKCE verifier, the 32-byte OAuth `state` and the age passphrase; no `SmallRng`, `StdRng::seed_from_u64` or time-based seeding was found on a security path. No home-rolled primitive exists. The one secret comparison that matters (capability token) is constant-time; the OAuth `state` compare is a plain `==`, which is fine because `state` is a public CSRF nonce, not a secret.

findings.title: TLS overrides: clean - no certificate verification is disabled anywhere; custom CAs are added, never substituted for verification
findings.description: The sweep for `danger_accept_invalid_certs`, `danger_accept_invalid_hostnames`, `rejectUnauthorized: false`, `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED` and `dangerous()` builders found nothing outside the string `is_dangerous` in command-safety tests. The single place TLS trust is shaped is `http-client/src/custom_ca.rs`: native roots are loaded, `CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE` (then `SSL_CERT_FILE`) adds roots through `add_root_certificate`, and a parse failure on the modern path fails construction rather than falling back to no verification. The MITM hook in the managed proxy is a corporate-deployment feature that terminates TLS for sandboxed commands, not for Codex's own model traffic, and is off unless configured. Network-scan owns the rest of the TLS configuration.

evidence.note: roots are added, verification stays on

findings.title: 818 unsafe blocks in 154 files, 63 SAFETY comments, no unsafe_code lint policy - the sandbox crates carry most of it
findings.description: `unsafe {` occurs 818 times (691 outside `*tests.rs` and `tests/` paths) across 154 files. The mass is where it must be: `linux-sandbox` (fork/exec, capabilities, inotify, seccomp), `windows-sandbox-rs` (tokens, ACLs, WFP firewall, job objects), `utils/pty`, `process-hardening`, the macOS proxy lookup and the IDE named-pipe code. These are exactly the load-bearing security paths, and only **63** blocks carry a `// SAFETY:` comment; `linux_run_main.rs` documents the capability ABI call but forks, `setpgid`s and `waitpid`s without a stated invariant. No crate sets `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` or `#![deny(unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn)]`, and `clippy.toml` has no `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, so the ratio is not enforced and will drift. The FFI seams themselves are thin libc/windows-sys calls rather than a large native library, and the two embedded engines (V8, Starlark) are consumed through safe Rust APIs. Testing-scan already notes the sandbox tests are the thinnest in the workspace.

evidence.note: load-bearing unsafe without a SAFETY comment

evidence.snippet: // SAFETY: capability ABI version 3 uses a [version, pid] header and
evidence.note: the documented style, used in a minority of blocks

findings.recommendation: Turn on `clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks` (warn first) for `linux-sandbox`, `windows-sandbox-rs`, `sandboxing`, `process-hardening` and `utils/pty`, add `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` to crates that have none today so the count cannot spread, and require a SAFETY comment stating the invariant on every fork/exec, token and ACL call.

attributes.ffi: libc / windows-sys / SystemConfiguration, no large native library

findings.title: Dynamic execution: model-written JavaScript runs in an in-process V8 isolate with the sandbox feature and a pruned global object
findings.description: Code mode (feature-flagged) lets the model write JavaScript that calls tools. It runs inside `code-mode-runtime` on `rusty_v8` built with `v8_enable_sandbox`, so heap corruption stays in the V8 sandbox region. The global object is pruned before the script runs: `console`, `Atomics`, `SharedArrayBuffer` and `WebAssembly` are deleted, and the only host functions are `tools`, `text`/`image`/`audio`, `store`/`load`, `notify`, `setTimeout` and `exit`. Every side effect therefore still goes through the same tool dispatch and approval gates as a direct tool call; the isolate gives the model compute, not capability. Execution yields on a time budget rather than a hard kill, so a CPU-burning script costs time, not a compromise. The other interpreter, Starlark for `execpolicy`, evaluates policy written by the user or administrator, not by the model. There is no `eval` of model text in Rust or TypeScript outside these two engines.

findings.title: Plugins, hooks and MCP servers: curated marketplace over TLS at a resolved commit, hooks hash-trusted, MCP servers unsandboxed by design
findings.description: Three kinds of third-party code run at runtime. **Plugins** from the OpenAI curated marketplace are synced by resolving the remote commit through the GitHub API and downloading `{repo}/zipball/{sha}` over HTTPS (with a chatgpt.com backup archive); there is no signature or pinned digest beyond the commit sha, so trust is TLS plus GitHub. Other marketplaces are user-configured git repositories, and `git_policy.rs` runs those git commands with repository-scoped environment stripped so a malicious project cannot redirect the clone. **Hooks** are gated by content hash: a user-layer hook runs only when its current hash equals the `trusted_hash` recorded at approval, so an edited hook flips to `Modified` and stops; managed-layer hooks are trusted implicitly, and `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` skips the check. **MCP servers** are launched as ordinary child processes with `sandbox: None`, which architecture-scan records; the gate is the install/approval decision and per-tool elicitation, not confinement. Skills and `AGENTS.md` are read as prompt content, which is the prompt-injection surface `model-output` discusses.

evidence.note: curated plugins fetched at a resolved commit

vetting.curated-plugins: TLS + GitHub API commit sha, no signature
vetting.hooks: content hash approved by user, managed implicit

findings.title: MCP tool auto-approval in the default `Auto` mode trusts the server's own readOnlyHint / openWorldHint annotations
findings.description: `AppToolApproval` defaults to `Auto`, and in that mode `requires_mcp_tool_approval` decides from the **server-declared** annotations: `destructiveHint: true` forces a prompt, `readOnlyHint: true` skips it, and otherwise a prompt is required only when `openWorldHint` is true (its absence counts as true). A server that labels a destructive tool `readOnlyHint: true` or `openWorldHint: false` therefore runs without a human in the loop, and the server is the very third party being trusted. The compensations are real: the user installed the server, per-server and per-tool `approval_mode` overrides (`Prompt`, `Writes`) exist, `restrict_to` composes a plugin's requested mode with the user's so the stricter wins, and MCP results are still untrusted text. This is the same shape as the exec policy trusting its heuristics, but the heuristics there are Codex's own; here the classifier is supplied by the party under review, which is why it is worth its own line.

evidence.note: default mode (the #[default] attribute is on the preceding line)
a server-declared read-only tool skips approval

findings.recommendation: Treat annotations as advisory for servers the user did not mark trusted: default unknown servers to `Writes` or `Prompt`, or require `destructiveHint`/`readOnlyHint` consistency (a tool cannot be both read-only and destructive) before honoring them.

findings.title: Dependencies and updates: locked and cargo-deny audited with three documented advisory ignores; forks pinned by rev; no in-binary updater
findings.description: Rust dependencies are pinned by `Cargo.lock`, audited in CI by `cargo-deny` whose `[advisories]` section carries three dated, justified ignores (unmaintained `derivative`, `fxhash`, `paste` pulled in through starlark and V8), and the four git dependencies (`nucleo`, `runfiles`, and the `openai-oss-forks` `crossterm`/`tungstenite` patches) are pinned to full commit hashes. `bubblewrap` is vendored under `codex-rs/vendor`. `openssl-sys` is a wildcard version, which tech-stack-scan already flags. At runtime Codex does **not** update itself: the doctor and TUI only print the package-manager command (`npm install -g @openai/codex`, `brew upgrade --cask codex`), so artifact verification is entirely the installer channels' job (sha256-checked archives, signed binaries, but a mutable `install.sh`, per cicd-scan). CVE status was not evaluated here.

findings.title: Model-output containment beyond the sandbox: every side effect passes a policy gate; what the model reads is ungated by design
findings.description: Treating model output as untrusted input, the paths from it to a side effect are: shell command (exec policy, dangerous heuristics, approval, sandbox), patch (`assess_patch_safety`, sandbox), MCP tool call (elicitation with persisted decisions, server-defined annotations), code-mode script (host functions map back to the same tools), network from a sandboxed command (OS cut-off, optional proxy with domain policy and credential broker), plugin install (`request_plugin_install` tool that asks), and sub-agent spawning (inherits the parent's policy). The optional guardian adds a model reviewer that fails closed. The inverse direction is deliberately open: project files, `AGENTS.md`, skills, MCP tool results and web content flow into the context with no filtering, so prompt injection can steer the model, but it can only act through the gates above. The design is thus **containment, not detection**; its weakest configurations are `AskForApproval::Never` combined with `DangerFullAccess`, which the `dangerously_*` naming and managed requirements make visible and governable.

evidence.note: MCP servers run outside the command sandbox

findings.title: Posture: a two-layer containment design (policy in front of an OS sandbox) with a clean code audit; the gaps are open defaults, not holes
findings.description: **Design.** Codex trusts one human and one credential and treats the model as the adversary: every model-proposed side effect crosses a policy layer (`exec_policy`, `assess_patch_safety`, MCP elicitation, optional guardian) and then a structural layer (Seatbelt / Landlock+seccomp / bwrap / Windows restricted token, plus network cut-off and an optional egress proxy with a credential broker). The layers are defense in depth on macOS and Linux and collapse to the policy layer alone on a default Windows install, which architecture-scan already rates medium. Secrets follow one pattern everywhere (keyring first, 0600 file second, age for managed secrets) and are redacted on the way to logs and memories. **Worst confirmed finding.** No credential leak, no injection path, no TLS override. Two mediums: model-run commands inherit `*KEY*`/`*SECRET*`/`*TOKEN*` variables by default because the documented exclude filter is opt-in, and the `unsafe` hygiene in the very crates that implement the sandbox (818 blocks, 63 SAFETY comments, no lint policy). Three lows: MCP `Auto` approval trusts server-declared annotations, the zip extractor is weaker than its tar sibling, and process hardening is linked only into the API proxy. **Coverage.** Swept clean: secrets in tree (13 candidates), SQL, command construction, path/zip traversal, TLS overrides, randomness, secret comparison, template/markup (TUI only; the login success page URL-encodes its query). Not covered: dependency CVE status (no database), the Windows sandbox internals beyond counting unsafe, exhaustive review of 691 unsafe blocks (a representative sample was read), and TypeScript SDK/CLI wrappers, which were skimmed only. **Probe next:** the environment-inheritance default against a prompt-injection scenario, the unsafe-block hygiene in the sandbox crates, and the MCP annotation trust in `Auto` mode.

evidence.note: the policy layer's hand-off to the structural layer
auto-approval exists only where a sandbox exists

layers: policy (exec_policy, patch safety, MCP elicitation, guardian)

findings.title: Data-class inventory: everything persistent lives under CODEX_HOME as append-only JSONL, six versioned SQLite files, atomically written TOML/JSON, encrypted age files and a few caches
findings.description: Codex is a desktop/CLI agent with a **single home directory** (`CODEX_HOME`, default `~/.codex`) and no server-side database of its own. Ten data classes live there. **Session rollouts** are append-only JSONL under `sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*.jsonl` (compressed to `.jsonl.zst` when cold) and are the canonical conversation record. **Runtime databases** are six SQLite files whose names carry a version suffix (`state_5.sqlite`, `logs_2.sqlite`, `goals_1.sqlite`, `memories_1.sqlite`, `queue_1.sqlite`, `thread_history_1.sqlite`) and are treated as rebuildable views over the rollouts. **User configuration** is `config.toml` plus layered profile files, written through `write_atomically`. **Credentials** are `auth.json` (0600, plain JSON) or the OS keyring; **managed secrets** are age-encrypted files (`local.age`, `codex_auth.age`, `mcp_oauth.age`) whose passphrase sits in the keyring. **Command history** is one global `history.jsonl`. **Memories** are DB rows plus a regenerated `raw_memories.md`. **Plugins** are staged directory trees under a versioned per-plugin root. **Caches** are small JSON files with a `schema_version` (remote plugin catalog, connector directory, apps tool cache, HMAC-signed cloud-config bundle). **Ephemera** are `shell_snapshots/`, `thread-writer-locks/`, `.tmp/` markers and `db-backups/`. Sensitivity is highest for `auth.json` and the rollouts (they contain prompts, tool output and file contents the agent read).

session-rollouts.writer: one background task per thread, guarded by writer lock

runtime-databases.writer: one process pool (5 conns) per db

caches.location: cache JSON files (plugin catalog, connectors, apps tools, cloud-config)
caches.format: JSON with schema_version, HMAC for cloud-config

ephemera.format: scripts, lock files, markers, moved db files

findings.title: Location resolution: CODEX_HOME env or ~/.codex, a separate SQLITE_HOME override for the databases, and a .tmp subfolder for cross-process markers
findings.description: All paths derive from one root. `find_codex_home` honours `CODEX_HOME` when set and **requires it to exist and be a directory** (a wrong value is fatal, not silently defaulted); otherwise it appends `.codex` to the platform home directory. The SQLite files have their own override: `resolve_sqlite_home_env` reads `codex_state::SQLITE_HOME_ENV`, which lets the databases live outside the home (and triggers a managed-requirements warning). Cross-process coordination artifacts (compression run marker, maintenance lock) are placed under `CODEX_HOME/.tmp`, and per-thread writer locks under `thread-writer-locks/`. Nothing is written relative to the working directory except the project's own `.codex/` config and instruction files, which are read, not persisted state.

findings.title: Session rollouts: append-only JSONL, one writer task per thread, compressed to zstd after 7 days, and the canonical source that every SQLite view is rebuilt from
findings.description: The rollout file is opened with `append(true)` and `create(true)` and the writer first makes sure the file is **newline-terminated** so a previous crash cannot glue two records together. Each thread has exactly one writer task; the live writer treats SQLite as a *rebuildable view* and forces the JSONL flush barrier to win before any projection into the database, so the database can lag the file but never lead it. A background worker compresses rollouts older than `MIN_ROLLOUT_AGE` (7 days) into `.jsonl.zst`; reading transparently handles both forms and appending to a compressed rollout materialises the plain file first. The first line is a `SessionMeta` record carrying `cli_version`, which is the only version marker in the format (see `schema-and-format/format-versioning`).

evidence.snippet: // SQLite is a rebuildable view. The flush barrier must win before projection starts so it

findings.title: Six independent SQLite databases opened in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL, incremental auto-vacuum, a 5-second busy timeout and a 5-connection pool each
findings.description: Instead of one database, `codex-state` keeps **six files** (`state_5`, `logs_2`, `goals_1`, `memories_1`, `queue_1`, `thread_history_1`) so that corruption or a breaking schema change in one does not take the others down. Every read-write pool is created with `journal_mode(Wal)`, `synchronous(Normal)`, `auto_vacuum(Incremental)`, `busy_timeout(5s)` and `max_connections(5)`; a separate single-connection read-only pool (`create_if_missing(false)`) serves `sqlite_integrity_check`. The state database is explicitly an **index over the rollouts** with a `backfill_state` row tracking how far the rebuild has progressed; `thread_history_1` is documented as the rebuildable paginated history. Failure to open the state database is a hard error at init, while the other five are opened best-effort with a warning. The bundled SQLite is pinned to a version with the WAL-reset corruption fix (tech-stack finding).

evidence.snippet: /// Open and migrate the rebuildable paginated thread-history database.

findings.title: Database access is hand-written SQL through SQLx with bound parameters and explicit transactions; no ORM
findings.description: All ~600 SQL sites are literal statements passed to `sqlx::query` / `query_scalar` with `.bind(...)` parameters (no string-built SQL, no ORM, no query builder except `QueryBuilder` for the log-pruning window query). Multi-statement updates in `projects.rs` and `memories.rs` open an explicit transaction with `self.pool.begin().await` and commit at the end; the memories store alone has 24 transaction sites. The `codex-rollout` crate talks to the state database only through `codex-state`'s `StateRuntime` API, and `thread-store` layers a `LocalThreadStore` over both the rollout files and the databases, so callers never hold a raw connection. Reads that must not create a database go through the read-only pool.

findings.title: Four lock layers guard concurrent writers: per-thread writer locks, a coordination lock over the lock directory, a rollout-maintenance lock, and an advisory lock with retry on history.jsonl
findings.description: Codex expects several processes (TUI, app-server daemon, `codex exec`) to share one home, and protects each shared artifact with OS file locks rather than a database. A thread's rollout may have one live appender: `WriterLockCoordinator::acquire` opens `thread-writer-locks/<thread_id>.lock` and `try_lock`s it, returning a `Conflict` error ("already has an active writer") instead of blocking; stale locks left by dead processes are removed under a `.coordination.lock` taken first. Jobs that **replace** rollout files (compression, legacy migration) take a separate nonblocking `rollout-maintenance.lock` under `.tmp` so they never rename over each other. `history.jsonl` is appended under `try_lock` with up to 10 retries at 100 ms, then fails with `WouldBlock` rather than blocking the TUI. SQLite concurrency is left to WAL plus the 5 s busy timeout. In-process, `codex_core::session` uses ~100 `.lock()` calls on mutexes, which the counting script mis-reports as file locks.

findings.title: Schema is owned by embedded SQLx migrations (50 for the state db, one migrator per database); newer-than-binary versions are tolerated, known versions are checksum-checked
findings.description: Each of the six databases has its own migration directory compiled in with `sqlx::migrate!` and applied at open. `runtime_migrator` wraps every migrator with `ignore_missing: true`, documented as deliberately relaxing the "database is ahead of me" case so an older binary can still open a database migrated by a newer one running in parallel, while migrations the binary does know are still validated by checksum. A one-off `repair_legacy_recency_migration_version` rewrites the `_sqlx_migrations` row for version 39 when its checksum matches under a different number, which is what a renumbered migration in the field required. Breaking changes are handled by **bumping the filename** (`state_5.sqlite` is the fifth incarnation) rather than by an in-place migration, and rollouts are backfilled into the new file. Migrations are forward-only; there are no down scripts, but since every database is rebuildable from JSONL that is a reasonable trade.

evidence.snippet: /// checksum, so this only relaxes the "database is ahead of me" case.

findings.title: On-disk formats are versioned inconsistently: SQLite by filename suffix, caches and secrets by an explicit version field, rollouts and auth.json by nothing
findings.description: Versioning exists wherever a format was designed recently and is absent in the two oldest, most valuable files. **Versioned**: SQLite files carry the version in the name; the remote plugin catalog cache, connector directory cache (`schema_version: 1`), apps tools cache (`CODEX_APPS_TOOLS_CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION = 4`) and cloud-config bundle cache (`version: 1`) all check the field and discard the file on mismatch; the encrypted secrets file has a `version: u8` and **refuses** files newer than `SECRETS_VERSION`; plugin install metadata has `schema_version`. **Unversioned**: rollout JSONL lines have no format version, only the `cli_version` string in the first `SessionMeta` line, so readers must infer the dialect (the legacy rollout canonicaliser exists because of this); `auth.json` and `config.toml` have no version and rely on tolerant parsing. The consequence is contained because rollout readers skip lines they cannot parse (reliability's finding) and because the legacy migration pipeline canonicalises old rollouts, but a future incompatible rollout record has no way to declare itself.

evidence.note: only version marker in a rollout

findings.recommendation: Add an explicit `format_version` (or `schema_version`) to `SessionMetaLine` and to `auth.json`, written by new binaries and ignored by old ones, so a future incompatible change can be detected on read rather than inferred from `cli_version` heuristics.

findings.title: Readers are tolerant by default: config.toml ignores unknown keys, rollouts skip unparseable lines, caches self-delete on version mismatch, secrets fail closed on a newer version
findings.description: Forward compatibility is handled per data class. `ConfigToml` is a plain serde struct with `Default`; `deny_unknown_fields` is applied only through `#[schemars(...)]` for the generated JSON schema, so the **TOML parser accepts unknown keys** written by a newer Codex and editors get a strict schema. Rollouts written by a newer version are read line by line and unknown or malformed lines are skipped with a counter (reliability's `rollout-resume-skips-malformed-lines`). Cache files with a different `schema_version` are simply deleted and refetched. The secrets file is the strict exception: a `version` greater than the binary's `SECRETS_VERSION` is an error, which is right for encrypted credentials. The database side is covered by `ignore_missing` in the migrator. Backward compatibility of old data is handled by the legacy rollout migration (`rollout_migration.rs`), which canonicalises pre-ordinal rollouts and notes that malformed legacy records cannot be repaired because they have no ordinals.

findings.title: Durability follows reliability-scan's verdicts (atomic temp+rename for config-style files, buffered-but-unfsynced rollout appends, WAL/NORMAL SQLite); the storage-specific additions are fsync'd staging in migration and compression
findings.description: Reliability already judged the write paths: config, caches and plugin metadata go through `write_atomically` (`NamedTempFile::new_in(parent)` + `persist`), plugin trees are staged and renamed with a backup-and-rollback sequence, the rollout writer retries but never calls `sync_all`, and SQLite runs `synchronous=NORMAL`. What that finding does not cover is the two **rollout-replacing** jobs, which are the only places that fsync: compression writes to a temp file in the same directory, verifies the zstd stream, checks the source is unchanged, `sync_all`s and publishes with `persist_noclobber`; the legacy migration writes a durable `.pending` journal (`sync_all` on the file and `sync_parent_directory`) before replacing a rollout so a crash between the JSONL publish and the SQLite metadata step can be finished by the next run. `write_atomically` itself does not fsync the temp file before rename, so on a power loss a config file can come back empty even though it is never half-written.

findings.title: auth.json is rewritten in place with truncate+write, so a crash mid-save leaves an empty or partial credentials file
findings.description: `FileAuthStorage::save` opens `auth.json` with `truncate(true).write(true).create(true)` and writes the serialized JSON directly, unlike every other config-style file, which goes through `write_atomically`. A crash, disk-full or kill between truncate and `write_all` leaves a zero-length or truncated file; the next `load` then fails to parse and the user is effectively logged out. The consequence is bounded: the file is small, the write is short, the data is regenerable by logging in again (or is in the keyring when `Keyring`/`Auto` store mode is selected), and the 0600 mode is preserved by `OpenOptions::mode`. That mitigation is why this is `low`, not `medium`. Security-design already covers the sensitivity of this file; this finding is only about write safety.
findings.recommendation: Route `FileAuthStorage::save` through `write_atomically` (or a `NamedTempFile` in `CODEX_HOME` with the 0600 mode set before `persist`) so the credentials file is never observed half-written; refresh-token rotation makes this save path run often, not just at login.

findings.title: Corruption is detected and recovered per artifact: corrupt SQLite files are moved to db-backups and rebuilt from rollouts, tampered caches fail closed via HMAC, compressed rollouts are verified before publish
findings.description: The recovery story is the strongest part of the storage design. **SQLite**: `is_sqlite_corruption_error` matches SQLite codes 11/26 (`SQLITE_CORRUPT`, `SQLITE_NOTADB`); `backup_runtime_db_for_fresh_start` moves only the affected database and its WAL/SHM sidecars into `db-backups/<unique>/`, the TUI wraps this in `LocalStateDbStartupError` so the user is told which file was quarantined, and the fresh database is refilled by the backfill from rollouts (`backfill_state` watermark). `sqlite_integrity_check` exposes `PRAGMA integrity_check` over the read-only pool for `codex doctor`. **Rollouts**: a corrupt line is skipped on read; the legacy migration keeps either the original rollout or a recoverable paginated one and never both half-done. **Compression**: `verify_zstd` re-reads the temp file before `persist_noclobber`, and a source file that changed meanwhile aborts the publish. **Caches**: the cloud-config bundle cache is HMAC-signed and rejects invalid signatures, unsupported versions, identity mismatches and expiry; the other caches delete themselves on schema mismatch. **Secrets**: the age ciphertext is hashed with the passphrase into an in-memory cache key, so an edited file simply fails to decrypt. The one class with no detection is `auth.json` (parse error equals logout), handled in `auth-json-overwrite`.

evidence.snippet: //! moves only that database file and its sidecars into a backup folder so the
//! short TTL, and is HMAC-signed so malformed or edited files fail closed.

findings.title: Session rollouts are never expired: they accumulate under sessions/ for the life of the install, only shrinking via zstd compression after 7 days or explicit user delete/archive
findings.description: There is no retention policy for the conversation record. `sessions/` grows by one file per thread forever; the only automatic process is the compression worker, which rewrites cold files as `.jsonl.zst` but deletes nothing. Removal happens only when the user runs `codex delete` (`delete_thread.rs` unlinks the canonical rollout) or archives (moves to `archived_sessions/`, which is likewise unbounded). Because rollouts contain prompts, tool output and the contents of files the agent read, this is also the largest **sensitive** footprint on the machine, and the performance scanner already noted that the filesystem listing fallback walks the whole tree. This is `low` rather than `high` because the data is user data the user expects to keep, it is compressed, and disk exhaustion in normal use is unlikely; it is not `info` because nothing bounds it and there is no configuration knob.

evidence.snippet: /// Starts a best-effort background job that compresses cold local rollout files.

findings.recommendation: Add an opt-in retention setting (e.g. `history.retention_days` or a size budget) applied by the existing compression worker, and surface the current `sessions/` size in `codex doctor`, so users with privacy or disk constraints are not left to prune the directory by hand.

findings.title: Ephemera are cleaned on best-effort triggers: stale shell snapshots and writer locks at session start, log rows after 10 days and a per-thread byte budget, the legacy TUI log at startup; db-backups, plugin backups on failed rollback, and an uncapped history.jsonl are not
findings.description: **Bounded**: `cleanup_stale_snapshots` runs in a spawned task on every session start and removes `shell_snapshots/` files whose owning thread is gone; `remove_stale_thread_locks` unlinks lock files that `try_lock` succeeds on; the logs database prunes rows older than `LOG_RETENTION_DAYS = 10` and enforces a strict per-thread byte cap after every insert; the compression run marker and staging temp files are considered stale after 6 hours and reclaimed; the legacy shared TUI log file is deleted at startup with a `TODO delete after 22/11/2026` marker. **Unbounded by default**: `history.max_bytes` is `Option<usize>` with no default, so the global `history.jsonl` grows without limit unless the user configures a cap, though it is then trimmed to an 80% soft cap under the write lock; `db-backups/` directories created by corruption recovery are never pruned; a plugin activation whose rollback also fails deliberately `keep()`s its backup directory for manual recovery. None of these is user data at risk, so the missing bounds are `info`.

findings.title: Import exists (external-agent migration from other coding agents); no export, backup or restore of CODEX_HOME itself
findings.description: The `external-agent-migration` crate and its app-server processor detect other agents' homes (config, hooks, MCP servers, memories, sessions) and import them into Codex, writing memories and config through the normal atomic paths and reporting what was migrated. In the other direction there is nothing: no `codex export`, no bundle of a thread for sharing beyond the `rollout-trace` debug bundle, and no backup/restore command. Because every database is rebuildable from `sessions/`, a user backup is simply a copy of `CODEX_HOME` minus the SQLite files, but that is undocumented and `auth.json` would be copied along with it. Uninstall leaves the whole directory behind.

findings.title: Posture: a home-directory store whose canonical record is append-only JSONL with SQLite as a rebuildable index; strong corruption recovery, tolerant readers, weak spots are an unversioned rollout format, an in-place auth.json write and no retention of sessions
findings.description: Per data class. **Session rollouts**: durable enough (append-only, newline-repair on open, single locked writer, no fsync per reliability), forward-compatible by tolerant reading only, retention none. **Runtime databases**: durable (WAL, NORMAL), compatible (checksummed migrations, `ignore_missing`, filename versioning), corruption quarantined and rebuilt from rollouts. **Config**: atomic, tolerant of unknown keys, user-managed. **Credentials**: 0600 but written in place; regenerable by re-login. **Managed secrets**: atomic, encrypted, versioned, fail closed. **Caches**: atomic, versioned, TTL-bounded, self-invalidating. **History**: locked appends, cap opt-in. **Ephemera**: cleaned on session start. The riskiest data class is the **session rollouts**, not because of write safety but because they are the only source of truth, carry the most sensitive content, have no format version and no retention. The strongest mechanisms are the SQLite backup-and-rebuild path and the fsync'd journal in the rollout migration. The three highest-leverage changes are `schema-and-format/format-versioning`, `integrity/auth-json-overwrite` and `lifecycle/retention-session-rollouts`.

findings.title: The protocol crate - 68 dependents - has the lowest ratio in the workspace: 1.5k LOC of sibling tests plus 6k inline for 18k LOC of vocabulary
findings.description: `codex-protocol` is the shared vocabulary that 68 of 133 crates depend on, and `risk-synthesis-scan` shows its `EnvironmentConfig` co-changing 100% with core validation. Its own tests are **eight small sibling files** (`error_tests`, `exec_output_tests`, `permission_profile_intersection_tests`, `request_user_input_tests`, `response_item_id_tests`, `shell_environment_tests`, `capabilities_tests`, `local_media_tests`) and inline modules concentrated in `models.rs` (68 tests), `protocol.rs` (59) and `permissions.rs` (42) - 293 test functions for 18,377 LOC, ratio **0.08 path-based, 0.33 inline**. They are serde round-trips and permission-intersection cases; the crate is otherwise tested only transitively, through every integration test that serialises an event. That is real coverage of the happy path but no direct guard on compatibility: a renamed variant fails downstream snapshot tests rather than a protocol test. The component is stable relative to its size, which keeps this at `low`.

findings.title: Sandboxing & policy (47k LOC, the security boundary) has a 0.26 ratio and its OS-level tests are platform-gated and self-skipping
findings.description: The **sandboxing & policy** component - Landlock/seccomp, Seatbelt, bubblewrap, the Windows sandbox, execpolicy and the network proxy - carries 12,095 LOC of path-based tests and 11,817 LOC inline for 47,258 main LOC (ratio **0.26 + 0.25**), 899 test functions. The tests that actually exercise an OS sandbox are few and conditional: `linux-sandbox/tests/suite/landlock.rs` is `#![cfg(target_os = "linux")]` with a separate `aarch64` branch, the Windows unified-exec tests are `#[ignore]`d for a ConPTY failure in CI, and the core-suite sandbox tests (`exec.rs`, `unified_exec.rs`, `windows_sandbox.rs`, `apply_patch_cli.rs`) call `skip_if_sandbox!`, which returns early when `CODEX_SANDBOX=seatbelt` is set - which is precisely when Codex runs its own tests. The policy layer (`execpolicy`, `policy_transforms_tests`, `violation_tests`, `seatbelt_tests`) is unit-tested in-process against the generated profile text, not against the kernel. CI's five-platform post-merge matrix runs these unsandboxed, which is the mitigation that keeps this `low` rather than `medium`; the gap is that a change to the sandbox is verified only after merge and never from inside a sandboxed agent.

findings.title: Whole-object pretty_assertions equality is the house style; the TUI is snapshot-heavy; the script's 63k assertions and 1,226 weak-assertion leads are both inflated
findings.description: AGENTS.md requires `pretty_assertions::assert_eq` on **entire objects** rather than field by field, and the suites follow it: `config_tests.rs` has 914 assertion sites for 314 tests, `session/tests.rs` 868 for 191. Integration tests assert on captured model requests (`ResponseMock::single_request()`), emitted events and filesystem state, not on "did not panic" - the four `*_does_not_panic` tests in `exec_policy.rs` are the exception. The **TUI is snapshot-first**: 683 `.snap` files, and in `history_cell/tests.rs` 63 `insta::assert_snapshot!` sit beside 139 `assert_eq!`; that is appropriate for rendering but means a UI regression is only as visible as the reviewer's diff of the accepted snapshot. Two script numbers should not be trusted as written: its **63,307 assertions** include every Rust `.expect("...")` (2,809 in `core/tests` and `app-server/tests` alone, which are unwraps, not assertions), and its **1,226 weak-assertion candidates** are mostly false - 256 are Python tests whose bare `assert x == y` statements the regex does not see, and the Rust ones are tests that assert through helpers (`wait_for_*`, `expect_*`) or through wiremock `.expect(n)` call-count expectations.

findings.title: Mocking stops at the model boundary: wiremock fakes /v1/responses and websocket streams, everything inside the process runs for real; the TS SDK's exec tests mock spawn
findings.description: The 2,411 mock sites the script counts are almost all one thing: **`wiremock` `MockServer`** instances (1,105 `wiremock` and 672 `MockServer` hits) standing in for the OpenAI Responses API, mounted through `core_test_support::responses` (`mount_sse_once`, `ResponseMock`, `WebSocketTestServer`, `ModelsMock`). There is no `mockall` and no trait-mocking of internal components; the session loop, tool router, sandbox, rollout writer and SQLite state run for real in a temp `CODEX_HOME`, so integration tests fail on real integration bugs. The app-server suite adds a `WebsocketDelayInterposer` to inject latency into the real transport rather than faking it. The TypeScript SDK is the one place that mocks the thing under test's neighbour: `exec.test.ts` replaces `child_process.spawn` with `jest.fn()` to assert on argv, while `run.test.ts` and `runStreamed.test.ts` spawn the real binary against `responsesProxy.ts`. Python mirrors that with a `ThreadingHTTPServer` fake of the Responses API.

findings.title: nextest retries every test once by default; four tests are ignored as flaky with only TODO names; leak-detection races are documented rather than fixed
findings.description: `.config/nextest.toml` sets **`retries = 1`** in the default profile with the comment that one transient failure should not fail full-CI - a blanket retry that masks intermittent failures in every crate, with no per-test justification and no tracking. Tests known to be flaky are parked with owner TODOs instead of issues: `pending_input.rs` `injected_user_input_triggers_follow_up_request_with_deltas` (`TODO(aibrahim): flaky`), `review.rs` `review_start_exec_approval_item_id_matches_command_execution_item` (`TODO(owenlin0): flaky`), and two Windows-only `flaky on windows` ignores in `review.rs` and `code_mode.rs`. `test_app_server.rs` and `mcp_process.rs` document that child cleanup timing is nondeterministic and can trip nextest's `LEAK` detection, and `tool_parallelism.rs` calls itself a timing-based test. The harness itself retries spawning the binary on `ExecutableFileBusy`. The script's 60 `flaky_markers` are mostly the `request_max_retries = 0` config line and should not be read as 60 flaky tests. cicd-scan already notes the arm Linux Bazel target disabled as flaky.

evidence.snippet: // child still alive at teardown and report `LEAK`, which makes the test flaky.

findings.recommendation: Move the blanket `retries = 1` into a named override for the few timing-sensitive tests and let the rest fail on first failure; replace `TODO(name): flaky` ignores with issue links and a quarantine filter so they stay visible in CI output.

findings.title: 381 sleeps in tests - sleep-then-assert-absence waits, 25 ms polling loops, 54 env mutations serialised with serial_test - but no real network on the default path
findings.description: The script finds **381 `sleep` sites** in test code, 608 wall-clock reads and 13 randomness uses. Two patterns dominate. **Poll-with-sleep loops** (`sqlite_state.rs` loops 100 times over `try_exists` with 25 ms sleeps; `wait_for_*` helpers in the app-server suite) are bounded and rarely flaky but add up. **Fixed sleep then assert nothing happened** - `plugin_list.rs` sleeps 100 ms and then asserts a remote request count of zero - is the shape that cannot be made reliable, only slow. Process environment is mutated in **54 places** despite AGENTS.md asking tests to avoid it; the mitigations are `#[serial(...)]` groups in 25 files and explicit comments where it is unavoidable (`client.rs` 3488). Real network is not on the default path: the 1,130 `network_in_tests` hits are URL string literals in config fixtures (`https://chatgpt.com`, `https://example.test`, `https://github.com`), and the only tests that reach the internet (`live_cli.rs`, the tmux resize smoke) are `#[ignore]`. Randomness is seeded or irrelevant (UUIDs for temp names).

findings.title: 1,320 skip-macro call sites turn integration tests green when run inside a sandbox; 74 attribute skips include two compaction tests ignored because current behaviour is known-incorrect
findings.description: Beyond the 74 `#[ignore]`/`cfg_attr(ignore)` sites the script counts, the dominant skip mechanism is invisible to it: **`skip_if_no_network!` (1,193 call sites) and `skip_if_sandbox!` (127)** print a line and `return`, so the test is reported as **passed**, not skipped. They fire whenever `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED` or `CODEX_SANDBOX=seatbelt` is set - which AGENTS.md says is always the case when Codex runs tests on itself - so an agent verifying its own change sees a green core suite that ran almost nothing. Of the attribute skips: 22 in `code_mode.rs` and others are honest platform gates (`no exec_command on Windows`, `covered by Linux and macOS CI`); 7 are child-process halves of subprocess tests; but two are behavioural: `compact.rs` 3601 and `compact_remote.rs` 3021 are ignored with the note that **current main behaviour around manual `/compact` failures is known-incorrect**, awaiting a follow-up PR - a shipped path (`functionality-scan/features/context-compaction`) with its regression test switched off. Four bare `#[ignore]` without a reason (`otel`, `absolute-path`, `tui_startup_tests`, `shell_snapshot`) are subprocess children or Windows-only manual runs.

evidence.note: returns from the test body, reported as pass

evidence.snippet: #[ignore = "behavior change covered in follow-up compaction PR"]
evidence.note: known-incorrect behaviour on a shipped path

evidence.snippet: - You operate in a sandbox where `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1` will be set whenever you use the `shell` tool. Any existing code that uses `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED_ENV_VAR` was authored with this fact in mind. It is often used to early exit out of tests that the author knew you would not be able to run given your sandbox limitations.
evidence.note: the skip is by design for sandboxed agents

findings.recommendation: Make the skip macros count: print a machine-readable `SKIPPED:` marker and have `just test` summarise how many tests early-returned, or convert them to nextest filters so skipped tests show as skipped. Track the two ignored compaction tests against the follow-up PR and re-enable them with it.

findings.title: core_test_support and app_test_support: a builder that boots a real Codex against wiremock, a test binary that impersonates codex/apply_patch/sandbox via arg0, and a subprocess JSON-RPC client
findings.description: **`core_test_support`** (`core/tests/common`, 14 modules) is the centre of gravity: `TestCodexBuilder` boots a real `Codex` in a temp `CODEX_HOME` bound to a `wiremock::MockServer`, with `build_with_auto_env()` (local or remote exec environment), `build_with_streaming_server()` and `build_with_websocket_server()` variants; `responses.rs` provides the SSE/websocket event builders (`ev_function_call`, `ev_apply_patch_custom_tool_call`, `sse_completed`, ...) and `ResponseMock` for asserting on captured requests; `lib.rs` holds the eight `skip_if_*` macros. A `#[ctor]` in `suite/mod.rs` makes the test binary answer as `codex`, `apply_patch` and `codex-linux-sandbox` depending on `arg0`, so tools that spawn helpers work without a separate build. **`app_test_support`** (`app-server/tests/common`, 15 modules) spawns the real binary and wraps every JSON-RPC method in a `send_*_request` method on `TestAppServer` (about 150 of them), with a websocket delay interposer, auth fixtures, analytics and models-cache servers and rollout fixtures. The **TUI** has `chatwidget/tests/helpers.rs` (`test_config`, `render_bottom_popup`) and a VT100 backend for terminal-level tests. **SDKs**: `responsesProxy.ts` records requests and replays SSE, `setupCodexHome.ts` builds a temp home; Python `app_server_harness.py` is a `ThreadingHTTPServer` fake. A separate `app-server-test-client` crate is a manual exploration client, not an automated suite. Mock servers beyond the model: `apps_test_server.rs`, `analytics_server.rs`, `rmcp-client` `test_stdio_server`/`test_streamable_http_server` binaries for MCP, and `exec-server/tests/common/relay.rs`.

findings.title: 737 insta snapshots reviewed through cargo insta, request-shape snapshots in the core suite, and app-server schema fixtures regenerated by an ignored test
findings.description: Three golden-file systems. **insta snapshots**: 737 `.snap` files, 683 under `codex-rs/tui` (126 in `tui/src/snapshots`, the rest beside their modules), 52 in `core`, one each in `cli/doctor` and `ext/skills`; AGENTS.md prescribes the review loop (`cargo insta pending-snapshots`, `show`, `accept -p codex-tui`) and asks that snapshot updates be reviewed as part of the PR "so UI impact is easy to review". The core suite uses 38 snapshots to freeze the **shape of model requests** after compaction and resume. **Schema fixtures**: `app-server-protocol` commits the generated TypeScript and JSON Schema; a normal test asserts the committed tree equals a fresh export, and the writer is an `#[ignore]`d test invoked by `just write-app-server-schema`, so the fixtures cannot silently drift. There is no snapshot pruning or unreferenced-snapshot check beyond what `cargo insta` offers. `scripts/mcp_conformance` keeps regression baselines (`regression-baseline-v1.json`) for the MCP compliance runner.
